sent.prompt: I have to declare a data retention policy for a table that gets millions of new rows a day. Why am I steered towards partitioning it and dropping old partitions rather than deleting old rows in batches, and when is deleting rows still acceptable?

output.text:
GitLab's data retention policy doc (`doc/development/database/database_growth_control/data_retention_policy.md`) covers this.

## Why partitioning is preferred

At millions of rows a day, deletes would have to keep pace with inserts, so every row inserted is eventually a row deleted. That cost recurs for as long as the table exists. The doc gives three reasons:

1. **Write amplification.** A `DELETE` leaves dead heap tuples and dead entries in every index. Autovacuum then re-reads and re-dirties those same pages. This roughly doubles the table's write load. If deletion can't keep up with insertion, the retention window is never actually enforced.
2. **The table never shrinks.** Vacuum makes space reusable, but the on-disk size stays at its high-water mark unless you rewrite the table, for example with `pg_repack`. Deletes can cap growth. They can't bring a table back under the size limit once it has crossed it.
3. **WAL and replication load.** WAL volume scales with the pages touched, not the rows deleted. Scattered deletes produce full-page images after each checkpoint, and vacuum then produces a second wave of WAL. All of it ships to every replica and the WAL archive, which adds lag.

`drop_partition` costs less over time. Detaching a partition with `DETACH PARTITION CONCURRENTLY` is a metadata operation. It produces no dead tuples and almost no WAL, however many rows the partition held. The main cost is one-time: converting an existing large table to a partitioned one is an expensive migration. A table partitioned from the start avoids that cost. Detached partitions are kept for a grace window (7 days by default) before being dropped, so the data stays recoverable during that window.

## When deleting rows is acceptable

`delete_rows` is the last resort in the decision tree. It fits when all of these hold:

- The data isn't removed by an existing feature lifecycle. If it is, use `transient_data` instead.
- The data can be deleted without archival first. If not, exclude the table with `needs_archival`.
- Partitioning isn't possible for the table.
- The table is under the 50 GB soft limit. The 100 GB hard limit applies on GitLab.com.

In practice that means narrow, lightly indexed, low-traffic tables with no viable partition key. Record the justification in the `work_item`. Deletion runs as batches through [Background operations](../background_operations.md). Rows are lost immediately, with no grace window.

A table over 50 GB must use partitioning. If that's impossible, you can't fall back to `delete_rows`. Instead, set `exclude.reason: technical_complexity` and justify the specific technical constraint in the work item. Team capacity doesn't count as a technical constraint.

## For your table

With millions of rows a day, your table will exceed 50 GB quickly. Plan on `drop_partition`, with a time-based key such as `created_at`. The doc's GitLab.com default retention window is 1 month. Your `db/docs/data_retention/<table_name>.yml` would look like this:

```yaml
---
retention_window: 30
enforcement_strategy: drop_partition
enforcing: true
work_item: https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/:issue_id
pause_mechanism: application_setting
pause_mechanism::name: <application_setting_name>
```

You can set `enforcing: false` at table creation and flip it once enforcement is in place. The partitioning approaches are described in `partitioning/date_range.md` and `partitioning/sliding_list.md`. Self-Managed instances need a way to disable retention, which is why the pause mechanism exists.

sent.prompt: When one collection is loaded into several resource groups, GetShardLeaders tags every leader with a resource group instead of taking a resource group in the request. Why was it done that way, and why can't the proxy just work out each leader's group from which nodes are in which resource group? output.text:
The code matches the design doc, `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260824-per-resource-group-load-and-shard-leader-readiness.md`. I read the proto, `utils/util.go:216-238` and `services.go:153-154`. I did not read the full progress function, `utils/resource_group_load_percentage.go`.

## Why the response carries a tag instead of the request taking a resource group

The first implementation did add a `resource_group` field to the request. It was replaced because it pushes a resource-group dimension into the proxy's shard-leader cache. The doc compares the two designs (§2.3):

| | Request filter | Response tag (current) |
|---|---|---|
| Proxy cache | Keyed by collection and resource group, so N fetches and N entries per collection | Unchanged: one copy per collection, filtered in memory per leader |
| `InvalidateShardLeaderCache` | Semantics would need rethinking | Untouched |
| Information per call | One group | Every group, so a caller can compare them |
| Old coordinator | Ignores the field and answers unfiltered, which the caller can't tell apart from a filtered answer | Leaves the field empty, which the caller can detect |

The tag is `ShardLeadersList.resource_groups`. It is a parallel array, so `resource_groups[i]` describes `node_ids[i]`. The proxy already uses a per-leader boolean (`serviceable`) to build its candidate set, and a per-leader string works the same way.

## Why the proxy can't work out each leader's group from node membership

The tag is the group of the replica the leader leads, not the group of the node. A replica can borrow nodes from another resource group (`num_outgoing_node` / `num_incoming_node`). Matching node IDs against a group's node set therefore gives the wrong answer, and it is wrong exactly during rebalances, when the check matters most.

The coordinator also flattens every replica into one list per channel, so the replica identity is gone once the response leaves QueryCoord. Only the coordinator can fill the tag, and it does so at `util.go:216` with `replica.GetResourceGroup()`.

Three details follow from this design:
- **Empty means unknown.** An old coordinator leaves the field empty, so an empty tag is not "no resource group". The proxy handles it defensively, and a tag array whose length doesn't match `node_ids` is treated as all-unknown.
- **Absence doesn't mean "no replica".** Query-invisible replicas are dropped before the tag is applied, so a group that is still coming up doesn't appear. The readiness surface is what tells "still coming up" apart from "nobody loaded here".
- **The proxy filter doesn't drop channels.** `FilterByResourceGroup` runs per channel in `lb_policy.go`. If the proxy filtered the channel map itself, a query could succeed over a subset of the shards with no error.
- **Nothing sets the scope yet.** No code on the proxy's request path sets `ChannelWorkload.ResourceGroup`, so deployed routing is unchanged for now.

## How one resource group's load progress is reported

- **Wire path:** set `ShowCollectionsRequest.resource_group` (proto line 225). `services.go:153-154` then calls `utils.LoadPercentageByResourceGroup(ctx, meta, targetMgr, dist, collectionID, rgName)`.
- **Scope:** `inMemory_percentages` then covers only the replicas in that group. `query_service_available` follows the same scope.
- **Empty name:** it keeps the collection-wide figure, so `Proxy.GetLoadingProgress` and existing callers are unchanged.
- **The number:** it is the minimum target coverage across the group's replicas, measured against `NextTargetFirst`. Query-invisible replicas are included.

Possible results:
- **`-1`, no error:** the group holds no replica of the collection.
- **`0`:** a replica exists but nothing is loaded yet.
- **`-1` with `ErrServiceNotReady`:** the coordinator is still starting, so retry.
- **`-1` with `ErrCollectionNotLoaded`:** the load failed terminally.
- **`-1` with `ErrResourceGroupNotFound`:** the group name is wrong.

Two cautions from the doc:
- **Progress, not a gate:** the figure can drop back below 100 when new segments land, and it can read 100 for a group that is not servable yet. Use `ShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup` to decide whether to route to a group.
- **Startup window:** `-1` can show up briefly while a load is being registered, so confirm it across two polls before treating it as terminal.

sent.prompt: With Cells, why can't we rely on a unique index for things like usernames and top-level group paths, and what do we do instead? And why do models that write with delete_all or insert_all need extra work for it?

output.text:
**Why a unique index isn't enough**

Each cell has its own database, and a unique index only enforces uniqueness inside one database. Usernames and top-level group paths appear in URLs, the REST and GraphQL APIs, and login. They must be unique across the whole cluster so the router can map each one to at most one cell. Two cells could each accept `gitlab` as a top-level path, and each local index would be satisfied.

**What we do instead**

We claim the attribute in the Topology Service, which has a cluster-wide database. Once one cell has claimed a value, no other cell can claim it.

- **Model setup:** A model includes `Cells::Claimable` and declares `cells_claims_attribute :username, type: ...`, plus `cells_claims_metadata` for the subject and source.
- **Live claiming:** `after_save` and `before_destroy` callbacks claim and release values on create, update and delete. A rename releases the old claim and creates the new one.
- **Only some values are claimed:** `if:` and `cells_claims_scope` filter what gets claimed. `Route` claims only top-level paths, meaning those with no `/`.
- **Backfill and drift correction:** `Cells::Claims::VerificationService` runs on a cron schedule. On its first run it backfills claims for existing records. After that it creates missing claims, destroys orphaned ones, and fixes claims whose values changed.

The details are in `doc/development/cells/claims.md`.

**Why `delete_all` / `insert_all` need extra work**

The claim logic lives in ActiveRecord callbacks. `delete_all`, `insert_all`, `upsert_all` and raw SQL skip callbacks, so rows get written or removed without the claim being created or released. That leaves the local database and the Topology Service out of sync. The consequences are:

- A deleted record keeps its claim, so nobody else can reuse the value.
- An inserted record has no claim, so another cell could take the same value.

The verification service would eventually repair this, but only after the cron runs, and it skips records updated in the last hour. So the doc tells you to audit these code paths and handle claims explicitly with `Cells::BulkClaimsWorker`:

- **Unclaiming:** Build the metadata with `build_destroy_metadata_for_worker` before deleting. After the delete the record no longer exists, so the metadata can't be built.
- **Claiming:** Pass `create_record_ids`. The worker loads the records and builds the claims.
- **Scheduling:** Schedule the worker with `run_after_commit`, in batches of `BULK_CLAIMS_BATCH_SIZE`. This keeps the Topology Service calls outside the database transaction. Check `cells_claims_enabled_for_attribute?` first.

MR !230849, which added bulk claiming for routes and emails, is the reference example.

## Why deleting in batches is a last resort

A `DELETE` is a write. To hold a retention window on a table that takes millions of rows a day, deletion has to keep pace with insertion. Every row inserted is eventually a row deleted, so you pay that cost for as long as the table exists.

1. **Write amplification.** A delete leaves a dead heap tuple and dead entries in every index. Autovacuum then re-reads and re-dirties the same heap pages and all the indexes to clean them up. The doc says this roughly doubles the table's write load. If deletion can't keep up with insertion, the retention window is never actually enforced.
2. **The table never shrinks.** Vacuum makes the space reusable for new inserts, but the on-disk footprint stays the same. Deletes can cap growth, but they can't bring a table back under the size limit once it has crossed it. The limits are a 50 GB soft limit and a 100 GB hard limit on GitLab.com.
3. **WAL and replication load.** WAL volume scales with pages touched, not rows deleted. Deletes scattered across cold pages emit a full-page image per page after each checkpoint. Vacuum then produces a second wave of WAL.

Any table over 50 GB must use partitioning. A non-partitioning proposal for such a table has to record its justification in the `work_item`.

Record the justification in the `work_item`. It is also a hard cutoff, because there is no soft-delete grace window as there is with detached partitions.

Your table gets millions of rows a day, so it is unlikely to fit that description. The decision flow in the doc reaches `delete_rows` only when the data can be deleted without archival, the feature lifecycle doesn't already delete it, and partitioning is not possible.

Two other outcomes are not row deletion:
- `transient_data`: the data is tied to a user or feature lifecycle that already deletes it.
- An `exclude` reason: `indefinite_retention`, `needs_archival`, or `technical_complexity`. The last one applies to tables over 50 GB that can't be partitioned. It needs a justification of the specific constraints in the `work_item`.

For your table, the practical choice is `enforcement_strategy: drop_partition`. Pick a partition key, usually a timestamp column, so that partitions age out cleanly. The policy file goes in `db/docs/data_retention/<table_name>.yml`.

Docs and code agree. The `Server` wrappers are `GetLoadPercentageByResourceGroup` and `GetShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup`.

The source for all of this is `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260824-per-resource-group-load-and-shard-leader-readiness.md`. I cross-checked it against `internal/querycoordv2/utils/util.go`, `resource_group_load_percentage.go`, `services.go` and `pkg/proto/query_coord.proto`.

## Why tag each leader instead of adding a request parameter

A request-side `resource_group` filter was built first and then replaced. Both approaches answer "which leaders can this group serve from?". The tag is cheaper for the proxy and safer during upgrades.

- **Proxy cache:** The cache is keyed by collection ID. A request filter would need a resource-group dimension: N fetches and N entries per collection. It would also force a rethink of what `InvalidateShardLeaderCache([]int64)` means. With the tag, the cache stays as it is, and the group is a per-leader attribute filtered in memory. It's the same shape as the existing per-leader `serviceable` flag.
- **Information:** One call returns every group, so a caller can compare them.
- **Rolling upgrades:** An old coordinator silently ignores a request field and returns an unfiltered answer that looks like a filtered one. With a response field, an old coordinator leaves `resource_groups` empty, which the proxy can detect. Empty means "unknown", not "no group". The proxy indexes the array defensively. If its length doesn't match `node_ids`, the proxy marks that channel's tags all-unknown with a rate-limited warning.

## Why the proxy can't derive it from node membership

There are two reasons.

1. **Replica identity is dropped.** The builder (`util.go:191-218`) flattens every replica of the collection into one `ShardLeadersList` per channel. Only the node ID, address and serviceable flag survive. The coordinator is the only place that still knows which replica a leader belongs to.
2. **Node membership isn't replica membership.** A replica can borrow nodes from another resource group (`num_outgoing_node` / `num_incoming_node`). Intersecting a leader's node with a group's node set can therefore give the wrong group. It goes wrong during rebalances, which is when a caller most needs the right answer.

So the coordinator appends `replica.GetResourceGroup()` at `util.go:216`. It's the replica's group, not the node's. The append sits in the same `info != nil` branch as the other three arrays, so a leader dropped for an unregistered node can't shift later tags.

The tag only says which group a leader belongs to. It doesn't say whether the group can serve. Query-invisible replicas are filtered out before the list is built. A group that is still coming up therefore doesn't appear at all, and absence doesn't mean the group has no replica. To tell those apart, use `ShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup`. It reports `ShardsWithoutLeader` for a group still coming up and `NoReplicaInResourceGroup` for a group nobody loaded into.

Nothing on the proxy's request path sets the scope yet. The doc says deployed routing is unchanged.

## How one resource group's load progress is reported

- **Wire path:** Set `ShowCollectionsRequest.resource_group` (`query_coord.proto:225`). `ShowLoadCollections` (`services.go:153-163`) then calls `utils.LoadPercentageByResourceGroup` and returns the result in `inMemory_percentages`. `query_service_available` is also scoped to that group. Empty keeps the old collection-wide figure, so `GetLoadingProgress` and other existing callers are unchanged.
- **Figure:** It takes only the replicas in that group and computes each one's target coverage. It reports the minimum, so the group counts as done only when its slowest replica is.

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-1`, no error | The group has no replica of this collection. Confirm across two polls, because there is a one-commit window during load registration. |
| `0` | A replica exists but carries no targets yet. Wait. |
| `-1` with `ErrServiceNotReady` (retriable) | The coordinator isn't initialized yet. |
| `-1` with `ErrCollectionNotLoaded` (non-retriable) | The load failed. The cause is in the message, normalized so a retriable sentinel isn't mistaken for "retry". |
| `-1` with `ErrResourceGroupNotFound` (input error) | The group name doesn't exist. This is checked first. |

sent.prompt: I'm about to start on the distributed query view work. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can, what it changes about who does what between Proxy, QueryCoord, StreamingNode and QueryNode and why, what a DataView version and a QueryView version are, how a query view moves through its states, how much of it serves production traffic today, and where each part is written down.

The code matches the docs. No Proxy code references the new path, so Proxy production routing is not switched over.

## What changes, by role

**Why:** If the old delegator logic moved onto StreamingNode, it would become a bottleneck for every sealed-segment load and release, every delete apply, every query, every reduce, and all QueryNode result traffic. The change spreads that work across the other roles.

| Role | Old model | New model |
|---|---|---|
| **QueryCoord** | Manages load targets. | Builds the full distributed query view for each shard and replica, and drives its state machine. It directly owns all sealed-segment load and release. |
| **StreamingNode** | Hosts the delegator, which forwards queries and applies deletes. | Only accepts view updates from the coordinator. It serves growing data and produces the query plan (MVCC, BM25 and pruning, view version). It no longer loads or releases sealed segments, forwards queries, or applies deletes. |
| **QueryNode** | Reached through the delegator. | Loads sealed segments for a view and subscribes to the delete stream itself. It executes queries directly. |
| **Proxy** | Sends to the delegator. | Phase 1 gets the plan from StreamingNode. Phase 2 sends the plan to StreamingNode and QueryNodes, then does the whole distributed reduce. |

If a node fails or a view is invalidated mid-query, the query is cancelled and retried.

## The two versions

- **DataView version** is `(streaming_version, compact_version)`, set per collection.
  - It is an immutable snapshot of loadable sealed segments, with a manifest version for each.
  - `streaming_version` goes up only on flush, which is the growing-to-sealed handoff.
  - `compact_version` goes up on every other membership change: compaction, import, truncate, partition drop, and L0 manifest advances.
- **QueryView version** is `((streaming, compact), query_version)`, set per shard and replica.
  - A new DataVersion creates a new view and resets `query_version` to 1.
  - `query_version` goes up for placement-only changes such as balance or node-crash recovery.

## State machine

```
Preparing → Ready → Up → Down → Dropping → Dropped
Preparing → Unrecoverable → Dropping → Dropped   (error path)
```

- QueryCoord leads the machine and pushes state to nodes through the single `SyncQueryView` RPC. Nodes always reply with their latest local state.
- **Ready:** QueryCoord moves a view to Ready once all StreamingNode and QueryNode report Ready. QueryCoord then tells StreamingNode to go Up. QueryNodes serve as soon as they are Ready and don't track Up or Down.
- **Down:** When a newer view becomes Up, the old Up view is sent to Down. StreamingNode delays that until its serving lease expires and no queries are using the view.
- **Unrecoverable:** The view is dropped once a replacement view is generated.
- **Persistence:** QueryCoord persists Preparing, Up, Down and Unrecoverable in etcd. Ready and Dropping are not persisted and are re-derived on recovery.
- **StreamingNode-only state:** After a crash, StreamingNode uses an extra `UpRecovering` state while it replays the WAL. QueryCoord sees it as Up.

## How much serves production traffic

Almost none. The code and docs agree on this.

- **Implemented, and tested at the component level:**
  - The StreamingNode query-plan and view-query path.
  - The QueryNode resource and view-query path.
  - An injectable query client in `internal/views/queryclient`.
  - The DataView manager.
- **Not wired:**
  - Proxy production routing is not switched. Nothing under `internal/proxy` references this path.
  - The QueryCoord runtime that generates QueryViews is not activated.
  - Legacy load APIs don't publish LoadInfo.
  - Remote TransformLog and delete-stream integration is partial.
  - Replica-level WAL-secondary routing isn't done.
  - Schema publication is not implemented.
  - DDL visibility for truncate and partition drop is a TODO.

## Where it's written down

All of it is under `docs/design-docs/design_docs/qviews/`, except the proto and the WAL view doc.

- **Overview (start here):** `README.md`. It covers the motivation, the two-phase query, the versions, the lifecycle and the production boundary.
- **DataView:** `data_view.md`, plus `data_view_schema.md`.
- **State machine:** `query_view_state_machine.md`, plus `query_view_lease.md`, `syncer.md` and `balancer_scanning.md`.
- **Query side:** `query/query_plan.md`, `query/query_client.md`, `query/query_execution.md` and `query/segment_pruning.md`.
- **QueryNode side:** `querynode_extraction.md` and `qnview/querynode_queryview_resource_preparation.md`.
- **StreamingNode side:** `../wal/streamingnode_vchannel_wal_view.md` and `snview/idf_oracle_runtime.md`.
- **Wire definitions:** `pkg/proto/view.proto`. It holds `DataVersion`, `QueryViewVersion`, `QueryViewState` and `SyncRequest`.

sent.prompt: With Cells, why can't we rely on a unique index for things like usernames and top-level group paths, and what do we do instead? And why do models that write with delete_all or insert_all need extra work for it?

output.text:
## Why a unique index isn't enough

Each cell has its own database, and a unique constraint only works inside one database. Two cells could each accept `username = "alice"` or the top-level path `gitlab`, and neither database would see the conflict. Usernames and top-level paths are used for routing and login, so each must belong to at most one cell across the whole cluster. (`doc/development/cells/claims.md`)

## What we do instead: claims

A cluster-wide service, the Topology Service, keeps a database of claims. Before an attribute is used, the cell claims it there, and once it's claimed no other cell can claim the same value.

In Rails, a model includes `Cells::Claimable` and declares what to claim:

```ruby
cells_claims_attribute :username, type: CLAIMS_CLAIM_TYPE::CLAIM_TYPE_USERNAME
cells_claims_metadata subject_type: CLAIMS_SUBJECT_TYPE::USER, subject_key: :id
```

- **Callbacks:** `after_save` and `before_destroy` callbacks claim and release values on create, update and delete. A rename releases the old claim and creates the new one.
- **Filtering:** `if:` limits which values are claimed. `Route` only claims top-level paths, so `gitlab` is claimed but `gitlab/project` is not.
- **New types:** each claim type must also be defined in the Topology Service protobufs.
- **Verification:** a cron-driven `Cells::Claims::VerificationService` backfills claims for existing rows. It then reconciles local records against the Topology Service, creating missing claims and removing orphaned or changed ones.

## Why `delete_all` and `insert_all` need extra work

The claiming is done by ActiveRecord callbacks. `delete_all`, `insert_all`, `upsert_all` and raw SQL skip callbacks, so no claim is created or released. The result is drift. Deleted rows keep holding their claims, which blocks other cells from using those values. Inserted rows are never claimed at all.

The fix is to handle claims explicitly with `Cells::BulkClaimsWorker`:

- **Deletes:** build the metadata with `build_destroy_metadata_for_worker` before deleting, because the record must still exist at that point. Pass it as `destroy_metadata`.
- **Inserts:** pass the new record IDs as `create_record_ids`. The worker loads the records and builds the claims.
- **Scheduling:** call the worker inside `run_after_commit`, so the Topology Service calls stay outside the database transaction. Batch the IDs with `BULK_CLAIMS_BATCH_SIZE`.
- **Feature flag check:** check `cells_claims_enabled_for_attribute?` before scheduling.

The docs list auditing for these code paths as a step when adding a new claimable model. They point to MR !230849, which added bulk claiming for routes and emails, as the reference implementation. The verification service acts as a safety net for anything missed, but it skips records updated within the last hour and runs on a schedule, so it doesn't replace handling bulk paths correctly.

sent.prompt: Why is the proxy's MetaCache keyed by collection ID, with collection names and aliases kept only as hints? And how are cache fills kept from racing the invalidations that DDL broadcasts send, so that a describe started before a DDL can't put stale metadata back?

output.text:
The cache is keyed by ID because an ID is the only stable identity a collection has. Fills are ordered against invalidations by a single RW lock, `fillMu`. I read `internal/proxy/metacache/meta_cache.go` and the broadcaster and collection/alias message docs. I did not read the rootcoord side, so the "commit before broadcast" ordering below is taken from the code comments.

## Why the cache is keyed by collection ID

- **Names change meaning.** The docs say `RenameCollection` keeps the collection ID and changes the name, and can move the collection to another database. A drop and recreate under the same name gives a new ID. A name-keyed entry could silently point at a different collection than the one it was filled for. An ID-keyed entry cannot.
- **IDs are unique and never reused.** The comment at `meta_cache.go:674` says so explicitly. It is also why the partition cache is keyed by ID: a drop and recreate can't alias into old partition entries, and invalidating partitions never needs name or alias expansion.
- **Aliases are an extra layer of indirection.** An alias resolves to a real name, which resolves to an ID. If aliases were first-class keys, every alias DDL would have to find and patch every copy of the entry.

So `collections` (ID → `CollectionInfo`) is the only source of truth, and an entry is live exactly when its ID is present (`meta_cache.go:365`). `nameIdx` (db → name → id) and `aliasInfo` (db → alias → real name) are only hints that point into it.

Every read validates the hint against the primary (`getCollection`, `meta_cache.go:479`). The ID must still exist, and the entry's name and database must still match what was asked for. After a rename, the old-name hint still points at a live ID but fails the name check, so it is a miss. A stale hint therefore costs at most one extra describe and can never return stale data.

Hints are written only together with their owning entry. `update()` writes the name and the entry's own declared `Aliases` (`meta_cache.go:590-612`). A single routine, `evictCollectionEntryLocked` (`meta_cache.go:1393`), removes the entry together with its alias hints, name hint and partition list. That is why no background GC is needed, and why a dropped collection's alias can't come back after a same-name recreate.

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

The mechanism is `fillMu`, an RW lock that replaced an earlier per-collection version floor (`meta_cache.go:399-420`).

- **Fills take the read side.** `updateWithSingleflight` takes `fillMu.RLock` around the whole `sfGlobal.Do` call (`meta_cache.go:698`). That covers the describe RPC, the write-back, delivery of the result, and singleflight's removal of the finished flight. Fills don't block each other, and cache hits never touch `fillMu`.
- **Invalidations take the write side.** `RemoveCollection`, `InvalidateCollectionMeta`, `RemoveCollectionsByID` and `RemoveDatabase` all take `fillMu.Lock()` before `m.mu`. The write lock waits for every in-flight fill to finish, so any fill that read pre-DDL state has already written back and returned. The eviction then deletes that write-back.
- **Fills after the invalidation read post-DDL state.** The comments state that rootcoord commits its metadata before broadcasting. Any describe issued after the eviction therefore sees the new state. This is also why a timestamp comparison isn't needed.

Two details close gaps:

- **The read lock covers the whole `singleflight.Do`, not just `update()`.** Singleflight keeps a completed call in its map until its own cleanup runs. If `fillMu` were released inside `update()`, an invalidation could evict the write-back. A caller arriving afterwards could still join the old flight and receive its pre-DDL result directly, bypassing the maps. There is a test for exactly this window (`internal/proxy/meta_cache_test.go:4252`).
- **This covers cases the old version floor could not.** Examples are alias-resolution entries and responses with `RequestTime == 0` from older rootcoords.

The costs are accepted in the comments. An invalidation waits for the slowest in-flight fill, and fills started while an invalidation is pending briefly block behind it. Fill RPCs use the caller's context with no extra deadline, so callers must supply one.

The lock order is `fillMu` before `m.mu`. The code says it is deadlock-free against rootcoord because ack callbacks release the meta lock before the expiration fan-out. A fill's describe RPC is therefore never stuck behind the DDL whose invalidation is waiting on that fill. I did not verify that on the rootcoord side.

`RemoveDatabase` is the one case that deliberately holds the write lock only for the drain and the O(1) bucket detach. It releases it before the O(N) walk. A fresh entry written during the walk may be over-deleted, which costs one extra describe and never a stale read.

sent.prompt: Why is the proxy's MetaCache keyed by collection ID, with collection names and aliases kept only as hints? And how are cache fills kept from racing the invalidations that DDL broadcasts send, so that a describe started before a DDL can't put stale metadata back?

output.text:
The code matches the design doc (`docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260716-proxy-metacache-id-inverted-index.md`). The implementation is in `internal/proxy/metacache/meta_cache.go`.

## Why the cache is keyed by collection ID

Invalidations arrive by id, alias or database, while the old store was keyed by `(db, name)`. Every eviction therefore had to scan. The doc lists O(all cached collections) for each Load, Release, Drop, Rename or Alter broadcast, plus scans over partition entries and aliases. The scans ran under the global write lock, so each broadcast stalled every query on the proxy.

The id is cluster-unique and never reused, so liveness is simply presence in `collections map[UniqueID]*CollectionInfo` (`meta_cache.go:371`). Names and aliases are only hints:

- `nameIdx` maps db and real name to an id.
- `aliasInfo` maps db and alias to a target name.

Every read validates the hint against the primary store. The id must be live, and the entry's name and db must still match. A failed check is a cache miss, which costs one extra describe, and never a stale read.

That makes hint bookkeeping simple:

- Hints are written only together with their entry (`update()`).
- `evictCollectionEntryLocked` (`meta_cache.go:1393`) is the only place that deletes from the primary store. It removes the entry plus everything it owns: its alias hints, its name hint (only while that hint still points at this id), and its partition list.
- After a rename, the old name's hint points at a live entry whose name no longer matches, so it misses. After drop and recreate under the same name, the new id replaces the old, so the old hint can't validate.
- Invalidation by id is O(1), and there is no background GC.

The remaining scans are rare cases. DropDatabase walks that database's name bucket. An AlterAlias whose old target is unknown falls back to a scan.

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

The old design used per-collection timestamp floors. They had gaps: alias write-backs weren't versioned, a `RequestTime == 0` compat path bypassed them, and the floors needed a tombstone lifecycle. The doc says this is replaced by one global lock, `fillMu sync.RWMutex` (`meta_cache.go:420`).

- **Fills take the read side.** `updateWithSingleflight` (`meta_cache.go:698`) holds `fillMu.RLock` across the whole `sfGlobal.Do`. That covers the describe RPC, the write-back, and delivery of the result. Fills don't block each other.
- **Invalidations take the write side.** `RemoveCollectionsByID` (`meta_cache.go:1365`), `RemoveDatabase`, `RemoveDatabaseInfo` and the alias and partition paths all take `fillMu.Lock()` first. That drains every in-flight fill before they evict.

This gives two outcomes:

- A describe that started before the DDL read a pre-DDL snapshot. It finishes, writes back, and the eviction then deletes that write-back.
- A describe that starts after the eviction reads post-DDL state, because rootcoord commits the DDL before it broadcasts.

So a pre-DDL describe can't put stale metadata back, and no timestamps are compared.

The read lock covers the whole singleflight call, not just `update()` (comment at `meta_cache.go:693-697`). Singleflight keeps a completed callback in its map until its own cleanup runs. If the lock were released inside `update()`, an invalidation could evict the write-back while a post-invalidation caller joined the old flight and received the pre-DDL result directly, bypassing the maps.

Lock order is `fillMu` then `m.mu`. `m.mu` is never held across an RPC. Cache hits touch neither lock.

Rootcoord's ack callbacks release the meta lock before the expiration fan-out. A fill's describe therefore can't be blocked by the DDL whose invalidation is waiting on that fill.

## Costs the doc accepts

- An invalidation, and so the broadcast ack, waits for the slowest in-flight fill. Fills use the caller's context with no MetaCache-specific timeout.
- Because Go's `RWMutex` blocks new readers once a writer is queued, a fill with no deadline that hangs below the transport could stall `fillMu`, the ack and later fills.
- `fillMu` is global, so a fill in one database can delay an invalidation in another. Sharding it is listed as future work.
- Duplicate or late broadcasts over-invalidate and cost an extra describe, instead of being filtered by version.

I read the type definition, the fill path and the eviction routine in the code. I didn't read the alias DDL ack callbacks or the tests, so the alias-DDL and rootcoord details above come from the doc alone.

**No, it has drifted.** The reversal branch is the main difference. The code, its spec and the module's own comments agree with each other. The spec was updated to match the code, so it can't catch this.

The intended behaviour is written in these places:
- `doc/development/namespaces_state_propagation.md:86-101`, the "State precedence" section. It has a table of expected results and the rule "higher precedence wins".
- The module header at `state_precedence.rb:9-15`, which says a descendant already in a higher-precedence state is not overwritten.
- `doc/development/namespaces_state_propagation.md:233` says `deletion_scheduled` outranks `archived`, so it survives an ancestor being archived.
- The service links the handbook ADR 003 ("state propagation model"). I couldn't open it from here, so I haven't checked it.

**Differences from that intent** (reversal branch, `state_precedence.rb:61-70`):

1. **Unarchive (`archived → ancestor_inherited`).** The doc says it returns `[:archived]` ("Unarchive, but stop at `deletion_scheduled`"). The code returns `[:archived, :deletion_scheduled, :maintenance]`. Unarchiving a parent therefore resets descendants that are pending deletion or in maintenance back to `ancestor_inherited`.
2. **Restore (`deletion_scheduled → ancestor_inherited`).** The doc says `[:deletion_scheduled, :archived]`. The code adds `:maintenance`, so a descendant in maintenance is also reset.
3. **Exit maintenance.** The code returns `[:archived, :deletion_scheduled, :maintenance]` for any target. That includes `:maintenance` itself, so descendants that were independently in maintenance are cleared too. The doc doesn't cover maintenance at all. The table has no maintenance rows, and the code treats `maintenance → maintenance` as a reversal.
4. **Equal precedence.** The doc (line 101) says equal source and target precedence returns `[]`. The code returns the lower states, for example `archived → archived` gives `[:ancestor_inherited]`, and `deletion_scheduled → deletion_scheduled` gives `[:ancestor_inherited, :archived]`. The code comment at lines 36-37 even says "higher- or equal-precedence". The one equal case that returns `[]` is `ancestor_inherited → ancestor_inherited`.

The header comment (lines 12-15, 41-52) also describes the reversal as returning "the whole subtree" to default. That contradicts its own "higher precedence wins" sentence.

The cause is that `reversal?` (line 88-90) and the `select { positive? }` on line 70 return every non-default state. They don't cap at the precedence of the state being reversed. A reversal that respected precedence would return the states at or below the source, so unarchive would give `[:archived]`.

Which side is right is a product decision. If the doc table is the spec, the code and spec need changing. If the "whole subtree" behaviour was deliberate, the doc table and the example at line 233 need updating. I haven't changed anything.

The StreamingNode splits oversized payloads in the WAL adaptor's append path and reassembles them in its scanner. The splitting switch is `streaming.splitChunkSN`.

## Splitting on append

- **`internal/streamingnode/server/wal/adaptor/wal_adaptor.go`**
  - `walAdaptorImpl.appendWithOptionalChunking` (line ~298) is called from the append callback. If `streaming.splitChunkSN` is false, it appends the message as a single record. Otherwise it compares the payload size with the per-record budget and splits when the payload is larger.
  - It calls `message.SplitIntoChunks(msg, chunkPayloadSize)`, then appends each chunk in index order through `appendOneWithRetry`. The message ID of the first chunk is returned to the caller as the logical message ID.
  - `chunkPayloadSize` and `computeChunkPayloadSize` (lines ~349–370) work out the budget. The budget is the backend's max message size minus a reserve. They use `paramtable.WALMaxMessageSize(...)` and `PulsarCfg.GetMessageSizeLimitsFor(...)`. The value is cached for one second (`chunkPayloadSizeRefresh`). A budget of 0, which RocksMQ gets, disables splitting.
- **`pkg/streaming/util/message/chunk.go`**: `SplitIntoChunks` slices the raw payload bytes without re-marshaling. Each chunk keeps the original properties and adds the index and total markers `_ci` and `_ct` (the `messageChunkIndex` and `messageChunkTotal` constants).
- **`internal/streamingnode/server/service/handler/producer/produce_server.go`**: `ProduceServer.validateMessage` rejects client messages that already carry the chunk markers, using `message.IsChunkedPayload`.

- **`internal/streamingnode/server/wal/adaptor/scanner_switchable.go`**: `catchupScanner` holds a `message.ChunkAssembler` field. sent.prompt: With Cells, why can't we rely on a unique index for things like usernames and top-level group paths, and what do we do instead? And why do models that write with delete_all or insert_all need extra work for it?

output.text:
**Why a unique index isn't enough**

Each cell has its own database, and a unique index only enforces uniqueness inside one database. Some values have to be unique across the whole cluster, such as usernames and top-level group paths. They are used for routing (URLs, REST and GraphQL APIs) and for logging in. If two cells each created `gitlab` as a top-level path, each cell's index would accept it, and the router couldn't tell which cell owns the URL. (`doc/development/cells/claims.md:12-24`)

**What we do instead: claims in the Topology Service**

The Topology Service is a cluster-wide database. A cell asks it to claim an attribute, and once claimed, no other cell can claim the same value.

A model opts in like this:

- It includes `Cells::Claimable`.
- It declares `cells_claims_attribute :username, type: ...`.
- It declares `cells_claims_metadata`, which sets the subject and source of the record.

`after_save` and `before_destroy` callbacks then claim and release values on every create, update and delete. A rename releases the old claim and creates the new one.

Verification backs this up. `Cells::Claims::VerificationService` runs on a cron schedule. On its first run it backfills claims for existing rows, because callbacks only cover new writes. After that it fixes drift: missing claims, orphaned claims and changed values.

**Why `delete_all` and `insert_all` need extra work**

The claiming is done by ActiveRecord callbacks. `delete_all`, `insert_all`, `upsert_all` and raw SQL skip callbacks. Rows written that way would never be claimed, and deleted rows would leave their claims behind. The verification service would only catch that later, on its next run.

For these paths, the doc says to schedule `Cells::BulkClaimsWorker` yourself:

- Capture `destroy_metadata` with `build_destroy_metadata_for_worker` **before** deleting. The worker can't build it afterwards because the records are gone.
- For inserts, pass `create_record_ids`. The worker loads the records and builds the claims.
- Schedule the worker inside `run_after_commit`, so the Topology Service calls stay outside the DB transaction.
- Check `cells_claims_enabled_for_attribute?` first.
- Send the work in slices of `Cells::Claimable::BULK_CLAIMS_BATCH_SIZE`.

When you add claims to a model, audit it for these bypass paths. MR !230849, which added bulk claiming for routes and emails, is the reference example (`claims.md:300-352`).

**Recommendation: don't go back to 5s. Keep 20s.**

**Why "well under a second" isn't the deciding number.** That figure holds for a colocated or single-AZ etcd and small snapshots. The commit history (a4e8295) and the comment on the constant record a real deployment where it doesn't hold. etcd spanned three AZs at about 40 ms per round trip, and releasing the pins of a large snapshot took 6–9 s. The 5s timeout cancelled the release partway, and the pins stayed until the next restart. Those pins held segments that GC should have freed. So 5s was already shown to fail on a real deployment.

**What decides the value.** The timeout needs to exceed the worst-case time to finish the cleanup, not the typical time. That time is roughly (number of etcd round trips) × (etcd latency), plus the tail when etcd is degraded. The number of round trips grows with snapshot size, so the cost scales with the snapshot. 20s is about 2× the observed worst case, which is a reasonable margin.

**Why the "fail fast" argument is weak here.**
- These are background cleanup paths, not user-facing calls. They use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or `m.ctx`, so nobody is waiting on them.
- A timeout doesn't fail anything usefully. It abandons a half-done release and leaves leaked pins, which is worse than waiting.
- A genuinely stuck etcd is detected elsewhere, and a shorter cleanup timeout doesn't improve that detection.
- The failures are already logged. The `RatedWarn` calls at `snapshot_export_manager.go:788` and `:777` show the cleanup is retried on a later pass.

**Caveat I'd flag.** The constant is shared by several sites in `snapshot_export_manager.go`, not just pin release:
- `updateFailedJob` at line 722
- `cleanupTerminalJob` at lines 767, 784, 797 and 818
- the export-completion cleanup at line 635
- the `CreateJob` failure path at line 192

Under a stuck etcd, each of these now holds for up to 20s. That includes `updateFailedJob`, which can be called with a lock held (`tryLock`), and I haven't checked whether holding it that long blocks anything. If someone wants a short timeout for those paths, the right change is a separate, shorter constant for them. Lowering the shared one would reintroduce the pin leak.

**If you want something between the two:** make the pin-release timeout scale with the work or with a config value, rather than picking one fixed number. I haven't tested this change at all, and the commit message says so too. If you do shorten it, test it against a high-latency etcd with a large snapshot.

- The old cache was keyed by (db, name). Every Load, Release, Drop, Rename or Alter broadcast therefore had to scan the whole cache to find the name keys for an ID.
- The same problem hit the partition sweep, alias cleanup, partition-DDL name expansion and `RemoveDatabase`.
- All of these scans ran under the global write lock, which stalls every query on the proxy. At the 1M-collection target, each broadcast would cost a full-cache sweep.

**An ID is cluster-unique and a name is not.**
- Names can be renamed, aliased, or dropped and recreated.
- Keying by ID makes the entry the single source of truth.

**Names and aliases are hints.**
- `nameIdx` maps db and name to an ID, and `aliasInfo` maps an alias to a real name.
- A read resolves the hint to an ID, then validates it against the primary entry. The ID must be live, and the entry's name and db must still match.
- A failed validation is a cache miss, which costs one extra describe. It is never a stale read.
- Hints are written only together with their entry, from its name and its declared aliases. One eviction routine, `evictCollectionEntryLocked`, removes the entry and everything it owns: its name hint, alias hints and partition list.
- No hint can dangle and no background GC is needed, so invalidation by ID is O(1).

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

The old design used a per-collection timestamp floor (`collectionCacheVersion`). It had gaps: alias write-backs were unversioned, a `RequestTime == 0` compat path bypassed it, and `RemoveDatabase` never raised it. It was replaced with pessimistic ordering through one global `fillMu sync.RWMutex`:

- **Fills** take `fillMu.RLock` for their whole duration, covering the describe RPC and the write-back (`meta_cache.go:698`, `:1051`). Fills don't block each other, and cache hits never touch `fillMu`.
- **Invalidations** take `fillMu.Lock` (`:866`, `:888`, `:1271`, `:1307`, `:1365`, `:1452`). That waits for all in-flight fills to finish before evicting.

This gives the ordering you asked about:
- **A describe started before the DDL.** It holds the read lock, so it finishes and writes back its pre-DDL snapshot before the invalidation can evict. The eviction then removes that snapshot.
- **A describe started after the eviction.** It reads post-DDL state, because rootcoord commits the DDL before it broadcasts the invalidation.
- **Stale write-backs.** A stale snapshot can therefore never land after the eviction that was meant to clear it.

Other details from the note and the code comments:
- **Lock order** is `fillMu` then `m.mu`. `m.mu` is never held across an RPC.
- **Deadlock-freedom against rootcoord.** DDL ack callbacks release the meta lock before the expiration fan-out, so a fill's describe is never blocked by the DDL that is draining it. `RemovePartition` runs its ensure-describe before taking the write side.
- **Alias DDL.** Rootcoord forwards both the old and new target IDs (`old_collection_id`). The proxy evicts both by ID, so a concurrent describe that re-points the alias hint can't cause a miss.
- **Database drop.** The write lock covers only the drain and the O(1) drop of the hint buckets. The walk over the database's entries runs afterwards, through the same eviction routine.
- **Alter database** invalidates only `dbInfo`, also under `fillMu`.
- **An id-only describe whose response has no db** (an older rootcoord during a rolling upgrade) is served uncached, because no database DDL could find it to invalidate it.

## Accepted trade-offs

- An invalidation, and so the broadcast ack, waits for the slowest in-flight fill. MetaCache imposes no timeout of its own, so the caller's deadline governs.
- A deadline-less RPC that hangs below the transport can pin `fillMu`. Because Go's `RWMutex` blocks new readers once a writer is queued, that can also stall later fills.
- Duplicate or late broadcasts over-invalidate and cost one extra re-describe. They are not filtered by version.

Callbacks don't run for these, so the code queues the claims explicitly in a Sidekiq worker.

sent.prompt: What does Import V3 change about how bulk import works compared with Import V2, and why was it needed? Is it what runs by default now?

output.text:
**No, V3 isn't the default.** `dataCoord.import.enableImportV3` defaults to `false`, so new imports still run on V2 unless an operator turns it on. I checked this in three places: `configs/milvus.yaml:1049`, `pkg/util/paramtable/component_param.go:8004`, and the design doc, which says "Implemented behind the one-way … gate (default `false`)".

## How the gate picks a version

The selection happens in `internal/datacoord/services.go:2085-2091`. A request with no version set resolves to V2. It resolves to V3 only when all of these hold:
- the gate is on;
- the import is not an L0 import;
- the import is not a snapshot source.

The resolved version is written into the WAL message and the job, so a job always finishes on the version it started with. The gate is meant to be one-way. Turning it back off after use is unsupported, and rolling back to a binary that doesn't know V3 is forbidden while any V3 job or temp data exists. It should only be enabled once every DataNode and every DataCoord that could become active supports V3.

The code and the design doc agree. I also saw a `.sloppy/notes/` copy of the doc, which I ignored.

## What changes from V2 to V3

**V2:**
- Every source file is read twice. `PreImportTask` parses the whole file and keeps only statistics. Then `ImportTaskV2` reads it again, hashes rows per file-group, and writes straight into pre-allocated segments.
- Each file-group task splits the same `(vchannel, partition)` bucket, which produces many small segments.
- A `hashed_stats` table grows with vchannels × partitions.
- Segments are sorted afterwards by a separate `Sorting` compaction.

**V3:**
1. **Count-only preimport.** It gets exact row counts and sizes. Parquet and NumPy counts come from file metadata, and JSON/CSV are scanned. Backup imports only size their object lists. The counts let ordinary imports get deterministic ID ranges (`AssigningIDRange`).
2. **Reshard.** Each source is parsed once. Rows are normalized, routed to a `(vchannel, partition)` bucket, sorted, and written as immutable Parquet fragments plus a manifest. Memory is bounded per slot, and overflow spills to local disk.
3. **Planning.** Fragments are packed per bucket across all reshard tasks into per-segment plans. The pipeline decides segment shape rather than the file-group boundary.
4. **Import.** Each `ImportTaskV3` does a k-way merge of one plan's fragments (fan-in 128 by default) and writes exactly one sorted segment through the existing Storage V2/V3 writers.
5. The job then goes straight to `IndexBuilding`, with no `Sorting` stage.

## Why it was needed (per the design doc)

- **Single read.** V2's preimport leaves nothing reusable.
- **Bucket ownership before task boundaries.** Routing inside per-file tasks makes cross-file segment planning impossible.
- **etcd size limit.** `hashed_stats` can exceed etcd's default 1.5 MiB request size. With V3, tables with 1024 partitions import natively.
- **One sorted write.** The output is already sorted, so the post-import sort is skipped.
- **Schema changes mid-import.** V2 can hang in `IndexBuilding` if the collection is altered during import. V3 compares an import-relevant schema projection at Planning, at each result acceptance, and before `IndexBuilding`. On a mismatch it fails with `ErrImportSysFailed` (2101).

L0 import stays on V2, and there are no new user-facing options or public API.

I read the design doc and the version-selection code, not the DataNode or checker implementations, so I haven't verified that V3 behaves the way the doc describes. This is a read-only explanation, so I didn't run any tests.

sent.prompt: With Cells, why can't we rely on a unique index for things like usernames and top-level group paths, and what do we do instead? And why do models that write with delete_all or insert_all need extra work for it?

output.text:
**Why a unique index isn't enough**

With Cells, each cell has its own database. A unique index only enforces uniqueness inside one database. Some attributes have to be unique across the whole cluster, because they're used for routing or login. Examples are a username or a top-level group path (a URL like `gitlab` must belong to exactly one cell). Two cells could each insert the same value without conflict, and the router couldn't tell which cell owns it. (`doc/development/cells/claims.md:12-24`)

**What we do instead: claims in the Topology Service**

The cluster has a shared Topology Service with its own database. A cell *claims* an attribute there, and once it's claimed, no other cell can claim it.

- A model includes `Cells::Claimable`. It declares `cells_claims_attribute` (for example `:username`) and `cells_claims_metadata`, which names the subject (the record that owns the claim) and the source.
- Rails `after_save` and `before_destroy` callbacks create and release claims in the Topology Service. A rename releases the old value and claims the new one. This happens for every create, update and delete.
- For top-level paths, `Route` claims only paths with no `/` in them. It does this with `if: ->(record) { record.path.exclude?('/') }`, plus a matching `cells_claims_scope` for verification.
- `Cells::Claims::VerificationService` runs on a cron schedule. On its first run it backfills claims for existing records. After that it fixes drift, meaning missing claims, orphaned claims and changed values.

**Why `delete_all`, `insert_all` and `upsert_all` need extra work**

Claiming lives in ActiveRecord callbacks, and those methods skip callbacks. So do raw SQL writes. Rows inserted that way never get claimed. Rows deleted that way never have their claims released, which leaves orphaned claims that block the value from being reused. (`claims.md:300-308`)

For those code paths, you schedule `Cells::BulkClaimsWorker` yourself:

- **Deletes:** call `build_destroy_metadata_for_worker` and pass the result as `destroy_metadata`. You have to build it *before* deleting, because it needs the record to still exist.
- **Inserts:** pass the new IDs as `create_record_ids`, and the worker loads the records and builds the claims.
- **Where to schedule:** use `run_after_commit`, so the gRPC calls to the Topology Service stay outside the database transaction. Batch with `BULK_CLAIMS_BATCH_SIZE`, and check `cells_claims_enabled_for_attribute?` first.

The doc points to MR !230849 (routes and emails) as the reference implementation. The verification service is a backstop for missed cases, but it skips records updated in the last hour, so it doesn't replace handling these paths explicitly.

sent.prompt: snapshotPinCleanupTimeout in internal/datacoord/snapshot_manager.go is 20 seconds. Someone points out that releasing pins normally finishes in well under a second and wants 5 seconds again so a stuck etcd fails quickly. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**Recommendation: don't go back to 5s. Keep 20s.** The "well under a second" figure holds for a single-AZ etcd or a small snapshot. It doesn't hold everywhere this code runs.

**What decides the value**

The timeout has to cover the slowest legitimate release, with headroom. It should not be set from the typical release time. The release time depends on:
- **etcd round-trip latency.** Releasing pins involves multiple sequential etcd operations, so the cost is roughly the number of operations times the round trip.
- **Snapshot size.** A larger snapshot has more pins and segments, so there are more operations.

The comment at `snapshot_manager.go:88-94` and the commit message `bba7d4c` give a measured case. With etcd spread over three availability zones (about 40 ms apart), releasing a large snapshot takes 6 to 9 seconds. At 5s the release was cancelled partway. The pins then stayed until the next restart and kept segments that GC should have freed.

Those figures come from the commit message and the code comment. I haven't reproduced them, and the commit says "Not tested".

**Why the asymmetry favors the longer value**
- **Timeout too short:** this fails silently and leaks. Cancelled cleanup logs a warning, and the pins persist, so storage is held indefinitely.
- **Timeout too long:** the only cost is that a call waits longer when etcd is stuck. These are background cleanup paths, not user-facing requests.

The "fail quickly" benefit is small. Of the sites I read, `cleanupTerminalJob` retries on its next pass and is only logged with `RatedWarn`. The job-creation failure path in `snapshot_export_manager.go:192` is the exception. It runs inline while the caller waits, so a stuck etcd delays that error by up to 20s. Its cleanup context is built with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` on purpose, so it wouldn't be cut short anyway.

**Caveats**
- The constant is shared. It covers every cleanup call in `snapshot_export_manager.go`: unpin, job update, job drop, and staging-metadata removal. Lowering it affects all of them.
- The 20s figure is only about 2x the worst measured case of 9s. A larger snapshot or a slower WAN link could exceed it.

**If you want fast failure on a stuck etcd**
- **Don't shorten the budget.** Make the unpin resilient instead, for example with retry on partial progress, so a cancelled release resumes rather than leaks.
- **Or make it configurable.** Moving the value into `paramtable` lets operators with single-AZ etcd tighten it.
- **Or bound the work, not the wall clock.** Apply a per-operation timeout rather than one budget for the whole release.

If the reviewer still wants 5s, ask for measurements of release time on a 3-AZ deployment with a large snapshot. Without that data, the safe choice is 20s.

output.text:
**Recommendation: keep it at 5. Don't revert to 4.** If the reviewer's real worry is bounded validation, ask for a hard ceiling or a benchmark instead of a lower number.

**Why it is 5.** The change is in `d268f6c`. The comment at `internal/proxy/search_agg/context_builder.go:234-241` records the reason. Nordwind Retail's catalogue search groups by region, store, department, brand and SKU family, and none of those levels can be flattened. A cap of 4 would reject that query outright. The old comment said 4 covers every real use and to raise it only when a concrete use case appears. Nordwind is that use case.

**The reviewer's concern.**
- **Validation cost:** The check at lines 251-257 is a linear walk down the `SubAggregation` chain. It stops with an error as soon as the depth passes the cap. Going from 4 to 5 adds one iteration. The comment also says validation at five levels stays under 2 ms on Nordwind's data. I didn't re-measure that figure, and the commit message says the tests were "Not run locally".
- **Downstream cost:** The cap also bounds the segcore topK/groupSize derivation, as the comment says. That cost is probably the real one, because the group count can grow multiplicatively with each level. I haven't traced that derivation, and neither the comment nor the commit has numbers for it. The 2 ms figure covers only proxy validation. It doesn't show that execution stays bounded at five levels.
- **The ES "≤3" guideline:** That is advice about Elasticsearch's own cost model. The existing cap of 4 already went past it, so it was never a hard rule here.

**What to do about the reviewer's request.**
1. Run `go test -tags dynamic,test -gcflags="all=-N -l" -count=1 ./internal/proxy/search_agg/...`, since the commit says the tests weren't run.
2. Ask the reviewer whether the concern is the nesting depth itself or the group explosion downstream. If it's the downstream cost, a bound on the product of `Size` across levels would limit it much better than any depth number.
3. If they still want 4, Nordwind loses a supported query. In that case someone should confirm with that user before reverting.

The test change is also a bit awkward. The six-level chain repeats `stock` because the schema has only five distinct fields. The depth check runs before the duplicate-field check, so the test still passes for the right reason. That is worth a second look, but it doesn't affect the choice of limit.

sent.prompt: Why is the proxy's MetaCache keyed by collection ID, with collection names and aliases kept only as hints? And how are cache fills kept from racing the invalidations that DDL broadcasts send, so that a describe started before a DDL can't put stale metadata back?

output.text:
The design doc (`docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260716-proxy-metacache-id-inverted-index.md`) and the code in `internal/proxy/metacache/meta_cache.go` agree on both points. I read the doc and the fill and invalidation paths in the code. I did not read the rootcoord ack-callback side or the partition and database fills, so the claim that rootcoord commits before it broadcasts rests on the doc.

## Why the cache is keyed by collection ID

**Invalidations arrive by ID, alias, or database, not by name.**
- Before this design the primary store was keyed by `(db, name)`. Every Load, Release, Drop, Rename or Alter broadcast therefore had to scan the whole cache to find the entry. It also scanned all partition entries and the database's aliases.
- That scan ran under the global write lock, so at around 1M cached collections each broadcast stalled every query on the proxy.

**IDs are cluster-unique and never reused.** This is what makes IDs safe as the key:
- A drop and recreate under the same name gets a new ID. Old partition entries can never be reached through the new collection.
- A rename only changes a hint. The entry itself stays put.

**Names and aliases are hints that are checked on every read.**
- The structures are `nameIdx` (db → name → id) and `aliasInfo` (db → alias → real name).
- A read goes alias → name → `nameIdx` → primary, and at each step it checks that the entry is live and that its name and db still match. See `getCollection` around `meta_cache.go:500-520`.
- A failed check counts as a cache miss and costs one extra describe. It is never a stale read.
- Hints are written only together with their entry. `update()` writes the name hint and the alias hints, and the alias hints come only from the describe response's declared `Aliases` (`meta_cache.go:590-612`).
- `evictCollectionEntryLocked` (`meta_cache.go:1393`) is the single routine that deletes a primary entry. It removes the entry's alias hints, its name hint (only if the hint still points at this ID) and its partition list. Every hint therefore has an owner that can find it, and no background GC is needed.

The result is that invalidating by ID is O(1).

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

The design drops the old per-collection timestamp floor, which had gaps: unversioned alias write-backs, a bypass when `RequestTime == 0`, and a tombstone lifecycle. It uses a global `fillMu sync.RWMutex` instead:

- **Fills take the read side.** `updateWithSingleflight` (`meta_cache.go:698`) takes `fillMu.RLock()` and holds it across the whole describe RPC and the write-back into the maps.
- **Invalidations take the write side.** `RemoveCollection`, `InvalidateCollectionMeta` and `RemoveCollectionsByID` all do `fillMu.Lock()` and then `mu.Lock()`. `fillMu.Lock()` waits for every in-flight fill to finish, so a fill started before the DDL writes its pre-DDL result into the cache before the eviction runs, and the eviction then removes it.
- **Fills started after the eviction see the new state.** The doc says rootcoord commits the DDL before it broadcasts the invalidation, so a describe issued after the eviction reads post-DDL metadata.
- **The lock also covers singleflight.** The comment at `meta_cache.go:693-697` says the read lock must wrap the whole `sfGlobal.Do` call. If it were released inside `update()`, a caller arriving after the invalidation could join a flight that had already completed and get its pre-DDL result straight from singleflight, bypassing the cache maps.
- **Lock order and deadlock avoidance:**
  - The lock order is `fillMu` then `mu`, and `mu` is never held across an RPC.
  - Cache hits take neither `fillMu` nor any invalidation state.
  - Rootcoord's DDL ack callbacks release the meta lock before they fan out the expiration. A describe RPC stuck inside a fill therefore can't be blocked by the DDL that is waiting to drain it.

## Trade-offs the doc accepts

- **Slow fills delay invalidations.** An invalidation, and so the broadcast ack, waits for the slowest in-flight fill. Go's `RWMutex` also blocks new readers once a writer is queued. A describe RPC with no deadline that hangs can therefore stall the ack and all later fills. The doc treats RPC deadlines as the caller's responsibility.
- **One gate for everything.** `fillMu` is global, so a fill in one database can delay an invalidation in another. Sharding it is listed as a follow-up.
- **Duplicate or late broadcasts over-invalidate.** They cost one extra describe and are not filtered by version.
- **The endgame is different.** The doc lists WAL-subscription metadata replication as the end state. Proxies would tail one ordered stream, and `fillMu` would go away.

sent.prompt: Look at `Namespaces::Stateful::StatePrecedence.overwritable_states` in app/models/concerns/namespaces/stateful/state_precedence.rb. Is it still doing what it was written to do? If it is not, say exactly what it does differently from what it is meant to do, and where the intended behaviour is written down.

output.text:
No, not entirely. The reversal branch does something different from what the design doc describes, and the code, its comments and the spec have all been changed to agree with each other.

**What the code does**

When the target is `:ancestor_inherited`, or the source is `:maintenance`, `overwritable_states` takes the reversal branch (`state_precedence.rb:61-70`). That branch returns every state with positive precedence: `[:archived, :deletion_scheduled, :maintenance]`.

- **Unarchive** (`archived → ancestor_inherited`) returns `[:archived, :deletion_scheduled, :maintenance]`.
- **Restore** (`deletion_scheduled → ancestor_inherited`) returns the same three states.

**What it is meant to do**

`doc/development/namespaces_state_propagation.md:93-99` is the written intent. It is the "State precedence" table, and the walkthrough at lines 233-234 says higher precedence wins. The table lists these rows:

| Transition | Doc says | Code returns |
|---|---|---|
| unarchive (`archived → ancestor_inherited`) | `[:archived]` ("Unarchive, but stop at `deletion_scheduled`") | `[:archived, :deletion_scheduled, :maintenance]` |
| restore (`deletion_scheduled → ancestor_inherited`) | `[:deletion_scheduled, :archived]` | `[:archived, :deletion_scheduled, :maintenance]` |

**Consequences**

- Unarchiving a parent now also resets descendants that are in `deletion_scheduled` or `maintenance` back to `ancestor_inherited`. The doc says it must stop at `deletion_scheduled`. This breaks the "higher precedence wins" rule that the module header comment (`state_precedence.rb:9-11`) and the doc both state.
- Restoring a parent also wipes descendants that are in `maintenance`.

The code does not say what it should do when exiting `maintenance`. The doc table has no maintenance rows at all, and it never mentions `maintenance` as a propagated state.

**Smaller mismatch**

The doc says that when the source and target have equal precedence, the method returns an empty array (line 101). The code does not. For example, `archived → archived` returns `[:ancestor_inherited]`, because the forward branch uses `<` against the target alone and ignores the source.

**Where the change shows up**

- The module comment (`state_precedence.rb:13-15, 41-52`) says "a reversal ... returns the whole subtree to its default state". That wording replaces the doc's per-source behaviour.
- The spec (`state_precedence_spec.rb:21-37, 242, 246`) asserts the broad reversal result and the non-empty equal-precedence results.
- The comment at `state_precedence.rb:18-21` and the `STATE_PRECEDENCE` table give `maintenance` the value 6, copied from the enum. That is harmless, because only the ordering matters.

I did not check git history or the linked design docs or ADR. So I can't say which side was changed deliberately. The doc and the code disagree, and the doc is the only place that states the original intent. It needs updating, or the code needs restoring to match it.

sent.prompt: We had a node crash during startup inside the AWS SDK when the S3 endpoint resolved to an auth scheme with an empty signer name. Where is the guard against that, and where does it get installed on the S3 client? Name the files, classes and functions, with paths relative to the repository root.

output.text:
The guard is a decorator class around the S3 client's endpoint provider. It's installed on the client by a helper that `MinioChunkManager::PreCheck` calls.

**The guard**
- File: `internal/core/src/storage/minio/GuardedS3EndpointProvider.h`
- Class: `milvus::storage::GuardedS3EndpointProvider`. It subclasses `Aws::S3::Endpoint::S3EndpointProviderBase` and wraps the client's existing provider (`delegate_`). Every other method forwards to that delegate, so region discovery, path-style addressing and ARN handling are unchanged.
- Check: `GuardedS3EndpointProvider::ResolveEndpoint(...)`.
  - It calls the delegate first and returns failures untouched.
  - On success, it looks at `outcome.GetResult().GetAttributes()`. If attributes exist and `authScheme.GetName()` is empty, it returns `Aws::Client::AWSError<CoreErrors>` with `ENDPOINT_RESOLUTION_FAILURE` and the name `InvalidS3EndpointAuthScheme`. The message points at `minio.region` and `minio.address`.
  - Without the guard, the SDK can return a successful endpoint with an empty auth scheme after failing to parse the endpoint's properties JSON. `AWSClient` then swaps its default signer for one with that empty name and dereferences a null signer, or asserts in Debug.
  - If there are no attributes, the SDK's default signer is used. An explicit `NullSigner` is also left alone.

**Installation**
- Helper: `InstallS3EndpointAuthGuard(Aws::S3::S3Client&)`, an inline function at the bottom of `internal/core/src/storage/minio/GuardedS3EndpointProvider.h`.
  - It takes `client.accessEndpointProvider()` and replaces it with `std::make_shared<GuardedS3EndpointProvider>(provider)`.
  - It does nothing if the provider is null or already guarded, so it is idempotent.
- Call site: `MinioChunkManager::PreCheck(const StorageConfig&)` in `internal/core/src/storage/minio/MinioChunkManager.cpp:407`. Its first line is `InstallS3EndpointAuthGuard(*client_);`, and the header is included at line 18 of that file.
- `PreCheck` is declared in `internal/core/src/storage/minio/MinioChunkManager.h:278`. It is called at `MinioChunkManager.cpp:640`, right after the client builders (`BuildGoogleCloudClient` and the other `Build*Client` variants) have created `client_`. So the guard is in place before the precheck request and before the client is used anywhere else.

**Tests**
- `internal/core/unittest/test_s3_endpoint_auth.cpp` covers the empty-signer case, a malformed region, idempotent installation, and retry behaviour.
- `internal/core/unittest/test_minio_endpoint_auth.cpp` also exists.

I traced this by reading the code. I didn't build it or run the tests.

sent.prompt: What does Import V3 change about how bulk import works compared with Import V2, and why was it needed? Is it what runs by default now?

output.text:
**Short answer:** No. Import V3 is not the default. It sits behind `dataCoord.import.enableImportV3`, which defaults to `false` in `pkg/util/paramtable/component_param.go:7997-8006` and in `configs/milvus.yaml:1049`. New imports still run on V2 unless an operator turns the gate on.

I took the V2/V3 comparison from the design doc's note, "MEP: Import V3 — Sort-Based Re-shard" (`docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260921-import-v3-reshard-design.md`). I did not read the V3 implementation files themselves, so the doc is the source for everything below. The config default is the one part I checked in code.

## What changes

**V2** reads every source file twice:
- `PreImportTask` parses the whole file and keeps only statistics.
- `ImportTaskV2` then re-reads the file, hashes rows per file group, and writes straight into pre-allocated segments.
- Every file-group task splits the same `(vchannel, partition)` bucket, so the result is many small segments.
- A `hashed_stats` table grows with V × P (vchannels × partitions).

**V3** parses each source once and lets the pipeline decide segment shape. It has three DataNode worker kinds:
- **`preimport`** only counts rows and sizes. Ordinary imports decode the file for this. Backup imports just size the object list.
- **`reshard`** reads each source once, normalizes it, routes rows to their bucket, sorts them, and writes immutable sorted fragments plus a manifest.
- **Planning** (DataCoord) packs fragments into per-segment, bucket-local plans across all source tasks.
- **`import`** (`ImportTaskV3`) does a k-way merge of one plan's fragments. It writes exactly one formal segment through the existing Storage V2/V3 writers.

The job state machine gains `AssigningIDRange`, `Resharding` and `Planning` stages. Ordinary imports need exact per-file row counts so that PK and RowID are deterministic, so they get ID ranges allocated before the reshard.

## Why it was needed (the doc's motivation)

- **Single read:** V2's preimport leaves no reusable output, so every file is read twice.
- **Fewer small segments:** V2 decides bucket ownership inside per-file tasks, which makes cross-file segment planning impossible.
- **etcd limit:** `hashed_stats` can exceed etcd's default 1.5 MiB request size. V3 has no such table, so tables with 1024 partitions import natively.
- **No sort step afterward:** V3 output is already sorted, so the post-import `Sorting` compaction is skipped.
- **No schema-change hang:** V2 can hang in `IndexBuilding` if the collection is altered mid-import. V3 compares an import-relevant schema projection and fails explicitly.

## Rollout caveats

- The gate is one-way. Open it only after all DataNodes and every DataCoord that could become active support V3.
- The version is persisted in the WAL and the job, so a job created as V3 always finishes as V3. Turning the gate off again after activation is unsupported.
- Rolling back to a binary that doesn't understand V3 is forbidden while any V3 job, task or temporary prefix still exists.
- L0 import stays on V2, and any request with an explicit or message version keeps the path it chose.
- The doc lists no new user-facing API or options. There are new tuning knobs, such as `fragmentSizeInMB` (128) and `fragmentMergeFanIn` (128).

I've found all three pieces. I'm writing up the answer now.

**1. Claiming on save/destroy**

- `app/models/cells/transaction_record.rb`, `Cells::TransactionRecord`, collects the claims on the current DB transaction. `Cells::Claimable` reaches it through `TransactionRecord.current_transaction(connection)`.
- `app/models/concerns/cells/serialization.rb` handles serialization for these records.
- I did not read the transaction-commit logic or the gRPC call sequence, so I can't say exactly when the claims are sent.

**2. Writes that skip callbacks (`delete_all`, `insert_all`, `upsert_all`, raw SQL)**
- `app/workers/cells/bulk_claims_worker.rb`, `Cells::BulkClaimsWorker#perform(model_name, attribute_name, payload)`.

  - It uses the private methods `build_create_metadata`, `build_destroy_metadata` and `enabled?`.

- Callers that enqueue it:
  - `app/services/routes/rename_descendants_service.rb`
  - `app/models/route.rb`, around line 80, for `RedirectRoute`
  - `lib/gitlab/background_operation/users_delete_unconfirmed_secondary_emails.rb`, for `Email`
- The developer guide `doc/development/cells/claims.md` recommends scheduling the worker with `run_after_commit`.

**3. Finding and fixing missing or stale claims**
- `app/workers/cells/schedule_claims_verification_worker.rb`, `Cells::ScheduleClaimsVerificationWorker#perform`. It finds the claimable models with `models_with_claims` and schedules one job per model.
- `app/workers/cells/claims_verification_worker.rb`, `Cells::ClaimsVerificationWorker#perform(model_name)`. It takes a lease and keeps its progress in Redis through `last_processed_id` and `save_last_processed_id`.
- `app/services/cells/claims/verification_service.rb`, `Cells::Claims::VerificationService#execute`.
  - It lists local records with `find_local_records` and Topology Service records with `list_ts_records`.
  - It compares them with `process_batch`, `compute_changes` and `diff_record`.
  - It repairs the differences in `reconcile_claims`, and it skips records that changed recently (`recently_changed_record?`).
  - It logs mismatches with `log_drift`.

Two related workers handle claims that were left in flight:

- `app/workers/cells/stale_requests_cleanup_cron_worker.rb`, `Cells::StaleRequestsCleanupCronWorker`.
