Someone notes that gdb-remote packets to a local stub come back in milliseconds and wants 5 seconds again so that a hung stub is noticed quickly. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**Not safe to revert as a blanket default. I'd keep 15s.**

**Why it was raised.** Commit 2e7564149 explains it. Velmora boards are debugged through a serial-over-IP bridge that adds about 1.5s per round trip. During attach, the slowest replies (reading the target's large register description) take 6–8s. With the old 5s default, lldb dropped the connection mid-attach. Going back to 5s would reintroduce that failure for those users.

**What decides the value.** The default has to exceed the slowest legitimate reply on the slowest transport you support. It doesn't depend on the typical reply time, and it doesn't depend on what a local stub does. Two things follow:

- The timeout is per packet. It is not a round-trip average, so one 6–8s reply is enough to trip it.
- For a local stub, millisecond replies don't matter. The timeout only fires when something is wrong, so a larger value costs nothing when the stub is healthy. It only delays noticing a hang, by about 10 extra seconds.

The sanitized builds already use 60s for the same reason: slow-but-correct replies shouldn't be treated as hangs.

**Recommendation.** Keep the 15s default. People who want fast hang detection against local stubs can set it themselves:

- `settings set plugin.process.gdb-remote.packet-timeout 5`
- Put that line in `~/.lldbinit`, or in test and CI configuration.

If you want a lower default for local stubs without breaking the bridge case, one option is to choose the value by connection type. For example, use a short timeout for `localhost` or a local pipe and keep 15s for remote connections. That is a code change, not a revert of the `.td` default, and I haven't looked at whether the client has a natural place for it. `GDBRemoteCommunicationClient::GetHostDefaultPacketTimeout` and `ProcessGDBRemote::GetPacketTimeout` are the places to start.

sent.prompt: I'd like to automate some of our contribution work: a bot that picks up issues labelled `good first issue`, has an AI coding agent write the fix and open the pull request by itself, and an AI reviewer that posts its comments on incoming PRs automatically. Would the project accept that? What does it require of contributions made with AI tools, and why does it draw the lines where it does?

output.text:
**No. As described, the project would reject all three parts of your bot.** The policy is in `llvm/docs/AIToolPolicy.md`.

## Your three ideas against the policy

**1. Bot that fixes `good first issue` issues with an AI agent: explicitly forbidden.**
The policy says (lines 56–62): "Using AI tools to fix issues labelled as 'good first issues' is forbidden." This applies "whether you are a newcomer or not." It would also break the "human in the loop" rule, because the bot opens the PR on its own.

**2. Agent that opens PRs by itself: banned.**
Lines 47–49 say the policy "bans agents that take action in our digital spaces without human approval." The GitHub `@claude` agent is named as an example.

**3. AI reviewer that posts comments automatically: banned.**
Line 50 says "automated review tools that publish comments without human review are not allowed." Comments and feedback on PRs are also listed as covered contributions (line 36).

## What is allowed

- **Any tool for your own work.** You can use AI to craft code, docs or descriptions, as long as you read and review everything before asking anyone else to look at it (lines 5–10).
- **Opt-in review tools with a human in the loop** (lines 50–51). For example, a tool that drafts review comments for a person to read, edit and post themselves.
- **Reviewed generated docs.** Generated documentation that a human checked and edited, then posted as a PR, is an approved use (lines 52–54).
- **Disclosure.** Substantial tool-generated content must be labelled, for example with an `Assisted-by: <tool>` commit trailer (lines 21–28).
- **Accountability.** You are the author and must be able to answer questions about the work during review.
- **The one exception.** The Bazel-fixer bot was approved through an RFC. Any further exception is judged individually (lines 148–156), so you would need to write an RFC and get project approval.

## Why the lines are where they are

- **Reviewing costs maintainers scarce time.** Unreviewed LLM output *extracts* work from maintainers. The "golden rule" is that a contribution must be worth more than the time it takes to review (lines 66–95).
- **Good first issues exist to teach people.** They are usually not urgent. They are meant to bring newcomers into the codebase, and automating them wastes that purpose while adding little value (lines 56–62). The policy also says passing maintainer feedback to an LLM "doesn't help anyone grow" (lines 17–19).
- **Newcomers matter to the project.** LLVM wants to grow its next generation of contributors and maintainers. It spends review time on new contributors for that reason (lines 97–106).
- **Accountability needs a person.** A bot can't answer review questions, so the policy requires a human author.
- **Copyright is the contributor's responsibility.** Regenerating copyrighted material with AI doesn't remove the copyright (lines 134–144).

## What happens if you do it anyway

Maintainers can paste a standard "doesn't comply with our policy" response. They can also label the PR `extractive`, and repeat offenders get escalated to moderators or admins (lines 110–132).

## What you could build instead

- A tool that **surfaces** `good first issue` items to human newcomers, or a triage dashboard.
- A local assistant that **drafts** review comments, with a person approving each one before it is posted.
- A pre-submission self-check that helps contributors review their own AI-assisted changes.

If you want to propose something beyond that, the Bazel-fixer RFC on Discourse is the precedent to follow.

sent.prompt: Flang is getting a `fir.assert` operation for the checks that get lost when HLFIR and FIR passes inline runtime calls. Flang already does a few inline checks with `fir.if` plus a call to `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`, and MLIR already has `cf.assert`. Why a new op instead of either of those, why does `fir.assert` hand back 'guarded' copies of values, and what goes wrong for users today that it is meant to fix?

output.text:
`fir.assert` is already in the repo. The design doc `flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md` and the op definition at `flang/include/flang/Optimizer/Dialect/FIROps.td:84` cover your questions. I haven't read the lowering or codegen code, so the codegen details below come from the doc and the op definition, not from the implementation.

## What goes wrong for users today

When an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code, the checks the runtime did are lost. Examples are DOT_PRODUCT or MATMUL shape agreement, array assignment conformance, and RESHAPE and CSHIFT argument checks. The doc (§1) lists three consequences:

1. **Behavior depends on the optimization level.** The inlining passes mostly run at `-O1` and above. A non-conforming program stops with `fatal Fortran runtime error(...)` at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`. This is why some gfortran tests had to be disabled.
2. **The inlined code can be memory-unsafe.** Loop bounds come from one operand and are used to index another. A size mismatch becomes an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error message.
3. **Some checks are missing everywhere.** Inline ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables don't check allocation status, though the standard requires it. That is the B1/B2 case (PR #223287).

## Why not `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

This is the pattern used today for MOD/MODULO, NEAREST and similar checks (§1, §3.6):

- **No data dependence.** Nothing ties the check to the operation it protects, and MLIR has no notion of an op that may not return. Any pass may hoist the protected `fir.load` or `arith.remsi` above the check.
- **Unknown memory effects.** The call blocks alias-based optimizations such as load CSE and store-to-load forwarding.
- **No `noreturn`.** The FIR declaration lacks `noreturn`, so LLVM can't use the checked condition afterwards. Once the protected op is hoisted above the check, LLVM may infer from its undefined behavior that the check can't fail, and delete it.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- It writes the default memory resource, so it blocks load CSE and store-to-load forwarding across it.
- It still doesn't order non-speculatable, effect-free ops such as `arith.remsi` after it.
- Its LLVM lowering prints with `puts` and calls `abort`. It doesn't go through the Fortran runtime, so the message format differs.
- It has no guarded results.

`fir.assert` instead writes a non-addressable `FortranRuntimeResource`. That keeps DCE from removing it and keeps it ordered with calls and I/O. FIR alias analysis and MLIR CSE ignore it for user memory. Codegen emits a `cond_br` with weights and a call to the Fortran runtime, then `unreachable`, with the declaration marked `noreturn`.

## Why it returns guarded copies

The assert takes `guard(%x...)` operands and returns one result per guarded value, with the same type. If the condition holds, each result equals its input. Operations that must not run before the check then consume the results (e.g. `hlfir.designate %a_ok (%i)`). Ordering is enforced by SSA dominance, so no pass needs to know about `fir.assert`.

The doc compares this with two alternatives:
- **A result-less assert** (the current revision of #223287) needs every pass to be taught not to move things across it. That PR patches only Flang LICM.
- **A region-based assert** (like `shape.assuming`) is structurally safe, but the region blocks the single-block and pattern-matching optimizations the checks must not block.

Guarding a value protects every access made through it, without wrapping a loop nest in a region.

The consequence is that nothing may rewrite through an assert, because that would drop the dependence. The op is not a view and has no folder that returns its operand, but analyses (alias analysis, origin and contiguity finders) must look through it.

Two design choices follow:
- **What gets guarded.** Conformance checks guard the arrays being accessed, not the extents. Extents stay unguarded so constant loop bounds remain visible.
- **Inlined elementals.** When an elemental expression is inlined, `hlfir::inlineElementalOp` moves the guard onto the arrays the body reads.

**What decides the value**

The commit message (`e65c534fb`) says the 180s default is there because some deployments put a caching proxy in front of the debuginfod server. On a cold cache the proxy only starts streaming after it has fetched the whole artifact. For very large binaries that took 110–150s at the Harrowgate build farm. With a 90s default, `llvm-symbolizer` gave up and crash reports came back unsymbolized.

So the value has to be longer than the slowest legitimate cold-cache response, plus some margin. 90s is below that observed 110–150s range, and 180s is above it. The reviewer's concern is real too: a hung server stalls a tool for up to the full timeout, so a larger default costs more in the failure case.

**Code check**

- The value is only used in `Debuginfod.cpp`. `getDefaultDebuginfodTimeout()` is called at line 179 and passed down to `Client.setTimeout(Timeout)` at line 254.
- `DEBUGINFOD_TIMEOUT` (whole seconds) still overrides the default.
- I found no tests or docs that depend on 90, so a revert wouldn't break anything. If you revert, you'd also need to change the comment, `Debuginfod.h` and the `llvm-debuginfod-find` help text back.
- I didn't verify whether `setTimeout` limits the whole request or only idle time. That decides how well the reviewer's "hung server" argument holds. If it's a whole-request limit, a stalled transfer costs the full timeout. If it limits idle time, the proxy's silent wait still counts against it.

**Options**

1. **Keep 180s.** This is the safest choice for users behind such proxies. The cost is slower failure when a server hangs.
2. **Revert to 90s.** The reviewer's expectation is met, but the Harrowgate-style deployments must then set `DEBUGINFOD_TIMEOUT=180` themselves, and anyone who doesn't know to will see silent symbolization failures again.
3. **Compromise.** Keep 90s as the default and have those deployments set `DEBUGINFOD_TIMEOUT` in their environment. This is reasonable if the proxy setup is rare. The evidence in the history comes from one site, so I can't tell how common it is.

Before settling, ask the reviewer whether the original reports are still happening and whether the farm can set the env var. If they can, option 3 is defensible. If you can't reach a decision, keep 180s. A slow failure on a hung server is less costly than quietly unsymbolized crash reports.

Velmora boards are debugged through a serial-over-IP bridge that adds
about 1.5s per round trip. During attach, the slowest replies (reading
the target's large register description) take 6 to 8s, so with the
5s default lldb dropped the connection while attaching.

Raise the non-sanitized default from 5s to 15s and document the reason
next to the setting. The sanitized default stays at 60s.

sent.prompt: I'm about to start contributing to ClangIR. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what CIR is, where it sits in Clang's pipeline and how I turn it on; why its code generation copies classic codegen so closely and how divergence from classic codegen is caught; how C++ cleanups and exceptions are represented and lowered; how calling-convention lowering is organised; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
## ClangIR (CIR) in brief

Everything below comes from the ClangIR docs in `clang/docs/CIR/`. I read the three design docs through the notes tool, not the source. I haven't checked the implementation under `clang/lib/CIR`, so some of the design may not have landed yet.

### What CIR is, where it sits, how to enable it
- **What it is.** CIR is a high-level IR that keeps C/C++ semantics. It is built as an MLIR dialect that lives inside the Clang project.
- **Where it sits.** Between Clang's AST and LLVM IR. The path is AST → CIR → CIR passes → LLVM IR → backend.
- **How to turn it on.** Pass `-fclangir` to the driver. Use `-emit-cir` to see the CIR, the way you'd use `-emit-llvm` for LLVM IR.
- **Build switch.** `-DCLANG_ENABLE_CIR=OFF` removes CIR from the build, and `-fclangir` is then unavailable.
- **Documented in:** `clang/docs/CIR/index.md`. It also lists the RFCs, talks and history, and links to the ClangIR-labelled issues and PRs on GitHub.

### Why codegen copies classic codegen, and how divergence is caught
- **Why it copies.** CIR codegen deliberately mirrors classic codegen. It uses the same structure, similar names, and often duplicated logic. The goal is CIR that is eventually semantically equivalent to classic output. Having near-identical code also lets you diff the two to find what's missing.
- **Known cost.** The duplication is accepted technical debt, because keeping the copies in sync is manual. Don't refactor to share code with classic codegen unless the refactor makes sense on its own. A comment noting the opportunity is acceptable instead.
- **How divergence is caught.** Each CIR codegen lit test carries two sets of LLVM IR checks:
  1. LLVM IR from CIR lowered to LLVM.
  2. LLVM IR from classic codegen.
- **Manual comparison.** When you add a test, you compare the two outputs by hand. Any difference should be a known missing feature, and you fix it in the same PR where you can.
- **Sentinel role.** If a classic codegen change breaks the classic checks, ClangIR contributors are expected to update the CIR side.
- **Planned.** Automated equivalence checking (`opt -pass-normalize`, Alive2) and running the whole classic test suite through CIR.
- **Documented in:** `clang/docs/CIR/CodeDuplication.md`.

### Cleanups and exceptions
- **Mechanism.** CIR codegen still drives cleanups with classic's `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`/pop. The output is structured, though, not unstructured LLVM-style blocks.
- **High-level form.** `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup [normal|eh|all] { ... }`.
  - Nested scopes give reverse-order destruction.
  - `break`, `continue`, `return` and `goto` implicitly run the cleanup region on the way out.
  - An EH-only cleanup is skipped on normal exit.
- **Try/catch.** `cir.try` has catch regions and an `unwind` region. Each receives a `!cir.eh_token`. `cir.begin_catch`/`cir.end_catch` bracket a handler, and `end_catch` sits in a cleanup scope.
- **Lowering, step 1: `cir::FlattenCFG`.**
  - Nested regions become explicit blocks. Branches through cleanups use the same destination-slot and switch scheme as classic.
  - Throwing calls become `cir.try_call`, with an unwind block that starts with `cir.eh.initiate`.
  - `cir.eh.dispatch` selects the handler. `cir.begin_cleanup`/`cir.end_cleanup` mark cleanups. `cir.eh.terminate` handles a throw inside an EH cleanup.
  - The result is still ABI-agnostic.
- **Lowering, step 2: a separate EH ABI-lowering pass.** It runs after flattening and is distinct from the CXXABI lowering pass, which runs before it. It adds the personality function and target-specific operations.
  - **Itanium:** `cir.eh.landingpad`, plus compare-and-branch on type ids and `__cxa_begin_catch`/`__cxa_end_catch` calls.
  - **Microsoft:** `catchswitch`/`catchpad`/`catchret`/`cleanuppad`/`cleanupret`.
- **Documented in:** `clang/docs/CIR/CleanupAndEHDesign.md`. It also covers dynamic exception specifications, which I skipped. For the original LLVM IR model see the Clang doc "LLVM IR Generation for EH and Cleanups".

### Calling-convention lowering
- **Design.** Classification is not reimplemented in CIR. The shared LLVM ABI library in `llvm/lib/ABI/` (`ABIInfo`, `abi::Type*`, per-target logic) classifies arguments and returns.
- **Dialect-specific parts.**
  - `ABITypeMapper` maps MLIR types to `abi::Type*`.
  - A generic MLIR ABI pass drives the classification.
  - Each dialect supplies an `ABIRewriteContext` for the rewriting. CIR's is `CIRABIRewriteContext`, with `rewriteFunctionDefinition` and `rewriteCallSite`. FIR can reuse the rest.
- **Pass name and position.** The pass is `cir-call-conv-lowering`. It runs after `cir-target-lowering` and `cir-cxxabi-lowering`.
  - It needs a `dlti.dl_spec` module attribute.
  - It takes exactly one of `target=<name>` or `classification-attr=<name>`. The second is for tests.
  - Classifier implementations live in `clang/lib/CIR/Dialect/Transforms/`.
- **Current limits.** It is on by default only for x86_64, because that is the only classifier implemented so far. Use `-fno-clangir-call-conv-lowering` or `-fclangir-call-conv-lowering` to turn it off or on. Both are `-cc1` options, so pass them with `-Xclang`.
- **Goal.** Call-compatibility with classic Clang CodeGen, validated by differential testing.
- **Documented in:** `clang/docs/CIR/ABILowering.md`.

### Where to start
1. Read `clang/docs/CIR/index.md`.
2. Read `CodeDuplication.md` before your first PR, since it sets the testing expectations.
3. Read the other two design docs when you touch cleanups or ABI.

sent.prompt: In lldb/source/Plugins/Process/gdb-remote/ProcessGDBRemoteProperties.td the default packet-timeout for non-sanitized builds is 15 seconds. Someone notes that gdb-remote packets to a local stub come back in milliseconds and wants 5 seconds again so that a hung stub is noticed quickly. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**Recommendation: don't revert to 5s as the global default.** It would bring back the attach failures that the 15s value was raised to fix.

**What decides the value:** the timeout has to exceed the slowest legitimate reply, not the typical one. Local stubs answer in milliseconds, but the default applies to every gdb-remote connection. The commit message and the comment in `ProcessGDBRemoteProperties.td:9-12` record the constraint that sets it:

- Velmora boards are debugged through a serial-over-IP bridge that adds about 1.5s per round trip.
- During attach, the slowest replies take 6-8s. The largest is reading the target's large register description.
- A 5s timeout is below that, so lldb dropped the connection while attaching.

15s leaves roughly 2x headroom over the worst observed 6-8s reply. A hung stub is still noticed, just 10s later than before.

**Why 5s is unsafe:** the failure mode is a spurious disconnect during attach on slow links. That is worse than waiting a bit longer on a real hang. The same logic is behind the sanitized builds' 60s default, since slower execution there also needs more headroom.

**If the goal is fast hang detection locally:** set the timeout per session or in `~/.lldbinit` instead of changing the shipped default:

```
settings set plugin.process.gdb-remote.packet-timeout 5
```

This works because the property is `Global` and user-settable. Test harnesses or local-only workflows can set it the same way.

**What would change my answer:** a measured worst-case reply time on the Velmora path comfortably under 5s, for example if the bridge or the register-description read got faster. I haven't measured that. The 6-8s figures come from the commit message, so check them before relying on them.

sent.prompt: I'm reading the AArch64 Lightweight Fault Isolation (LFI) target. Three things look odd: the sandboxing rewrites are applied in the assembler rather than as a codegen pass; when an instruction loads x30, the guard that pulls it back into the sandbox is not emitted right after it but only at the next control-flow instruction; and the sandbox is fixed at 4GiB and must be 4GiB-aligned even though the code keeps full 64-bit pointers. Why each of these?

output.text:
All three reasons are in `llvm/docs/LFI.md` and the rewriter sources. I read the doc and `AArch64MCLFIRewriter.{h,cpp}`. I didn't build or run anything.

## 1. Rewrites happen in the assembler, not a codegen pass

The doc says it directly (`LFI.md:51-53`): the expansions run "at the very end of the LLVM compilation pipeline (during the assembler step). This allows the rewrites to be applied to hand-written assembly, including inline assembly."

- **Coverage:** LFI is meant to sandbox existing code, including assembly, unmodified (`LFI.md:9-10`). A codegen pass never sees `.s` files or inline `asm`.
- **Trust:** The rewriter is the last thing that touches each instruction before it is encoded. So nothing later can reintroduce an unsafe instruction, and the set of code that has to be trusted stays small, which is the "simple and verifiable" goal (`LFI.md:19-20`).
- **Opt-out:** The same layer provides `.lfi_rewrite_disable` / `.lfi_rewrite_enable` (`LFI.md:79-96`) for assembly that is already safe.
- **Where it lives:** It is an `MCLFIRewriter` hooked into the streamer. `rewriteInst`, `onLabel` and `finish` are in `AArch64MCLFIRewriter.h:54-58`.
- **X86:** `X86LFIRewritePass.cpp` also exists, so x86 may use a somewhat different arrangement. I didn't read it.

## 2. The x30 guard is deferred to the next control-flow instruction

The reason is pointer authentication (`LFI.md:295-303`, `AArch64MCLFIRewriter.h:64-69`). The guard is `add x30, x27, w30, uxtw`, which replaces the upper 32 bits of x30 with the sandbox base. A PAC-signed return address keeps its signature in those upper bits. In the usual `-mbranch-protection=pac-ret` sequence, `ldr x30, [...]` is followed by `autiasp` and then `ret`. If the guard ran right after the load, it would erase the signature before `autiasp` could check it. That would defeat PAC and make `autiasp` fail.

So the rewriter sets `DeferredLRGuard` (`rewriteLRModification`, cpp ~484-496) and emits the guard only when x30 could be used. In the code:

- **Control flow:** Before any return or indirect branch (cpp ~922-927).
- **Labels:** In `onLabel` (cpp ~307-311), because a label is a potential branch target. Temporary labels are excluded.
- **End of stream:** In `finish` (cpp ~319-322).

The invariant "x30 always holds an address within the sandbox" is therefore only temporarily false, and never at a point where x30 is used as a branch target.

Related details:

- Per the doc, `retaa`/`retab` expand to `autiasp`/`autibsp`, then the guard, then `ret` (`LFI.md:372-396`).
- `svc` emits its own guard, so any pending deferred guard is discarded in that case (cpp ~915-918).
- Without `FEAT_FPAC`, the mask overwrites the poison bits from a failed authentication (`LFI.md:344-348`). The pointer stays confined, but you lose the PAC fault.

## 3. The sandbox is fixed at 4GiB and 4GiB-aligned, with full 64-bit pointers

The doc's rationale is at `LFI.md:132-136`. The ABI stores pointers as their full 64-bit values, not as 32-bit offsets from the base. That gives two benefits:

- It enables stores-only mode (`+no-lfi-loads`), where loads are not sandboxed and so must work on ordinary pointers.
- The host can pass pointers straight into the sandbox with no translation.

The guard `add xD, x27, wN, uxtw` takes the low 32 bits of the pointer as an offset and adds the base. For this to reproduce the original pointer for in-sandbox addresses, the base's low 32 bits must be zero. That means 4GiB alignment (`x27` "must be aligned to the size of the sandbox", `LFI.md:124-125`). It also ties the size to 4GiB: `uxtw` is a 32-bit zero-extend, so the offset width is fixed at 32 bits. The doc says "the current design only supports 4GiB sandboxes", so this is a limitation of the current design rather than something fundamental.

Paths are relative to the repository root.

**MLIR type → shared ABI type**
- `mlir::abi::ABITypeMapper` in `mlir/include/mlir/ABI/ABITypeMapper.h` converts an `mlir::Type` into the `abi::Type*` that the shared classification code in `llvm/lib/ABI` works on. I only saw the header, and I'm inferring the `.cpp` is alongside it.

- `mlir::abi::ABIRewriteContext` is declared in `mlir/include/mlir/ABI/ABIRewriteContext.h`. Each dialect implements it. It takes a `FunctionClassification` and rewrites function signatures, bodies and call sites to match.

sent.prompt: With -gkey-instructions, when an optimization duplicates code (loop unrolling, jump threading), the copies need source-atom numbers of their own so both get stepped on. Where is that done when a block is cloned and when a cloned instruction is remapped, and where is the counter the new numbers come from? And on the Clang side, what does codegen use to open an atom and add instructions to it? Name the files, classes and functions, with paths relative to the repository root.

output.text:
**LLVM side: giving clones new atom numbers**

- **Block cloning.** `llvm::CloneBasicBlock` in `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp` (around line 162) does this. After it clones each instruction, and when its `MapAtoms` flag is set, it calls `mapAtomInstance(DL, VMap)` on the new instruction's `DebugLoc`.
- **`mapAtomInstance`.** It is defined in the same file at line 48 and declared in `llvm/include/llvm/Transforms/Utils/Cloning.h:145`.
  - It looks up `{InlinedAt, atomGroup}` in `VMap.AtomMap`. If there's no entry yet, it allocates a fresh group with `LLVMContext::incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` and records it. It does not modify any instruction.
  - `AtomMap` is a member of `ValueToValueMapTy`, declared in `llvm/include/llvm/IR/ValueMap.h:123` and cleared at line 152.
- **Remapping a cloned instruction.** `llvm::RemapSourceAtom(Instruction *I, ValueToValueMapTy &VM)` in `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.cpp:1320` does this.
  - It finds the instruction's `{InlinedAt, atomGroup}` in `VM.AtomMap`, builds a new `DILocation` with the mapped group and the same rank, and calls `setDebugLoc`.
  - It is declared in `llvm/include/llvm/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.h`.
  - `RemapInstruction` in the same file calls it at line 1029.
- **Callers of `mapAtomInstance`** (in the passes that duplicate code):
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/JumpThreading.cpp`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/SimpleLoopUnswitch.cpp`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/LoopRotationUtils.cpp`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/SimplifyCFG.cpp`
- **Callers of `RemapSourceAtom`:**
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/JumpThreading.cpp` (through its `remapSourceAtoms` helper)
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/LoopUnroll.cpp`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/BreakCriticalEdges.cpp`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/SimplifyCFG.cpp`

**LLVM side: the counter**

- The counter is `uint64_t NextAtomGroup = 1;` in `LLVMContextImpl` (`llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContextImpl.h:1933`). It is per-context and global, not per-function.
- `LLVMContext::incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` (declared in `llvm/include/llvm/IR/LLVMContext.h:372`, defined in `llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContext.cpp:403`) returns `NextAtomGroup++`.
- A neighbouring function in `LLVMContext.cpp` (line 400) bumps the counter to `max(NextAtomGroup, V)`, so it stays ahead of groups already seen.
- `llvm/lib/IR/DebugInfoMetadata.cpp:469` also calls the increment function.
- `llvm/docs/HowToUpdateDebugInfo.md` and `llvm/docs/KeyInstructionsDebugInfo.md` describe the scheme.

**Clang side: opening an atom and adding instructions**

The code is in `clang/lib/CodeGen/CGDebugInfo.h` and `clang/lib/CodeGen/CGDebugInfo.cpp`.

- **`ApplyAtomGroup`** is an RAII class (constructor at `CGDebugInfo.cpp:227`).
  - The constructor saves `CurrentAtom` and sets it to `NextAtom++`.
  - The destructor rewinds `NextAtom` if the group was never used, based on `HighestEmittedAtom`. It then restores the saved `CurrentAtom`.
  - Code opens an atom by creating one of these in the scope that emits the statement or expression.
- **`CGDebugInfo::KeyInstructionsInfo`** is the struct (`CGDebugInfo.h:~202`) holding `CurrentAtom`, `NextAtom` and `HighestEmittedAtom`. These are function-local, and `CGDebugInfo::completeFunction()` resets them.
- **Adding instructions to the atom:**
  - `CGDebugInfo::addInstToCurrentSourceAtom(Instruction *KeyInstruction, Value *Backup)` (`CGDebugInfo.cpp:182`) uses the current atom.
  - `CGDebugInfo::addInstToSpecificSourceAtom(KeyInstruction, Backup, uint64_t Group)` (`CGDebugInfo.cpp:188`) uses an explicit group. It tags the key instruction with rank 1, the backup instruction with rank 2, and any chain of casts feeding the backup with ranks 3 and up.
  - Both go through `CGDebugInfo::addInstSourceAtomMetadata`, which builds the new `DILocation` with the group and rank and also updates `HighestEmittedAtom`.
- **Where codegen calls them:** `CGExpr.cpp`, `CGExprScalar.cpp`, `CGStmt.cpp`, `CGDecl.cpp`, `CGClass.cpp`, `CGExprAgg.cpp`, `CGExprComplex.cpp`, `CGAtomic.cpp` and `ItaniumCXXABI.cpp`, all under `clang/lib/CodeGen/`.

I didn't open `addInstSourceAtomMetadata`'s signature line. Its role comes from the body I read (lines 160–180) and its callers.

sent.prompt: In lldb/source/Plugins/Process/gdb-remote/ProcessGDBRemoteProperties.td the default packet-timeout for non-sanitized builds is 15 seconds. Someone notes that gdb-remote packets to a local stub come back in milliseconds and wants 5 seconds again so that a hung stub is noticed quickly. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**Recommendation: don't revert to 5s.** Keep the default at 15s. Fast local stubs are better served by a per-user or per-site override.

**Why it isn't safe.** Commit `ceaa4835b` raised the default from 5s to 15s because of a concrete failure. Velmora boards are debugged through a serial-over-IP bridge that adds about 1.5s per round trip. During attach, the slowest replies (reading the target's large register description) take 6–8s. With a 5s timeout, lldb dropped the connection mid-attach. The comment at `ProcessGDBRemoteProperties.td:9-13` records this and warns against going below about 15s. A 5s default would bring back that attach failure for those users.

**What decides the value.** The timeout has to cover the slowest legitimate reply, not the typical one. That is the worst-case stub latency plus transport delay, with some headroom.
- Local stubs reply in milliseconds, so any timeout works for them. The value only matters for slow or high-latency targets.
- The timeout only affects how quickly a hung stub is noticed. A too-low value drops healthy but slow connections. A too-high value only delays detection of a dead one. The first is a hard failure and the second is a wait, so the default should lean high.
- The sanitized-build default is 60s for the same reason: instrumented builds are slower.

**What to do instead.** The setting is user-configurable, so people who want fast hang detection can set it themselves:
- `settings set plugin.process.gdb-remote.packet-timeout 5` in `~/.lldbinit`.
- Or set it per target or per session.

If a project wants a lower default for local debugging, a sound approach is to choose it by transport. For example, use a short timeout for local or loopback connections and keep the longer one for serial or bridged ones. That is a code change and goes beyond editing this `.td` default.

sent.prompt: Flang is getting a `fir.assert` operation for the checks that get lost when HLFIR and FIR passes inline runtime calls. Flang already does a few inline checks with `fir.if` plus a call to `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`, and MLIR already has `cf.assert`. Why a new op instead of either of those, why does `fir.assert` hand back 'guarded' copies of values, and what goes wrong for users today that it is meant to fix?

output.text:
`fir.assert` is designed in `flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md` (sections 1 and 3) and defined in `FIROps.td:84`. I read those two places. I didn't build or run anything.

## What goes wrong for users today

When an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code, the checks the runtime did are lost with it. Three things follow:

1. **Behavior depends on optimization level.** The inlining passes mostly run at `-O1` and above. A non-conforming program stops with a clear message at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`. Examples are a DOT_PRODUCT size mismatch, an array assignment with mismatched shapes, or an ALLOCATE of an already allocated variable.
2. **It becomes memory-unsafe.** The inline loops take their bounds from one operand and index another. A shape mismatch turns into an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error.
3. **Some checks are missing on every path.** The doc's example is inline ALLOCATE/DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables, which don't check allocation status. The standard requires that check.

## Why not `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

- The `fir.if` has no data dependence on the operation it protects. MLIR has no notion of an op that may not return, so a pass can hoist a `fir.load` or `arith.remsi` above the check.
- The call has unknown memory effects, which blocks alias-based optimizations.
- The FIR declaration isn't `noreturn`, so LLVM can't use the checked condition afterwards.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- It writes the default resource, so it blocks store-to-load forwarding and load CSE across it.
- It still doesn't order non-speculatable ops that have no memory effects, such as `arith.remsi`.
- Its LLVM lowering prints with `puts` and calls `abort`. It doesn't report through the Fortran runtime, so the message format differs.
- It has no guarded results.

## Why `fir.assert` hands back guarded copies

The result-less version in PR #223287 keeps a runtime-only effect (`MemWrite<FortranRuntimeResource>`) and teaches Flang's LICM not to hoist across it. That protects only one pass. Sinking, scheduling and patterns that create ops elsewhere would each need the same fix. If a protected `fir.load` or `arith.remsi` does end up above the check, LLVM can use its undefined behavior to conclude the check can't fail, and delete it.

The guarded results move the ordering into SSA. Each result equals its guarded operand when the condition holds. Anything that must run after the check consumes the result, not the original value. SSA dominance then enforces the order in every pass, and no pass has to know about `fir.assert`.

For example, in the doc's DOT_PRODUCT case the loop reads `%a_ok` and `%b_ok`, not `%a` and `%b`. The loop bound stays the unguarded extent, so constant bounds stay visible to loop optimizations.

Two design choices follow from this:

- **Not transparent to rewrites.** The op is neither speculatable nor view-like, so a fold can't look through it to the original operand. That would drop the dependence. Analyses such as alias analysis and origin or contiguity queries must look through it.
- **Why not a region-based assert.** A region would also give structural ordering, but it would wrap whole loop nests. That gets in the way of single-block pattern matching, store-to-load forwarding and LICM, and merging asserts would mean merging regions.

The remaining design points:

- **Effect.** The write goes to a non-addressable resource. DCE keeps the assert, it stays ordered with calls and I/O, and it doesn't block memory optimizations.
- **Code generation.** It becomes `cond_br` plus a `noreturn` runtime call. Messages use the runtime's format, with file and line taken from the assert's location.
- **Check categories.** Each assert has a kind (`status`, `conformance`, `argument`, `bounds`, `pointer`, `do`, `bits`, `divide`). The first three are on by default and the rest are opt-in. Checks are gated where they're emitted.

One caveat: the doc is marked "draft design, for discussion". The op itself is already in `FIROps.td`, with tests under `flang/test/Fir/assert*.fir`. Section 9 lists open questions such as option names and whether the new elemental and WHERE/FORALL checks belong in the default-on `conformance` kind.

output.text:
**No. As described, the project would not accept any of the three parts.** The policy is `llvm/docs/AIToolPolicy.md`.

## What the policy rules out

- **Autonomous PR bot:** Contributors may use any tool, but there must be a human in the loop (lines 5–12). The policy "bans agents that take action in our digital spaces without human approval," and names the GitHub `@claude` agent as an example (lines 47–50). A bot that writes a fix and opens the PR by itself falls under this ban.
- **`good first issue` automation:** This is a separate, explicit ban. "Using AI tools to fix issues labelled as 'good first issues' is forbidden" (lines 56–62). It applies whether or not the contributor is a newcomer. So even a human-supervised AI fix to those issues is not allowed.
- **AI reviewer that posts on its own:** "Automated review tools that publish comments without human review are not allowed" (lines 48–50). The policy also covers comments and feedback on PRs (line 36).

## What would be acceptable

- **Opt-in AI review tool with a human in the loop:** The policy says this is acceptable (lines 50–51). For example, a tool that drafts comments, which a reviewer reads, edits and posts under their own name.
- **AI-assisted contributions in general:** The contributor must read and review all LLM-generated code or text before asking anyone to review it (lines 8–10). They are the author, they are accountable, and they must be able to answer questions during review.
- **Labelling:** Contributions with substantial tool-generated content should be labelled, for example with an `Assisted-by: <tool>` commit trailer (lines 21–28).
- **PR descriptions:** Contributors are strongly encouraged to write these themselves (lines 40–45).
- **Copyright:** The contributor is responsible for it (lines 134–144).
- **The only exception:** The Bazel-fixer bot, approved through an RFC. Any future exception would be judged individually on whether it helps the project or extracts work from maintainers (lines 146–156). A new bot would need its own RFC.

## Why the lines are drawn there

- **Reviewer time is the scarce resource.** The policy calls unreviewed LLM output an "extractive contribution." It moves effort from the author to the maintainers who do design and code review (lines 66–73).
- **Golden rule:** A contribution should be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review (line 75). An autonomous bot can send PRs faster than people can review them.
- **`good first issue` is about growth, not urgency.** These issues are generally not urgent. They exist so newcomers can learn the codebase, and automating them "squanders the learning opportunity and doesn't add much value" (lines 56–62). Lines 97–106 add that LLVM wants to grow new contributors and maintainers. The policy also says that passing maintainer feedback to an LLM "doesn't help anyone grow" (lines 18–19).
- **Accountability needs a person.** An agent can't answer questions in review, so the policy requires a human author.

## If you want to automate something

- **Reviewer:** Build a drafting assistant that a human triggers and approves before anything is posted.
- **Fixes:** Use AI on non-`good first issue` work, with a human who reviews the output and opens the PR. Add the `Assisted-by:` label.
- **Bot:** If you still want a bot, propose it as an RFC on Discourse, as the Bazel bot was.

If a maintainer finds a contribution non-compliant, they paste a standard response asking for justification. They can also apply the `extractive` label, and persistent cases are escalated to moderators to lock the conversation (lines 110–132). An autonomous bot would likely hit that quickly.

  - It skips locations whose atom group is 0.
  - It looks up `{DL.getInlinedAt(), CurGroup}` in `VMap.AtomMap`.
  - If there is no entry yet, it asks the context for a new group with `DL->getContext().incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` and stores that in the map.

  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/JumpThreading.cpp` (lines 2079, 2109, 2730)

  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/LoopRotationUtils.cpp` (line 576)
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/SimplifyCFG.cpp` (lines 1198 and 3826)

- `llvm::RemapSourceAtom(Instruction *I, ValueToValueMapTy &VM)` is defined at line 1320.
- It looks up `{inlinedAt, atomGroup}` in `VM.AtomMap`.

**The counter:**

sent.prompt: I'm about to start contributing to ClangIR. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what CIR is, where it sits in Clang's pipeline and how I turn it on; why its code generation copies classic codegen so closely and how divergence from classic codegen is caught; how C++ cleanups and exceptions are represented and lowered; how calling-convention lowering is organised; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
# ClangIR (CIR) for a newcomer

## What it is, where it sits, how to enable it
- **What:** CIR is an MLIR dialect that keeps C/C++ constructs visible (scopes, cleanups, C++ ABI types, loops). It sits between Clang's AST and LLVM IR.
- **Pipeline:** AST → CIR → CIR-to-CIR passes → LLVM dialect → LLVM IR → the normal backend. The backend is classic CodeGen's `emitBackendOutput`, so optimisation and object emission are shared.
- **Turn it on:** pass `-fclangir`. `-emit-cir` is the CIR equivalent of `-emit-llvm`, and it is refused without `-fclangir`.
- **Build:** `CLANG_ENABLE_CIR` is ON in the monorepo build. It is off and refused in a standalone Clang build.
- **Tools:** `cir-opt`, `cir-translate` and `cir-lsp-server` work on `.cir` files.
- **Status:** it is incomplete. Gaps are tracked in code, not issues. `MissingFeatures.h` has about 250 guards that return false, and there are about 760 `errorNYI` sites.

## Why it copies classic codegen, and how divergence is caught
- **Why the copy:** CIRGen deliberately uses the same file layout, class names and logic as classic codegen. Directly comparing the two was judged the surest way to get equivalent output.
- **Cost:** every fix or feature in classic codegen needs a manual twin in CIR. The team accepts that as short-term debt.
- **Sharing:** whether to refactor shared code is left to the author and reviewers. The default is to refactor only when it makes sense independent of the long-term sharing plan.
- **Long term:** high-level CIR will drop target-specific handling. That handling moves into later lowering passes and shared classes, which shrinks the duplication.
- **Catching divergence:** CIR codegen lit tests carry two sets of LLVM IR checks, one for CIR then LLVM and one for classic codegen.
  - When you add a test, compare the two by hand. Any difference should be a known missing feature, and you should fix it in the same PR where you can.
  - The classic-codegen checks also act as sentinels. If a classic change breaks them, the CIR contributors are expected to update CIR.
  - The plan is to automate the equivalence check (`opt -pass-normalize`, Alive2) and eventually run all classic tests through CIR.

## Cleanups and exceptions
**High-level, structured form:**
- CIRGen still drives this with `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`.
- A scope that needs cleanup becomes `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup [normal|eh|all] { ... }`.
- `break`, `continue` and `return` implicitly run the cleanup region first. Nested scopes give reverse-order destruction.
- `try/catch` is `cir.try` with catch and unwind regions that take a `!cir.eh_token`.
- Handlers use `cir.begin_catch`, and `cir.end_catch` sits in a cleanup scope.

**Flattening:**
- The `FlattenCFG` pass turns this into plain blocks.
- Branches through cleanups use the same slot-and-switch scheme as classic codegen.
- Throwing calls become `cir.try_call`, which has normal and unwind destinations.
- Unwind blocks start with `cir.eh.initiate`, and `cir.eh.dispatch` selects the handler.
- `cir.begin_cleanup`/`cir.end_cleanup` mark EH cleanups.
- A throw inside an EH cleanup goes to `cir.eh.terminate`.
- At this stage the form is still ABI-agnostic.

**ABI lowering of EH (a separate, later pass from C++ ABI lowering):**
- It adds a personality function.
- Itanium: `cir.eh.landingpad`, plus type-id compares and branches. `begin_catch` and `end_catch` become `__cxa_begin_catch` and `__cxa_end_catch`.
- Microsoft: `catchswitch`/`catchpad`/`catchret` and `cleanuppad`/`cleanupret`.
- This is described as a design. Check the source for how much of it exists today.

## Calling-convention lowering
- **Where classification lives:** `llvm/lib/ABI/` holds `abi::Type*`, `ABIInfo` and the per-target classifiers (x86_64, with AArch64 planned). It is the single source of truth for the rules.
- **MLIR adapter:** `ABITypeMapper` converts `mlir::Type` to `abi::Type*`. A generic ABI lowering pass then runs these steps:
  1. Read the signature through `FunctionOpInterface`.
  2. Map the types.
  3. Call `ABIInfo::computeInfo`.
  4. Rewrite the signature and call sites.
- **Dialect glue:** each dialect implements only `ABIRewriteContext`, which creates its own ops (`createFunction`, `createCall`, `createExtractValue`, `createAlloca`, and so on).
- **Goal:** call-compatibility with classic CodeGen, checked by differential testing.
- **Today:** it works for x86-64 System V only. Other targets pass through unchanged.
- **Related code:** CIR's `TargetLowering` code is in `clang/lib/CIR/Dialect/Transforms/`, and the design's migration path ports useful algorithms from the incubator into the ABI library.

## Where it is written down
| Topic | Location |
|---|---|
| Overview, usage, RFCs, talks, history | `clang/docs/CIR/index.md` |
| Codegen duplication and testing strategy | `clang/docs/CIR/CodeDuplication.md` |
| Cleanups and EH | `clang/docs/CIR/CleanupAndEHDesign.md` |
| Calling-convention lowering | `clang/docs/CIR/ABILowering.md` |
| Driver and frontend action selection | `clang/lib/Driver/ToolChains/Clang.cpp`, `clang/lib/FrontendTool/ExecuteCompilerInvocation.cpp` |
| AST to CIR | `clang/lib/CIR/CodeGen/` |
| Pass pipeline | `clang/lib/CIR/Lowering/CIRPasses.cpp` |
| Passes | `clang/lib/CIR/Dialect/Transforms/` |
| Lowering to LLVM | `clang/lib/CIR/Lowering/DirectToLLVM/LowerToLLVM.cpp` |
| Op definitions | `clang/include/clang/CIR/Dialect/IR/CIROps.td` |
| Missing-feature tracker | `clang/include/clang/CIR/MissingFeatures.h` |

I read these through the project notes and did not open the source files themselves, so check line-level details against the code before relying on them.

sent.prompt: With -gkey-instructions, when an optimization duplicates code (loop unrolling, jump threading), the copies need source-atom numbers of their own so both get stepped on. Where is that done when a block is cloned and when a cloned instruction is remapped, and where is the counter the new numbers come from? And on the Clang side, what does codegen use to open an atom and add instructions to it? Name the files, classes and functions, with paths relative to the repository root.

output.text:
The work is split in two. When a block is cloned, a new atom number is allocated and recorded in the value map. When a cloned instruction is remapped, its debug location is rewritten with that number.

## LLVM side

**Cloning a block** (`llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp`)
- `llvm::CloneBasicBlock` copies each instruction and calls `cloneDebugInfoFrom`. If `MapAtoms` is set, it then calls `mapAtomInstance(DL.get(), VMap)` (around line 162).
- `llvm::mapAtomInstance(const DebugLoc &, ValueToValueMapTy &)` is at line 48. Its declaration is in `llvm/include/llvm/Transforms/Utils/Cloning.h:145`.
- It skips instructions whose atom group is 0.
- It inserts `{DL.getInlinedAt(), oldGroup} -> newGroup` into `VMap.AtomMap`. That map is a member of `ValueMap` in `llvm/include/llvm/IR/ValueMap.h:123`. If the entry already exists, it does nothing, so every instruction of one atom in the clone shares one new number.
- The new number comes from `DL->getContext().incNextDILocationAtomGroup()`. It also updates the `RemappedAtomMax` statistic.
- Other passes that duplicate code call `mapAtomInstance` directly: `JumpThreading.cpp`, `LoopRotationUtils.cpp`, `SimplifyCFG.cpp` and `SimpleLoopUnswitch.cpp`.

**Remapping a cloned instruction** (`llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.cpp`)
- `llvm::RemapSourceAtom(Instruction *, ValueToValueMapTy &)` is at line 1320. Its declaration is in `llvm/include/llvm/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.h:306`.
- It looks up `{inlinedAt, group}` in `VM.AtomMap`. If found, it builds a new `DILocation` with the new group and the same line, column, scope, inlinedAt, implicit-code flag and rank, then calls `setDebugLoc`.
- `ValueMapper.cpp:1029` calls it from the general instruction remapper (`Mapper::remapInstruction`, going by the call site; I didn't read the enclosing function name).
- Loop unrolling (`LoopUnroll.cpp:1285-1287`), `JumpThreading.cpp:2033-2036`, `BreakCriticalEdges.cpp:413-415` and `SimplifyCFG.cpp:1251` call it explicitly.

**The counter**
- It is `uint64_t NextAtomGroup = 1;` in `LLVMContextImpl` (`llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContextImpl.h:1933`). It is a per-`LLVMContext` counter, not per function.
- `LLVMContext::incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` (`llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContext.cpp:403`) returns `NextAtomGroup++`. Its declaration is in `llvm/include/llvm/IR/LLVMContext.h:372`.
- `LLVMContext::updateDILocationAtomGroupWaterline(uint64_t)` (`LLVMContext.cpp:399`) raises the counter to the maximum of its current value and the argument.
- `DILocation` construction at `llvm/lib/IR/DebugInfoMetadata.cpp:469` also calls `incNextDILocationAtomGroup()`. I didn't read the surrounding code, so I'm not sure what that path is for.

## Clang side

**Class `CGDebugInfo`** (`clang/lib/CodeGen/CGDebugInfo.h` and `CGDebugInfo.cpp`)
- It holds `KeyInstructionsInfo`, whose fields are `NextAtom`, `CurrentAtom` and `HighestEmittedAtom`. These are reset per function in `CGDebugInfo::completeFunction()` (`CGDebugInfo.cpp:220`).

**Class `ApplyAtomGroup`** (declared at `clang/lib/CodeGen/CodeGenFunction.h:246`, defined at `CGDebugInfo.cpp:227`)
- This RAII class opens an atom. Its constructor saves `CurrentAtom` and sets `CurrentAtom = NextAtom++`.
- Its destructor winds `NextAtom` back to `min(HighestEmittedAtom + 1, NextAtom)` if the number went unused, then restores `CurrentAtom`.
- It is a friend of `CGDebugInfo` (`CGDebugInfo.h:62`).
- It is used in many places, for example `CGStmt.cpp`, `CGExprScalar.cpp`, `CGExprComplex.cpp`, `CGClass.cpp` and `CGDecl.cpp`.

**Adding instructions to an atom** (`CGDebugInfo.cpp`)
- `CGDebugInfo::addInstToCurrentSourceAtom(Instruction *KeyInstruction, Value *Backup)` (line 182) forwards to the function below with `CurrentAtom`.
- `CGDebugInfo::addInstToSpecificSourceAtom(Instruction *, Value *Backup, uint64_t Group)` (line 188) returns early unless `-gkey-instructions` is on (`DebugKeyInstructions`) and the function's `DISubprogram` has key instructions enabled.
  - It tags the key instruction with rank 1.
  - It tags the backup value, if it is an instruction, with rank 2.
  - It then walks back through chains of casts, giving ranks 3 and up.
- `CGDebugInfo::addInstSourceAtomMetadata(Instruction *, uint64_t Group, uint8_t Rank)` (line 152) does the actual write.
  - It caps the rank at 7.
  - It keeps the existing group if the instruction already has a lower rank there.
  - It raises `HighestEmittedAtom` and replaces the instruction's `DILocation` with one that has the group and rank.

**The `CodeGenFunction` wrappers** (`clang/lib/CodeGen/CodeGenFunction.cpp:3494-3512`; declared in `CodeGenFunction.h` near lines 1813-1822)
- `CodeGenFunction::addInstToCurrentSourceAtom` and `addInstToSpecificSourceAtom` forward to `CGDebugInfo`.
- `CodeGenFunction::addInstToNewSourceAtom` creates a temporary `ApplyAtomGroup` and then calls `DI->addInstToCurrentSourceAtom`. Call sites such as `CGStmt.cpp` and `CGBuiltin.cpp` use these wrappers.

Clang's atom numbers are function-local and restart at 1 per function. LLVM's clone counter is context-wide, and `mapAtomInstance` asserts that the new group is greater than the old one.

sent.prompt: I'd like to automate some of our contribution work: a bot that picks up issues labelled `good first issue`, has an AI coding agent write the fix and open the pull request by itself, and an AI reviewer that posts its comments on incoming PRs automatically. Would the project accept that? What does it require of contributions made with AI tools, and why does it draw the lines where it does?

output.text:
**No, the project wouldn't accept that as you've described it.** Each of the three parts conflicts with `llvm/docs/AIToolPolicy.md`.

## What conflicts

1. **An autonomous bot that fixes `good first issue` issues and opens PRs.**
   - The policy bans agents that "take action in our digital spaces without human approval". It names the GitHub `@claude` agent as an example (lines 47–51).
   - Separately, it says "Using AI tools to fix issues labelled as 'good first issues' is **forbidden**" (lines 56–62). That applies whether or not a human is involved, and to newcomers and experienced contributors alike.

2. **An AI reviewer that posts comments automatically.**
   - "Automated review tools that publish comments without human review are not allowed" (lines 49–50).
   - The policy covers "comments and feedback on pull requests" explicitly (line 36).

## What is allowed

- **You can use AI tools freely, with a human in the loop.** You must read and review all LLM-generated code or text before asking anyone to review it. You remain the author, you're accountable for it, and you must be able to answer questions about it in review.
- **Opt-in review tools that keep a human in the loop are fine.** For example, a tool could draft review comments for you, and you would read, edit and post them yourself.
- **Disclosure is required.** Label contributions with substantial tool-generated content in the PR description, the commit message, or wherever authorship is normally indicated. A trailer like `Assisted-by: <tool>` works.
- **You should write PR descriptions yourself.** Using tools for translation or copy-editing is fine.
- **Copyright is your responsibility.** You must make sure you have the right to contribute the code under the project's license.
- **Exceptions are rare and judged individually.** The only current one is the council-approved Bazel-fixer bot (lines 148–153).

## Why the lines are drawn there

- **Maintainer time is the scarce resource.** The policy calls unreviewed LLM output an "extractive contribution". It pushes design and code review work onto maintainers. The golden rule is that a contribution must be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review it. Automation makes sending PRs cheap and doesn't make reviewing them any cheaper.
- **Good first issues exist for people, not for the fixes.** They're described as generally non-urgent and meant as learning opportunities for new contributors. Automating them "squanders the learning opportunity and doesn't add much value". The project wants to grow future contributors and maintainers. It also notes that passing maintainer feedback to an LLM "doesn't help anyone grow".
- **Accountability needs a person.** A bot can't answer questions or take responsibility for a change, so the policy requires a human author.
- **Enforcement is by maintainer judgment.** Maintainers can ask for justification using a template response and apply the `extractive` label. They can also escalate to moderators to lock the conversation.

## What you could build instead

- A **local assistant that drafts review comments**, which you approve one by one before they're posted.
- A **tool that triages or summarizes issues for you**, not for the project's issue tracker.
- Working on **non-`good first issue` tickets** with AI help, reviewing everything yourself and labelling it `Assisted-by`.
- If you want a real bot, **propose it as an RFC** on Discourse, as the Bazel-fixer bot did. The policy says exceptions are considered individually on whether they help the project or extract work from maintainers.

**Recommendation: don't revert to 90 unless you have a different fix for the Harrowgate case. Keep 180, but fix the stale docs.**

**Is reverting safe?** Technically yes. The change is one constant, and `DEBUGINFOD_TIMEOUT` still overrides it. Functionally it brings back the bug the commit fixed. Per the commit message, a caching proxy at the Harrowgate build farm only starts streaming after it has fetched the whole artifact. Cold-cache fetches of the largest binaries take 110–150 s. Under a 90 s default, `llvm-symbolizer` gives up and crash reports come back unsymbolized. Those failures would return for anyone who hasn't set the variable.

**What decides the value** is a trade-off between two failure modes:
- **Too short:** legitimate slow fetches are abandoned. This is a silent loss of symbolization, and it is hard to diagnose.
- **Too long:** a hung server stalls the tool for the full timeout. This is the reviewer's concern, and it is real, but the cost is bounded and visible.

The evidence is on the "too short" side. The commit message gives measured latencies of 110–150 s, and 90 s is below all of them. 180 s clears the worst reported case with some margin. "90 was the default for years" is not an argument for the value, because it was never tied to a measurement. The commit message doesn't say whether 90 was ever validated against slow servers.

**If the reviewer's concern should win**, the options are:
- Keep 90 and have Harrowgate users set `DEBUGINFOD_TIMEOUT=180`. This is reasonable if that deployment is niche and you'd rather keep the default conservative. The cost is that every affected user has to discover the variable.
- Keep 180 and let users who care about hangs lower it with the variable. This is the current behavior.

I haven't checked whether the timeout covers the whole transfer or only connection or stall time. That affects how much the hung-server worry applies. It is passed at `Debuginfod.cpp:179`, so check how `HTTPClient` applies it before deciding.

**Stale references to 90 s.** Whichever value you choose, these still say 90 and now disagree with the code:

- `llvm/tools/llvm-debuginfod-find/llvm-debuginfod-find.cpp:76` (says "defaults to 90s")

sent.prompt: Look at `SemanticSignatureElement::getNeverWritesMask` in llvm/include/llvm/Frontend/HLSL/SemanticSignatures.h. Is it still doing what it was written to do? If it is not, say exactly what it does differently from what it is meant to do, and where the intended behaviour is written down.

output.text:
No, it has drifted from the documented behaviour.

**What the code does** (`llvm/include/llvm/Frontend/HLSL/SemanticSignatures.h:179-181`):

```cpp
return static_cast<uint8_t>(~UsageMask & getDeclaredMask());
```

It limits the result to the element's declared components, `((1 << Cols) - 1) << StartCol`. For example, with `Cols=2`, `StartCol=1` and `UsageMask=0x2`, it returns `0x4`.

**What it is meant to do** (`llvm/docs/DirectX/SemanticSignatures.md:115-118`, "Derived Container Fields"):

> for outputs `NeverWrites = ~UsageMask & 0xF`. The output mask includes components outside the declared mask. These conventions apply to validator version 1.5 onward.

The same spec is repeated in the sloppy note `.sloppy/notes/01M7064FFGSQ22J99WBRCEC3R9.md:128`. For the example above, the documented result is `~0x2 & 0xF = 0xD`. That sets bits 0 and 3, which lie outside the declared mask `0x6`.

**The difference:** the code masks with `getDeclaredMask()` where the doc masks with `0xF`. It therefore leaves out every undeclared component, which the doc says must be included. For any element that doesn't use all four columns starting at column 0, the code returns a smaller mask than documented.

**The test hides this.** `llvm/unittests/Frontend/HLSLSemanticSignatureMetadataTest.cpp:223-224` asserts the declared-mask behaviour (`// NeverWrites stays within the declared mask`, expecting `0x4`). It agrees with the code and contradicts the doc, so it would need changing along with the fix.

The mask feeds the output side of `llvm/lib/Target/DirectX/DXILSignatureAnalysis.cpp:608`.

I didn't check git history, so I can't say whether the doc or the code changed first. The doc is the only written statement of the intent. If the declared-mask behaviour was a deliberate change, the doc and note are what's stale.

## Why the lines are drawn there

- **Review time is scarce.** The policy calls unreviewed LLM output an "extractive contribution". It pushes design and code review work onto maintainers, and the golden rule is that a contribution must be worth more than the time it takes to review (lines 66–95). Automated PR and review bots make that imbalance worse at scale.
- **Good first issues exist for learning.** They're usually not urgent. Their value is in getting newcomers familiar with the codebase and growing future maintainers, so automating them "squanders the learning opportunity and doesn't add much value" (lines 56–62). The project sees reviewing newcomers as how it sustains itself (lines 97–106).
- **Accountability needs a person.** The contributor is always the author. Passing maintainer feedback straight to an LLM doesn't help anyone grow (lines 18–19).
- **Copyright is unresolved.** Contributors remain responsible for having the right to contribute what a tool produced (lines 134–144).

## Enforcement

Maintainers can paste a stock reply asking for justification. They can also apply the `extractive` label, and repeat offenders get escalated to moderators who can lock the conversation (lines 110–132). A bot like this would likely trigger that quickly.

## What you could do instead

- Build a tool that helps a human contributor. It could triage issues that are *not* `good first issue`, or draft a fix or review comments for a person to review, edit and submit under their own name with the `Assisted-by` label.
- If you still think full automation is worthwhile, propose it as an RFC on Discourse, as the Bazel bot was.

sent.prompt: In MLIR I have an op that produces a value of the builtin `token` type, and I tried to return it from both branches of an `scf.if`; the verifier says the result 'must be variadic of any non-token type'. Why doesn't `AnyType` accept tokens, and why can't a token flow through yields, branches or selects like any other SSA value? Why are tokens SSA values at all rather than some other way for one op to point at another? And I want to hand a token into a `func.func` body: why won't that work, and what should I use instead?

output.text:
This is covered by `mlir/docs/Tokens.md` and the LangRef "Token Type" section in your checkout. I haven't run your IR, so the `scf.if` diagnosis rests on the docs and on the error text matching their example.

## Why `AnyType` rejects tokens
`AnyType` was changed to mean "any non-token type". That is the `any non-token type` wording in your error. It is deliberate opt-in. Any op declared with `AnyType` (`scf.if` results, `scf.yield` operands and so on) has forwarding semantics. If tokens were allowed there, they could be passed through such ops by accident. An op that really wants a token has to say so with the `Token` constraint (`Token:$scope`). ODS then adds `TokenProducerTrait` or `TokenConsumerTrait` for you.

## Why tokens can't flow through yields, branches or selects
A token is meant to work like a pointer to a specific op, through an OpResult, or to a region, through an entry block argument. The invariant is that from any use of a token you can walk back to its semantic producer. Anything that forwards or merges values breaks that. Examples are:
- `scf.yield` and region results
- `cf.br` successor operands
- non-entry block arguments
- call arguments and results
- `arith.select`

In your `scf.if`, the result would be either of two different producers, so the use no longer identifies one op. Generic passes are also not allowed to add a forwarding step between a token's use and its producer. For the same reason there are no token constants, so tokens can't constant-fold.

## Why SSA values
This is from the "Design Rationale" section.
- Tokens reuse the existing def-use machinery. That means no parallel def-use system for ops, no change to the generic op syntax or bytecode, and no change to core `Operation` APIs.
- The chain is one-way, from use to definition. A pass can delete a token use without touching or inspecting the definition.
- CSE, DCE and hoisting behave as usual, and a token user follows the normal `isTriviallyDead()` rules.

## Handing a token into a `func.func` body
There are two reasons it fails:
1. A token can't be an argument or result type of a `FunctionOpInterface` op. It also can't be a forwarded operand or result of a `CallOpInterface` op.
2. `func.func` is `IsolatedFromAbove`, and SSA values, tokens included, can't cross that boundary. The doc says this is intentional, so passes can process isolated regions concurrently without racing on def-use chains.

**What to use instead:** the docs say to use another mechanism, for example a symbolic reference through an attribute. Concretely, you could:
- Give the producing op a symbol name, or an attribute such as a `SymbolRefAttr` or an ID. Inside the function, a consumer op takes that attribute instead of a token operand and looks the producer up by symbol.
- Alternatively, restructure so the consumer stays in the same region as the token producer. A non-isolated region-holding op, such as an `scf` op or your own op with `TokenProducerTrait`, can have a token-typed entry block argument. The docs allow that only for entry blocks.

If you tell me what the token represents, I can suggest a specific shape for the symbolic reference.

sent.prompt: I'm reading the AArch64 Lightweight Fault Isolation (LFI) target. Three things look odd: the sandboxing rewrites are applied in the assembler rather than as a codegen pass; when an instruction loads x30, the guard that pulls it back into the sandbox is not emitted right after it but only at the next control-flow instruction; and the sandbox is fixed at 4GiB and must be 4GiB-aligned even though the code keeps full 64-bit pointers. Why each of these?

output.text:
All three are design choices recorded in `llvm/docs/LFI.md` and the rewriter's comments. The docs state most of the reasons, and I mark the parts I inferred.

## 1. Rewrites happen in the assembler, not as a codegen pass

`LFI.md:51-53` says the rewrites are applied "at the very end of the LLVM compilation pipeline (during the assembler step). This allows the rewrites to be applied to hand-written assembly, including inline assembly."

A codegen pass only sees what the compiler generates. LFI's goal (`LFI.md:9-10`) is to sandbox existing C/C++ *and assembly* unmodified. Doing the rewrite at the `MCStreamer` level, in `AArch64MCLFIRewriter::rewriteInst`, covers every instruction that reaches the object file, whatever its source. That includes `.S` files, inline asm, and instructions that late passes or the linker-facing emitter insert.

It also makes the trusted part small. The rewriter is the one place that has to be right, which fits the "simple and verifiable" goal (`LFI.md:19-20`). Hand-written code that is already safe can opt out with `.lfi_rewrite_disable` / `.lfi_rewrite_enable`.

## 2. The x30 guard is deferred to the next control-flow instruction

The reason is pointer authentication (`LFI.md:295-303`, `AArch64MCLFIRewriter.h:64-69`). The guard is `add x30, x27, w30, uxtw`, which keeps only the low 32 bits of x30. A PAC-signed return address keeps its signature in the upper bits, so guarding immediately after `ldr x30, [...]` would destroy the signature. The following `autiasp` would then have nothing to authenticate.

With the guard deferred, the sequence is:

```
ldr x30, [...]
autiasp
add x30, x27, w30, uxtw
ret
```

The invariant that x30 is always in the sandbox is only needed when x30 is *used* for control flow. So `rewriteInst` flushes the pending guard before any return or indirect branch (`AArch64MCLFIRewriter.cpp:922-927`). It also flushes at non-temporary labels, since a label is a possible branch target (`:307-311`), and at `finish()` (`:319-322`).

The `svc` expansion already emits its own guard, so it discards any pending one (`:915-918`).

I didn't trace every path, but the window where x30 is unguarded looks bounded. It lasts until the next branch, label or end of stream, and a plain `bl` overwrites x30 anyway.

## 3. A fixed 4GiB sandbox, 4GiB-aligned, with full 64-bit pointers

`LFI.md:132-136` gives the reason. The ABI keeps pointers as full 64-bit values, not 32-bit offsets from the base. That is what enables stores-only mode, where loads aren't sandboxed but stores are, and it lets the host pass pointers straight into the sandbox.

The alignment requirement follows from the guard `add xD, x27, wN, uxtw`, which takes `x27` plus the zero-extended low 32 bits. Because `x27` is 4GiB-aligned, that sum is the same as replacing the top 32 bits with the base. A pointer that is already inside the sandbox therefore guards to itself, and a stray one is forced inside. The program never needs to see a translated pointer, which is the inferred part. A different sandbox size would need a different masking sequence, which is why 4GiB is hard-wired for now. It is also the natural fit for the `uxtw` addressing mode, `[x27, wM, uxtw]`, which makes the common load/store safe with no extra instruction.

sent.prompt: With -gkey-instructions, when an optimization duplicates code (loop unrolling, jump threading), the copies need source-atom numbers of their own so both get stepped on. Where is that done when a block is cloned and when a cloned instruction is remapped, and where is the counter the new numbers come from? And on the Clang side, what does codegen use to open an atom and add instructions to it? Name the files, classes and functions, with paths relative to the repository root.

output.text:
**LLVM side: giving the copies new atom numbers**

- **Block clone:** `llvm::CloneBasicBlock` in `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp` (~line 162).
  - After it clones each instruction and calls `cloneDebugInfoFrom`, it calls `mapAtomInstance(DL.get(), VMap)` on the new instruction's `DebugLoc`.
  - This only happens when the `MapAtoms` flag is set.
- **`mapAtomInstance`:** defined at `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp:48` and declared in `llvm/include/llvm/Transforms/Utils/Cloning.h:145`.
  - It looks up `{DL.getInlinedAt(), atomGroup}` in `VMap.AtomMap`. This is the `AtomMap` member of `ValueToValueMapTy`.
  - If there is no entry yet, it allocates a fresh group with `DL->getContext().incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` and records it.
  - It also updates the `RemappedAtomMax` statistic.
- **Instruction remap:** `llvm::RemapSourceAtom(Instruction *I, ValueToValueMapTy &VM)` at `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.cpp:1320`.
  - It looks up the instruction's `{inlinedAt, atomGroup}` in `VM.AtomMap`.
  - If it finds one, it rebuilds the `DILocation` with the new group and the same line, column, scope, inlinedAt, implicit-code flag and rank, then calls `setDebugLoc`.
  - It is called from `llvm::RemapInstruction` (`ValueMapper.cpp:~1028`), unless the `RF_DoNotRemapAtoms` flag is set.
- **Other callers of `mapAtomInstance`:** passes that duplicate code without going through `CloneBasicBlock` call it directly:
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/JumpThreading.cpp` (three places)
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/SimpleLoopUnswitch.cpp`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/LoopRotationUtils.cpp`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/SimplifyCFG.cpp` (two places)
- **The counter:** `NextAtomGroup` in `LLVMContextImpl` (`llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContextImpl.h:1933`, starts at 1). It is per `LLVMContext`.
  - `LLVMContext::incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` returns it and post-increments it (`llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContext.cpp:403`).
  - `LLVMContext::updateDILocationAtomGroupWaterline(V)` raises it to `max(current, V)` (`LLVMContext.cpp:399`).

**Clang side: opening an atom and adding instructions**

All of this is in `clang/lib/CodeGen/CGDebugInfo.cpp` and `CGDebugInfo.h`.

- **Opening an atom:** the RAII class `ApplyAtomGroup`, declared in `clang/lib/CodeGen/CodeGenFunction.h:246` and defined at `CGDebugInfo.cpp:227`.
  - Its constructor saves `KeyInstructionsInfo.CurrentAtom` and sets it to `KeyInstructionsInfo.NextAtom++`.
  - Its destructor gives back the number if it went unused and restores the previous `CurrentAtom`.
  - It is used all over codegen, for example in `CGStmt.cpp`, `CGExprScalar.cpp`, `CGExprComplex.cpp`, `CGClass.cpp`, `CGDecl.cpp`, `CGAtomic.cpp` and `CGExpr.cpp`.
- **State:** the `KeyInstructionsInfo` struct in `CGDebugInfo.h:~202`.
  - Its fields are `NextAtom`, `HighestEmittedAtom` and `CurrentAtom`.
  - They are function-local and reset in `CGDebugInfo::completeFunction()`.
- **Adding instructions:**
  - `CGDebugInfo::addInstToCurrentSourceAtom(KeyInstruction, Backup)` uses `CurrentAtom`.
  - `CGDebugInfo::addInstToSpecificSourceAtom(KeyInstruction, Backup, Group)` does the work. It returns early unless `DebugKeyInstructions` is on and the function's `DISubprogram` has key instructions enabled.
  - Both call `CGDebugInfo::addInstSourceAtomMetadata(I, Group, Rank)`. It rebuilds the `DILocation` with the group and rank (rank is capped at 7) and updates `HighestEmittedAtom`.
  - The key instruction gets rank 1. The optional backup instruction gets rank 2, and any chain of casts feeding it gets rank 3 and up.

**When a block is cloned**
- `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp`, `llvm::CloneBasicBlock` (line 142). After it clones each instruction (around lines 153–165), it calls `mapAtomInstance(DL.get(), VMap)`. This only happens when `MapAtoms` is set.
- `mapAtomInstance` is defined at `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp:48`, and declared in `llvm/include/llvm/Transforms/Utils/Cloning.h:145`.
- It looks up the instruction's `{DL.getInlinedAt(), AtomGroup}` pair in `VMap.AtomMap`. If there is no entry yet, it asks the context for a fresh group number and records it. Every instruction in the clone that shares the old atom then maps to the same new number.
- Other transforms call `mapAtomInstance` directly when they clone instructions themselves:
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/LoopRotationUtils.cpp:576`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/SimpleLoopUnswitch.cpp:304`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/SimplifyCFG.cpp:1198` and `:3826`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/JumpThreading.cpp:2079`, `:2109` and `:2730`

- `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.cpp`, `llvm::RemapSourceAtom(Instruction *I, ValueToValueMapTy &VM)` (line 1320, declared in `ValueMapper.h:306`).
- It finds the instruction's `{InlinedAt, AtomGroup}` in `VM.AtomMap`. If there is a mapping, it rebuilds the `DILocation` with the new group and keeps the other fields, including the rank, then calls `setDebugLoc`.
- `ValueMapper.cpp:1028` calls it from `Mapper::remapInstruction`, unless the caller passed `RF_DoNotRemapAtoms` (defined at `ValueMapper.h:115`).
- Some passes call it explicitly instead:
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/LoopUnroll.cpp:1287`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/BreakCriticalEdges.cpp:415`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/SimplifyCFG.cpp:1251`
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/JumpThreading.cpp`, through its own static wrapper `remapSourceAtoms` (line 2031), used at lines 2335, 2461 and 2770

**Where the counter lives**
- `llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContextImpl.h:1933` holds `uint64_t NextAtomGroup = 1;`, which is per `LLVMContext`.
- `LLVMContext::incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` (`llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContext.cpp:403`, declared in `llvm/include/llvm/IR/LLVMContext.h:372`) returns it and then increments it. `mapAtomInstance` calls this.
- `llvm/lib/IR/DebugInfoMetadata.cpp:469` also calls it.

- **`ApplyAtomGroup`**
  - It is a scoped RAII class declared in `clang/lib/CodeGen/CodeGenFunction.h:246`, with its constructor and destructor in `clang/lib/CodeGen/CGDebugInfo.cpp:227` and `:234`.
