**No. As described, LLVM would not accept this.** Each of the three parts conflicts with `llvm/docs/AIToolPolicy.md`.

## What the policy requires

LLVM allows any tool, but there must be a human in the loop (`AIToolPolicy.md:5-12`):

- **Review before submission.** Contributors must read and review all LLM-generated code or text before asking anyone else to review it.
- **Accountability.** The contributor is always the author and must be able to answer questions about the work during review.
- **Disclosure.** Contributions with substantial tool-generated content must be labelled, for example with an `Assisted-by: <tool>` commit trailer (`:21-28`). The labelling is meant to help reviewers, not to track which parts of LLVM are generated.
- **Scope.** The policy covers code, RFCs, issues and security reports, and comments on PRs (`:30-36`).
- **Descriptions.** PR descriptions should be written by the contributor, with tools used only for translation or copy-editing (`:40-45`).
- **Copyright.** The contributor is responsible for having the right to submit the code (`:134-144`).

## How your three pieces fare

1. **Bot fixing `good first issue` issues: forbidden outright.** The policy says AI tools must not be used to fix these issues, whether or not you're a newcomer (`:56-62`).
2. **Agent opening PRs by itself: banned.** The policy bans agents that act in LLVM's spaces without human approval. It names the GitHub `@claude` agent as an example (`:47-49`).
3. **AI reviewer posting comments automatically: banned.** Automated review tools that publish without human review aren't allowed (`:49-51`). An opt-in reviewer that keeps a human in the loop is acceptable.

## Why the lines are drawn there

- **Review time is the scarce resource.** Sending unreviewed LLM output to maintainers *extracts* design and code review work from them (`:66-73`). The golden rule is that a contribution must be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review (`:75-77`). An autonomous bot makes the cost of producing a PR almost zero while the review cost stays the same, which is the imbalance the policy targets (`:93-95`).
- **Good first issues exist for people.** They're not urgent. Their purpose is to teach newcomers the codebase, and automating them wastes that purpose and adds little value (`:56-60`). The policy also says that passing maintainer feedback to an LLM doesn't help anyone grow (`:18-19`).
- **Growing contributors matters to LLVM.** The project wants to welcome and recruit new contributors (`:97-106`). An autonomous bot takes the place of that pipeline instead of feeding it.

## Consequences and exceptions

- Maintainers can reply with the standard "doesn't comply" message and apply the `extractive` label. Persistent non-compliance gets escalated to moderators, who can lock the conversation (`:110-132`).
- The only exception is the Bazel-fixer bot, which the project council approved through an RFC (`:146-153`). Any further exception is judged individually on whether it helps the project or extracts work from maintainers (`:155-156`).

## What you could do instead

- **Assist the author, not replace them.** Use AI to help you draft a fix for a non-`good first issue` issue. Read and understand every line, write the PR description yourself, add an `Assisted-by:` trailer, and submit it under your own name.
- **Run an opt-in reviewer.** A tool that drafts review comments privately, which you read, edit and post yourself, is fine. Only the auto-posting is the problem.
- **Propose an exception.** If you think a bot would help the project, put an RFC on Discourse, as the Bazel-fixer did. Make the case that it reduces maintainer work. Don't expect an issue-fixing bot for `good first issue` to pass, since the policy rules that out explicitly.

sent.prompt: Flang is getting a `fir.assert` operation for the checks that get lost when HLFIR and FIR passes inline runtime calls. Flang already does a few inline checks with `fir.if` plus a call to `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`, and MLIR already has `cf.assert`. Why a new op instead of either of those, why does `fir.assert` hand back 'guarded' copies of values, and what goes wrong for users today that it is meant to fix?

output.text:
`fir.assert` is already in this tree, and the design doc `flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md` answers your question. I haven't built or run anything here.

## The problem for users

Flang leaves most dynamic checks to the Fortran runtime. These include shape conformance, allocation status, and DIM and SHAPE argument validity. When an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code, the check disappears (doc §1). Users see three effects:

1. **Behavior depends on `-O` level.** A non-conforming program stops with a clear message at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`.
2. **The inline code is memory-unsafe on bad input, not just wrong.** Loop bounds come from one operand and are used to index another. A size mismatch in `DOT_PRODUCT`, `MATMUL` or an array assignment becomes an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error.
3. **Some standard-required checks are missing on every path.** Inline ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables don't check allocation status (F2023 9.7.1.3, 9.7.3.2, 9.7.4). This is why `-mllvm -use-alloc-runtime` is the workaround today.

## Why not `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

- **No data dependence.** Nothing ties the protected operation to the check, so a pass can move it above the check. MLIR has no way to say an operation may not return.
- **Optimization cost.** The call has unknown memory effects, which blocks alias-based optimizations.
- **Missing `noreturn`.** The FIR declaration lacks `noreturn`, so LLVM can't use the checked condition afterward.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- It writes the default resource. That blocks store-to-load forwarding and load CSE across it.
- It doesn't order non-speculatable, effect-free ops such as `arith.remsi` after it.
- It lowers to `puts` plus `abort`, not the Fortran runtime. The message format therefore differs from `fatal Fortran runtime error(<file>:<line>): ...`.
- It has no guarded results.

## Why guarded copies

`fir.assert` takes `guard(%x...)` operands and returns one result per guarded value, with the same type. If the condition holds, each result equals its input. Otherwise the program terminates.

Anything that must not run before the check consumes the guarded result. SSA dominance then enforces the ordering, for every pass, without any pass knowing about `fir.assert`. The doc contrasts this with the current PR #223287, a result-less assert. There, LICM had to be taught not to hoist across it, and every other pass that moves or recreates ops would need the same fix.

The ordering matters beyond MLIR. If a protected load or remainder ends up above the check, LLVM can infer from its undefined behavior that the check can't fail, and delete it.

The doc also rejects a region-based assert, because the region boundary gets in the way of the single-block pattern matching that bufferization and forwarding rely on.

## Supporting design choices

- **Effect model.** The op is `MemWrite<FortranRuntimeResource>`, a non-addressable resource. It is never dead and stays ordered with calls and I/O, but alias analysis and CSE ignore it (`FIROps.td:84-88`).
- **Not transparent to rewrites.** It is not a view, has no folder that returns the guarded operand, and no other rewrite may look through it. Looking through it would drop the dependence. Analyses, however, must look through it.
- **What gets guarded.** Conformance checks guard the arrays being accessed, not shapes or extents. That keeps constant loop bounds visible to MLIR loop optimizations.
- **Code generation.** It becomes `cond_br` plus a `noreturn` runtime call, so messages match the runtime's.

The doc is marked "draft design, for discussion", so details such as option names and kind defaults are still open.

If you need "one of two producers", this design doesn't allow it. You'd have to make each branch consume its own token inside the branch. Or you'd model the dependency with something forwardable, such as a value of a different type that your dialect defines.

## Why SSA values instead of another reference mechanism

The Design Rationale (`Tokens.md:19-35`) gives these reasons:

- It reuses the existing def-use machinery. There's no parallel def-use system for operations, and no change to generic op syntax, bytecode, or the core `Operation` APIs.
- The chain is unidirectional, like normal SSA. A use points at its definition, so a transformation can drop a token use without touching the definition.
- CSE, DCE and hoisting keep working unchanged. A token user is side-effect free and follows the normal `isTriviallyDead()` rules.

## Handing a token into a `func.func` body

There are two separate blockers:

1. **A function can't take or return a token.** An argument or result type of a `FunctionOpInterface` op may not be a token, and call operands and results can't be tokens either (`Tokens.md:76-86`). A call would be a forwarding step.
2. **Tokens can't cross `IsolatedFromAbove` boundaries.** `func.func` is isolated from above, so a token defined outside can't be used inside it. This is intentional: passes can then process isolated regions concurrently without racing on def-use chains (`Tokens.md:31-35`).

## What to use instead

The docs say that when a token-like dependency must cross an isolated boundary, "another mechanism must be used (e.g. a symbolic reference using an attribute)" (`Tokens.md:33-35`). In practice:

- **Symbol reference.** Give the producing op a symbol name and have the consumer inside the function refer to it with a `SymbolRefAttr`. This is the approach the docs suggest.
- **Inline the region.** If the function body is just a scoped region, use an op with a non-isolated region. Its entry block argument can be a `token`, as long as the parent op has `TokenProducerTrait`. That keeps the token inside a single region and avoids the function boundary.
- **A dialect-specific forwardable type.** If you really need the value to be passed through calls and yields, define your own type, which isn't subject to the token restrictions. You then give up the "always walk back to one producer" guarantee.

If you tell me what your token represents (an async dependency, a scope, a handle to an op), I can say which of these fits best.

That only works if you can always walk back from a use and say "this token came from *that* op". `AnyType` is the constraint ops use for values they forward, so `mlir/docs/Tokens.md` excludes tokens from it by default. Without that, a token could be passed along by accident as an operand with forwarding semantics. `AnyType` now means "any non-token type", which is what it meant before tokens existed. Ops that really take or return a token have to opt in with the `Token` constraint. For example, `(outs Token:$token)` on a producer, or `(ins Token:$scope, AnyType:$value)` on a consumer.

**Why yields, branches and selects can't carry a token.** Those ops merge or forward values without understanding them. Once a token has gone through one of them, it could have come from either branch, and the "which op produced it" chain is lost. The doc lists the forms that are disallowed:
- forwarded operands or results of `CallOpInterface` ops;
- argument or result types of `FunctionOpInterface` ops;
- successor operands of `BranchOpInterface` ops;
- block arguments of non-entry blocks;
- iter-args, region results and yielded values of `RegionBranchOpInterface` ops;
- the result of `arith.select` and similar ops.

Your case fails because `scf.if` results are `Variadic<AnyType>` and `scf.yield` operands are `AnyType`. Both the result and the yield get rejected, which is the "must be variadic of any non-token type" error you saw.

**Why tokens are SSA values at all.** This is so ops can refer to other ops without a second def-use system. Tokens reuse the existing SSA machinery. They need no changes to the generic op syntax, the bytecode, or the core `Operation` C++ APIs. The def-use chain is one-directional: a use points to its definition. A pass can therefore drop a token use without touching or inspecting the definition.

**Why a token can't go into a `func.func` body.** Two reasons:
- Function arguments and results are forwarding positions, and the rules above forbid tokens there.
- Because tokens are SSA values, they can't cross `IsolatedFromAbove` boundaries. `func.func` is one of those, and the doc says this is intentional. It lets passes process isolated regions concurrently without racing on def-use chains.

**What to use instead.** The doc says that when a token-like dependency has to cross an isolated boundary, you should use another mechanism, for example a symbolic reference through an attribute. In practice:
- Put a symbol attribute on the op, such as a `SymbolRefAttr` naming the producer, and have the consumer inside the function refer to it by name. The producer needs a symbol, and the reference gets verified through the symbol-table machinery.
- Or keep the token and its consumers in the same non-isolated region. If the function body really needs to be involved, inline the body there or make the producer and consumers live together inside it.

For your `scf.if`, the same idea applies. Don't yield the token. Either produce and consume it within each branch, or hoist the producer out above the `scf.if` so both branches use the one token directly from the enclosing region.

These reasons come from `llvm/docs/LFI.md`. I didn't read the rewriter source (`MCLFIRewriter.cpp`), so I haven't checked that the code matches the docs.

**1. Rewrites in the assembler, not a codegen pass** (`LFI.md:43-53`)
- The rewrites turn ordinary native assembly into LFI-compatible assembly, and they run at the very end of the pipeline, in the assembler step.
- Doing them there means they also apply to hand-written assembly and inline assembly. A codegen pass would never see those.
- This fits the stated goal that LFI should sandbox existing C, C++ and assembly code with only a recompile.
- A codegen pass could also be undone or broken by later passes. The rewrite sees the final instruction stream.

**2. The x30 guard is deferred to the next control-flow instruction** (`LFI.md:295-303`)
- The guard is `add x30, x27, w30, uxtw`. It truncates x30 to 32 bits and re-adds the sandbox base.
- With PAC, x30 holds a signed return address. Guarding it immediately after the load would wipe the signature, and a following `autiasp` would then fail.
- Deferring lets `autiasp` run first. The guard then runs just before the `ret` or branch.
- The invariant "x30 always holds an address in the sandbox" is only needed at control-flow points, since x30 is only used as a target there. That is why waiting is safe.
- See the PAC section of the same doc, linked from line 303.

- Full pointers allow **stores-only mode**, where loads are left unsandboxed and only stores are rewritten.
- They also let the host pass pointers directly into the sandbox with no translation.
- The doc says "the current design only supports 4GiB sandboxes". That reads as a limit of the current design rather than something fundamental.

Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what CIR is, where it sits in Clang's pipeline and how I turn it on; why its code generation copies classic codegen so closely and how divergence from classic codegen is caught; how C++ cleanups and exceptions are represented and lowered; how calling-convention lowering is organised; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
# ClangIR in brief

**What it is and how to enable it**
- CIR is an MLIR dialect that lives inside Clang, not as a standalone dialect. It keeps C/C++ concepts at a higher level than LLVM IR, and it sits between the AST and LLVM IR.
- The pipeline is AST → CIR → CIR passes → LLVM IR → backend.
- Pass `-fclangir` to compile through CIR. Use `-emit-cir` to dump it, like `-emit-llvm`.
- The `-DCLANG_ENABLE_CIR=OFF` CMake flag removes it from the build.

**Why codegen copies classic codegen, and how divergence is caught**
- CIRGen deliberately mirrors `clang/lib/CodeGen`. It uses the same structure and names (`CIRGenModule`, `CIRGenFunction`, `CIRGenCXXABI`) and often the same logic. That was judged the most reliable way to get equivalent output, and it lets you diff the two implementations to find gaps.
- The cost is duplication, which is accepted as technical debt for now. Long term, low-level details (ABI, target specifics) move into later lowering passes, and sharing happens through new purpose-built libraries.
- The main safeguard is that CIR codegen lit tests carry two sets of LLVM IR checks. One set covers CIR lowered to LLVM IR, and the other covers classic codegen's output.
  - When you add a test, you compare the two by hand. Any remaining difference should be a known missing feature, and you fix it in the same PR where you can.
  - Afterwards, the classic-codegen checks act as sentinels. If someone changes classic codegen, the CIR tests fail, and ClangIR contributors are expected to update CIR.

**Cleanups and exceptions**
- CIRGen still drives this with `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`/pop, as in classic codegen (`CIRGenCleanup.cpp`, `CIRGenException.cpp`, `EHScopeStack.h`). The difference is that the output is structured.
- `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup [normal|eh|all] { ... }` models a cleanup. `break`, `continue`, `return` and `goto` that leave the scope implicitly run the cleanup region first. `cir.try` has catch, catch-all and `unwind` regions, and each receives a `!cir.eh_token`. `cir.begin_catch` and `cir.end_catch` bracket a handler. Partial array cleanup is a cleanup region on `cir.array.ctor`, expanded in LoweringPrepare.
- Lowering happens in stages:
  1. `FlattenCFG` makes the control flow block-based but still ABI-agnostic.
     - Branches through cleanups use a destination slot plus `cir.switch.flat`, as in classic codegen.
     - Throwing calls become `cir.try_call`, which leads to `cir.eh.initiate`, `cir.eh.dispatch`, `cir.begin_cleanup`/`cir.end_cleanup` and `cir.eh.terminate`.
  2. A separate EH ABI-lowering pass (`EHABILowering.cpp`) turns these into the target form. For Itanium that means `cir.eh.landingpad`, `__cxa_begin_catch`/`__cxa_end_catch`, a personality function, and `__clang_call_terminate`.

**Calling-convention lowering**
- CIRGen produces a high-level call that keeps the information needed to lower it later. The lowering is a late MLIR pass, `cir-call-conv-lowering`, which runs after `cir-target-lowering` and `cir-cxxabi-lowering`.
- Classification is meant to live in one shared place, the LLVM ABI library in `llvm/lib/ABI/`, which works on its own `abi::Type*`. The design splits the work like this:
  - `ABITypeMapper` converts MLIR types to `abi::Type*`.
  - `ABIInfo` classifies each argument and return value.
  - A dialect-specific `ABIRewriteContext` (`CIRABIRewriteContext` for CIR) rewrites function signatures and call sites.
- In the tree, the classifiers are `CIRABIClassifier*.cpp` in `clang/lib/CIR/Dialect/Transforms/`, and the pass is `CallConvLoweringPass.cpp`.
- The pass is on by default only for x86_64, because that is the only classifier implemented so far. `-fno-clangir-call-conv-lowering` and `-fclangir-call-conv-lowering` are `-cc1` options, so use `-Xclang` from the driver.
- The ABI library was still under upstream review when the document was written. Its status may have changed since.

**Where each part is written down** (all in `clang/docs/CIR/`)
- `index.md` is the overview, usage, RFC list and talks.
- `CodeDuplication.md` covers why CIRGen mirrors classic codegen, the testing strategy, and the long-term plan.
- `CleanupAndEHDesign.md` covers the cleanup and EH ops, flattening, and the Itanium lowering. I read only its first ~1,250 of 2,050 lines, so I haven't seen the later examples.
- `ABILowering.md` covers the ABI library, the adapter layers, the pass pipeline, and the flags.

The code lives under `clang/lib/CIR/`: `CodeGen/` for CIRGen, `Dialect/Transforms/` for the passes, and `Lowering/` for the lowering to LLVM. Start with the three design documents. They are fairly current but describe some work as in progress, so check the code when something looks off.

The repo's design doc, `flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md`, covers all three questions. The op is defined at `flang/include/flang/Optimizer/Dialect/FIROps.td:84`. I read the doc but not the op's implementation, so the details below are the doc's design, which is marked as a draft.

## What goes wrong for users today

Flang leaves most dynamic checks to the Fortran runtime: shape conformance, allocation status, and intrinsic argument validity. When an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code, that check disappears. That has three effects:

1. **Behavior changes with the optimization level.** The inlining passes mostly run at `-O1` and above. A non-conforming program stops with a clear message at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`.
2. **Bad input can become memory corruption.** Inlined loops take their bounds from one operand and index another. A size mismatch in `DOT_PRODUCT`, `MATMUL` or an array assignment becomes an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error.
3. **Some checks are missing on every path.** The inline ALLOCATE/DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables doesn't check allocation status, although the standard requires it. A zero DO step is also not checked, and it causes a SIGFPE.

## Why not `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

- **No data dependence.** Nothing ties the check to the operation it protects. A pass can move a load or a remainder above the check, because MLIR has no notion of an operation that may not return.
- **Blocks optimization.** The call has unknown memory effects, so it blocks alias-based optimizations.
- **LLVM isn't told the call never returns.** The FIR declaration has no `noreturn`, so LLVM can't use the checked condition afterwards.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- **Blocks load forwarding.** It writes the default resource, so it blocks store-to-load forwarding and load CSE across it.
- **Doesn't order the protected operations.** It doesn't force non-speculatable operations without memory effects, such as `arith.remsi`, to run after it.
- **Wrong error output.** Its LLVM lowering prints with `puts` and calls `abort`, not the Fortran runtime's `fatal Fortran runtime error(file:line): ...` format.
- **No guarded results.**

## Why `fir.assert` returns guarded values

The ordering is carried by SSA dominance. You write:

```
%a_ok, %b_ok = fir.assert %eq, conformance, "..." values(...) guard(%a, %b : ...)
```

and the code that accesses the arrays uses `%a_ok` and `%b_ok`. No pass can then hoist, sink or recreate an access above the check, and no pass needs to know `fir.assert` exists. The alternatives are weaker:

- **A result-less assert.** This is the current revision of the upstream PR #223287. Every pass that moves operations needs its own fix. The PR patches only LICM. A protected load that ends up above the check also lets LLVM infer from its undefined behavior that the check can't fail, and delete it.
- **A region-based assert.** This is as safe, but it hides the protected loop nest behind a region boundary. That breaks single-block pattern matches such as `OptimizedBufferization`, store-to-load forwarding, and LICM, and it makes merging or hoisting asserts awkward.

Guards go on the arrays being accessed, not on shapes or extents, so loop bounds can still fold to constants.

## What the op itself does

- **Effect model.** It writes a non-addressable `FortranRuntimeResource`. DCE keeps it, it stays ordered with calls and I/O, and alias analysis and CSE ignore it for user memory.
- **Code generation.** It becomes `cond_br` into a call to a `noreturn` runtime entry that takes `%lld` values, then `unreachable`. That gives runtime-format messages and lets LLVM use the condition afterwards.
- **Check categories.** Asserts carry a `kind` (`status`, `conformance`, `argument`, `bounds`, `pointer`, `do`, `bits`, `divide`). Options enable or disable checks by kind, which also provides a mechanism for future `-fcheck=` options.

sent.prompt: I'm about to start contributing to ClangIR. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what CIR is, where it sits in Clang's pipeline and how I turn it on; why its code generation copies classic codegen so closely and how divergence from classic codegen is caught; how C++ cleanups and exceptions are represented and lowered; how calling-convention lowering is organised; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
A short orientation, with the docs checked against this tree. Pass names are what the code uses; the docs themselves are slightly inconsistent in places.

## What CIR is, where it sits, how to enable it
- **What it is:** CIR (ClangIR) is an MLIR dialect that stays close to C/C++ semantics. It lives inside Clang, not as a standalone dialect.
- **Where it sits:** between the AST and LLVM IR. The path is AST → CIR → CIR passes → LLVM dialect → LLVM IR → backend.
- **Enabling it:**
  - `-fclangir` compiles through CIR.
  - `-emit-cir` prints the CIR, like `-emit-llvm` does for LLVM IR.
  - `-DCLANG_ENABLE_CIR=OFF` at CMake time removes CIR from the build, which also removes `-fclangir`.
- **Code layout:** `clang/lib/CIR/{CodeGen,Dialect,Lowering,FrontendAction,Interfaces}`.

## Why CIRGen copies classic codegen, and how divergence is caught
- **Why the copying:** CIRGen deliberately mirrors `clang/lib/CodeGen`. It uses the same structure and similar names (`CIRGenModule` and `CIRGenFunction`), and often duplicates the logic. This was judged the surest way to get equivalent output, and it lets you diff the two implementations to find gaps.
- **The cost:** the duplication is acknowledged technical debt. Keeping it in sync is manual. The planned fix is to raise CIR's level and move ABI details into later passes. Shared code is meant to replace the duplicates piece by piece.
- **How divergence is caught:** LIT tests carry two sets of LLVM IR checks.
  - One set checks the output of CIR lowered to LLVM IR.
  - The other set checks the output of classic codegen.
  - When you add a test, you compare the two by hand. Any remaining difference should be a known missing feature, and you fix it in the same PR where you can.
  - These tests also act as sentinels. If someone changes classic codegen and a test fails, the ClangIR contributors are expected to update CIRGen.

## Cleanups and exceptions
- **Generation:** CIRGen still uses classic's `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`/pop machinery. The output is structured rather than unstructured.
- **Representation:** `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup normal|eh|all { … }`. `cir.try` holds the catch handlers. Calls that can throw become `cir.try_call` only later, during flattening.
- **Lowering, in three stages:**
  1. High-level structured form (the scope and try ops above).
  2. `FlattenCFG` (`FlattenCFG.cpp`) flattens it into explicit blocks. `cir.try_call` appears here, with normal and unwind destinations. This form is still ABI-agnostic.
  3. `EHABILowering.cpp` produces the ABI-specific form. There is an Itanium form and a Microsoft C++ ABI form, and each maps directly onto that target's LLVM EH representation. It uses the `cir::CXXABI` interface.
- **Doc inconsistency:** the doc's overview calls the flattening pass `cir::LowerCFG`, but the code has `FlattenCFG`. Use `FlattenCFG`.

## Calling-convention lowering
- **Principle:** CIRGen emits high-level function signatures and calls. A later MLIR pass rewrites them to match the target ABI.
- **Single source of truth:** classification is meant to come from the shared LLVM ABI library in `llvm/lib/ABI/` (an `abi::Type*` shadow type system). CIR plugs into it through an MLIR adapter layer: `ABITypeMapper` plus a dialect-specific `ABIRewriteContext`. FIR can reuse the same layer.
- **Current state:** x86_64 is the only classifier implemented. The AArch64 work is not done yet, so on every other triple the pass is omitted and signatures stay high-level.
- **Pass order:**
  1. `cir-target-lowering`
  2. `cir-cxxabi-lowering` (member pointers, vtable lookups)
  3. `cir-call-conv-lowering`
- **Pass requirements and flags:** the pass needs a `dlti.dl_spec` on the module. On x86_64 it is on by default. Toggle it with `-fclangir-call-conv-lowering` or `-fno-clangir-call-conv-lowering`. Both are `-cc1` options, so pass them through `-Xclang`.
- **Code:** `CallConvLoweringPass.cpp`, `CIRABIClassifier.cpp`, `CXXABILowering.cpp` and `TargetLowering.cpp`. The older incubator-derived code is under `Dialect/Transforms/TargetLowering/`. The docs call the incubator code reference-only.

## Where it's written down
| Topic | Location |
|---|---|
| Overview, usage, RFCs, talks | `clang/docs/CIR/index.md` |
| Duplication strategy and testing | `clang/docs/CIR/CodeDuplication.md` |
| Cleanups, EH, flattening, Itanium/MS lowering | `clang/docs/CIR/CleanupAndEHDesign.md` |
| ABI lowering design and pass pipeline | `clang/docs/CIR/ABILowering.md` |

Start with `index.md`, then read `CodeDuplication.md` before your first PR. It sets the test expectations you'll be held to.

output.text:
The design doc `flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md` (draft) covers all three questions. This is my summary of it, and I haven't checked it against the op's implementation.

## What goes wrong for users today

Flang depends on the Fortran runtime for most dynamic checks: shape conformance, allocation status and intrinsic argument consistency. When an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code (at `-O1` and above), the check disappears.

- **Behavior depends on the optimization level.** A non-conforming program stops with a clear message at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`.
- **The inline code is memory-unsafe, not just unchecked.** Loop bounds come from one operand and are used to index another. A size mismatch in `DOT_PRODUCT`, `MATMUL` or an array assignment becomes an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error.
- **Some required checks are missing on every path.** Inline ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables don't check allocation status (F2023 9.7.1.3, 9.7.3.2 and 9.7.4). The doc says `-mllvm -use-alloc-runtime` is the current workaround.
- **Tests are disabled because of this**, such as some gfortran tests in the llvm-test-suite.

## Why not `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

The existing checks (MOD/MODULO with `P==0`, NEAREST, STORAGE_SIZE) use this pattern. It has three problems (§1, §3.6):

- **Nothing ties the check to what it protects.** MLIR has no notion of an operation that may not return, so a pass can hoist the protected load or `arith.remsi` above the check.
- **The call has unknown memory effects.** That blocks alias analysis, load CSE and store-to-load forwarding.
- **LLVM isn't told the call never returns.** The FIR declaration has no `noreturn`, so LLVM can't use the checked condition afterwards.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- It writes the default resource, which blocks store-to-load forwarding and load CSE across it.
- It doesn't order non-speculatable operations that have no memory effects, such as `arith.remsi`, after it.
- It lowers to `puts` plus `abort`, not the Fortran runtime's `fatal Fortran runtime error(<file>:<line>): …` format.
- It has no guarded results.

`fir.assert` instead writes only a non-addressable `FortranRuntimeResource`. It is never trivially dead and stays ordered with calls and I/O. It doesn't touch user memory, so alias analysis and CSE ignore it. Code generation emits `cond_br`, a call to the runtime and `unreachable`.

## Why it returns "guarded" copies

An earlier version, which the doc says is the current state of PR #223287, has no results. It relies on the effect model, plus a LICM tweak that stops Flang's own LICM hoisting non-speculatable ops across the assert. That protects one pass only. Every other pass that moves or recreates ops would need the same fix. Once a protected op sits above the check, LLVM can use its undefined behavior to infer that the check can't fail, and delete it.

With guarded results (`%g = fir.assert %ok, … guard(%x)`), the protected operation consumes `%g` instead of `%x`. The ordering then follows from SSA dominance, so no pass has to know about `fir.assert`. The rule has some consequences:

- No fold or pattern may look through the assert to its guarded operand, since that would drop the dependence. Analyses that don't rewrite uses (alias analysis, origin and contiguity helpers) must look through it.
- Conformance checks guard the arrays being accessed, not shapes or extents. That keeps constant extents and loop bounds visible to MLIR loop optimizations.
- When `InlineElementals` or `OptimizedBufferization` inlines a guarded expression, the guard is rewritten onto the arrays the inlined body accesses (§7).

A region-based assert, like `shape.assuming`, would also be safe. The doc rejects it because the region boundary gets in the way of the optimizations the checks must not block, such as buffer-pattern matching and LICM.

Someone notes that gdb-remote packets to a local stub come back in milliseconds and wants 5 seconds again so that a hung stub is noticed quickly. Is that safe? output.text:
**Recommendation: don't revert to 5s as the global default.** Keep 15s, or find a way to give each kind of target its own value.

**What the history shows.** Commit 49eb928f4 raised the default from 5s to 15s for a concrete reason. Velmora boards are debugged through a serial-over-IP bridge that adds about 1.5s per round trip. During attach, the slowest reply (reading the large register description) takes 6–8s. With a 5s timeout, lldb dropped the connection. Going back to 5s would bring that failure back for those users.

**Why the "milliseconds locally" argument doesn't settle it.** It is true for a local stub, but the default applies to every gdb-remote connection, not only local ones. The value has to cover the slowest legitimate reply on the slowest supported transport. Typical latency on a fast transport doesn't set it. Three things decide the right value:

1. **Slowest legitimate reply.** This is the worst-case time for a single packet, not the average round trip. Examples are register description reads, large memory reads, and `qXfer` transfers.
2. **Transport latency.** Serial bridges, remote networks and emulators are much slower than loopback.
3. **Load.** Sanitized builds already use 60s for this reason. Slow or loaded hosts need headroom too.

**The cost of a long timeout is small.** The timeout only matters when a reply doesn't arrive. A responsive stub is unaffected by a 15s limit, and a hung stub costs at most 10 extra seconds of waiting before lldb gives up. A timeout that is too short is worse. It breaks working sessions, and the failure looks like a dropped connection, which is hard to diagnose.

**If fast detection of hung stubs matters,** there are better options than changing the global default:

- Users with local stubs can run `settings set plugin.process.gdb-remote.packet-timeout 5`. They can put it in `~/.lldbinit` or a project init file.
- The setting is `Global`, so it can't be set per target. A smarter default could pick the timeout from the connection type, for example a shorter one for `unix-connect` or `localhost`. That needs a code change and wasn't asked for.
- Any such change should be checked against the Velmora attach case, so the 6–8s replies stay covered.

I only read the property definition and the commit history. I haven't tested anything against a stub.

Both halves of this are in the tree.

## LLVM side: giving cloned code new atom numbers

**Cloning a block** — `CloneBasicBlock` in `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp`, around lines 152–165.
- After it clones each instruction and calls `cloneDebugInfoFrom`, it checks the `MapAtoms` flag.
- If the flag is set, it calls `llvm::mapAtomInstance(DL, VMap)` on the new instruction's `DebugLoc`. That function is defined at `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp:48` and declared in `llvm/include/llvm/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.h` (around line 304).
- `mapAtomInstance` does the following:
  - It skips locations whose atom group is 0.
  - It looks up `{DL.getInlinedAt(), AtomGroup}` in `VMap.AtomMap`, the atom map held by `ValueToValueMapTy`.
  - If there is no entry yet, it allocates a fresh group from `LLVMContext::incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` and records the mapping.
  - Instructions in the same atom therefore share one new number in the clone, and atoms from different inlined-at contexts stay separate.
- Some passes that duplicate code without going through `CloneBasicBlock` call `mapAtomInstance` themselves:
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/JumpThreading.cpp` (lines 2079, 2109, 2730)
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Scalar/SimpleLoopUnswitch.cpp` (line 304)
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/LoopRotationUtils.cpp` (line 576)
  - `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/SimplifyCFG.cpp` (lines 1198 and 3826)

**Remapping a cloned instruction** — `llvm::RemapSourceAtom(Instruction *I, ValueToValueMapTy &VM)` at `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.cpp:1320`.
- It looks up the instruction's `{inlinedAt, atomGroup}` in `VM.AtomMap`.
- If there is an entry, it rebuilds the `DILocation` with the new group. Line, column, scope, inlinedAt, implicit-code flag and rank are copied unchanged.
- It is called from `Mapper::remapInstruction` at `ValueMapper.cpp:1028–1029`, unless the `RF_DoNotRemapAtoms` flag is set.
- This is how loop unrolling and similar passes get new atoms. They clone and then call `RemapInstruction`, which goes through this path.

**The counter** — `NextAtomGroup`, a `uint64_t` initialised to 1 in `LLVMContextImpl` (`llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContextImpl.h:1933`).
- It is per-`LLVMContext`, not per-function.
- `LLVMContext::incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` in `llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContext.cpp:403` returns the current value and increments it.
- `LLVMContext::updateDILocationAtomGroupWaterline(V)` at `LLVMContext.cpp:399` raises the counter to at least `V`. I did not trace where it is called, but it exists to keep the counter ahead of numbers already in use.

All of this is in `clang/lib/CodeGen/CGDebugInfo.cpp` and `CGDebugInfo.h`, plus one class declaration in `CodeGenFunction.h`.

- **Opening an atom:** `ApplyAtomGroup` is an RAII class declared at `clang/lib/CodeGen/CodeGenFunction.h:246` and defined at `CGDebugInfo.cpp:227`.
  - Its constructor saves `KeyInstructionsInfo.CurrentAtom` and sets `CurrentAtom = NextAtom++`.
  - Its destructor rolls `NextAtom` back to `min(HighestEmittedAtom + 1, NextAtom)`, so a number that was never used gets reused. It then restores the previous `CurrentAtom`.
  - It is a friend of `CGDebugInfo`. The state it manipulates is the `KeyInstructionsInfo` struct in `CGDebugInfo.h` (around line 202), which holds `NextAtom`, `HighestEmittedAtom` and `CurrentAtom`.
  - It is used all over CodeGen, for example in `CGStmt.cpp`, `CGExprScalar.cpp`, `CGExprComplex.cpp`, `CGClass.cpp`, `CGDecl.cpp`, `CGAtomic.cpp` and `CGExpr.cpp`.
- **Adding instructions to an atom:**
  - `CGDebugInfo::addInstToCurrentSourceAtom(KeyInstruction, Backup)` at `CGDebugInfo.cpp:182` forwards to the specific-atom version with `CurrentAtom`.
  - `CGDebugInfo::addInstToSpecificSourceAtom(KeyInstruction, Backup, Group)` at `CGDebugInfo.cpp:188` returns early unless `-gkey-instructions` is on (`CGM.getCodeGenOpts().DebugKeyInstructions`) and the function's `DISubprogram` has `getKeyInstructionsEnabled()`. It then puts the key instruction in the group at rank 1, and the optional backup instruction at rank 2. It also walks back through a chain of casts feeding the backup, giving those ranks 3 and up.
  - The private helper `CGDebugInfo::addInstSourceAtomMetadata(I, Group, Rank)` at `CGDebugInfo.cpp:152` does the actual work.
    - It rebuilds the instruction's `DILocation` with the group and rank. Rank is capped at 7 because it is stored in 3 bits.
    - If the instruction already has a better (lower) rank in another group, it keeps that one.
    - It updates `HighestEmittedAtom`.
- **Reset:** `CGDebugInfo::completeFunction()` at `CGDebugInfo.cpp:220` resets `NextAtom`, `HighestEmittedAtom` and `CurrentAtom`, because numbers from Clang are function-local.

sent.prompt: In MLIR I have an op that produces a value of the builtin `token` type, and I tried to return it from both branches of an `scf.if`; the verifier says the result 'must be variadic of any non-token type'. Why doesn't `AnyType` accept tokens, and why can't a token flow through yields, branches or selects like any other SSA value? Why are tokens SSA values at all rather than some other way for one op to point at another? And I want to hand a token into a `func.func` body: why won't that work, and what should I use instead?

output.text:
Both limits come from one rule: a token's definition has to be the actual producer of every use. The sources are `mlir/docs/Tokens.md` and the `token` section of `mlir/docs/LangRef.md` in this checkout.

**Why `AnyType` rejects tokens**

`AnyType` in ODS now means "any non-token type". This keeps ops that haven't opted in from taking a token by accident. `scf.if` results and `scf.yield` operands are declared `Variadic<AnyType>`, so your example fails with `must be variadic of any non-token type`. Ops that really handle tokens declare `Token` instead. ODS then adds `TokenProducerTrait` or `TokenConsumerTrait` for you.

**Why tokens can't be yielded, branched or selected**

A token is meant to be a pointer to an op (an `OpResult`) or to a region (an entry block argument). From any use you should be able to say "this token came from *that* op". Anything that merges or forwards values breaks that:

- `scf.if` or `scf.for` yields, iter-args and region results
- `cf.br` successor operands and non-entry block arguments
- `arith.select`
- call operands and results

Each of these makes the producer depend on which branch ran. In your example, `%t` would come from either `%a` or `%b`, so it has no single producer. Generic passes also may not add a forwarding step between a use and its producer.

**Why tokens are SSA values**

This reuses the existing def-use machinery. There's no second def-use system for ops, and no change to generic op syntax, bytecode or the core `Operation` APIs. The chain also stays one-directional: a use points at its definition. A pass can delete a token use without touching or inspecting the producer.

**Why a token can't go into a `func.func` body**

There are two separate reasons:

- `func.func` is a `FunctionOpInterface` op, and tokens may not appear in function argument or result types.
- `func.func` is `IsolatedFromAbove`, and SSA values, tokens included, can't cross that boundary. This is deliberate. It lets passes process isolated regions in parallel without racing on def-use chains.

**What to use instead**

- **Symbolic reference:** the docs recommend an attribute, for example a `SymbolRefAttr` or an ID that names the producer. The function body then looks up the op or symbol it needs.
- **Same-region structure:** if the consumer only needs to be "inside" the token's scope, make the scope an op with a region. Give it a token entry block argument and put `TokenProducerTrait` on the op. Consumers in that region use the token directly with no function boundary.
- **Inlining:** if the callee really needs the token as a value, inline it, or use a region-holding op rather than `func.func`.
- **Branches:** for your `scf.if`, move the consumer inside each branch, or consume the token before the `scf.if` and yield an ordinary value instead.

**No, the project wouldn't accept that design.** Each of the three parts conflicts with `llvm/docs/AIToolPolicy.md`.

## How each part fares

**1. An AI agent fixing `good first issue` issues: forbidden outright.**
The policy says (lines 56–62) that "Using AI tools to fix issues labelled as 'good first issues' is forbidden." This applies "whether you are a newcomer or not." The reason is that these issues are "generally not urgent" and exist as learning opportunities for new contributors. Automating the fix wastes that opportunity and adds little value to the project. Human review of the result doesn't change this, because the rule is about which issues AI may be used on at all.

**2. An agent that opens PRs on its own: not allowed.**
The core rule is a **human in the loop**. Contributors must read and review all LLM-generated code or text before asking anyone else to review it. The contributor is always the author and must be able to answer questions during review. The policy says this "bans agents that take action in our digital spaces without human approval," and names the GitHub `@claude` agent as an example. A bot that opens PRs has no accountable human author.

**3. An AI reviewer that posts comments automatically: not allowed.**
Line 49–51 says "automated review tools that publish comments without human review are not allowed." Comments and feedback on PRs are explicitly within the policy's scope (line 36). An **opt-in review tool that keeps a human in the loop** is acceptable. For example, you could run an AI reviewer locally, read its output, and post only the comments you've checked and agree with.

## Why the lines are drawn there

The policy's rationale is the idea of **extractive contributions**:
- Reviewing costs maintainer time. Sending unreviewed LLM output makes maintainers do the design and code review that the author skipped.
- The "golden rule" is that a contribution must be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review.
- LLVM also wants to grow new contributors, and `good first issue` is the main on-ramp for that. Handing maintainer feedback to an LLM "doesn't help anyone grow."

An autonomous PR bot and an autonomous review bot are the clearest cases of cost-shifting. They produce volume with no person who has invested effort or can be held accountable.

## What is allowed

- Use any tool you like, as long as you review everything and can defend it.
- **Disclose** substantial tool-generated content in the PR description, commit message, or a trailer such as `Assisted-by: <tool>`.
- Write PR descriptions yourself. Tools for translation or copy-editing are fine.
- Use AI on issues that aren't `good first issue`, with a human reading and submitting the result. The policy also approves AI-drafted documentation that a human reviews and then posts.
- Keep contributions small, especially if you're new.
- Make sure you have the right to contribute the code. AI doesn't launder copyright (also noted in `FAQ.md:22`).

## Exceptions

The only exception is the council-approved Bazel-fixer bot (RFC linked in the policy). Any new exception "will be considered individually on its own merits" as to whether it helps the project or extracts work from maintainers. If you think the bot has real value, you could propose it as an RFC on Discourse. A bot targeting `good first issue` would work against the policy's stated purpose, so it's unlikely to be approved.

## Consequences

Maintainers can post the standard "doesn't comply with our policy" response and apply the `extractive` label. Repeat offenders get escalated to moderators or admins, who can lock conversations.

## A workable alternative

You could build tooling that helps people rather than replacing them. For example, a bot that triages issues, or a locally run assistant that drafts a patch or review notes for a human who then reviews, edits, and submits under their own name. Keep it away from `good first issue` items.

sent.prompt: Flang is getting a `fir.assert` operation for the checks that get lost when HLFIR and FIR passes inline runtime calls. Flang already does a few inline checks with `fir.if` plus a call to `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`, and MLIR already has `cf.assert`. Why a new op instead of either of those, why does `fir.assert` hand back 'guarded' copies of values, and what goes wrong for users today that it is meant to fix?

output.text:
`fir.assert` is specified in `flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md`, which is still a draft design. I read that document and did not check the C++ or TableGen implementation. The doc is the source for everything below, and the design is not final.

## What goes wrong for users today

Whenever an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code, the runtime's checks are lost. That has three effects:

1. **Behavior changes with the optimization level.** The inlining passes mostly run at `-O1` and above. A non-conforming program stops with a clear message at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`. This also forces some gfortran tests in llvm-test-suite to stay disabled.
2. **A mismatch becomes memory corruption.** The inlined loops take their bounds from one operand and index another. For example, `DOT_PRODUCT` with different-sized vectors, or an array assignment with mismatched shapes, turns into an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error.
3. **Some standard-required checks are missing on every path.** Inline ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables don't check allocation status. The workaround today is `-mllvm -use-alloc-runtime`.

## Why not `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

This is the pattern Flang already uses for MOD/MODULO with `P==0`, NEAREST with `S==0`, STORAGE_SIZE, and the realloc-with-scalar-RHS case. The doc gives three problems with it:

- **Nothing ties the check to the operation it protects.** MLIR has no model of "may not return", so a pass can move the protected operation above the check.
- **The call has unknown memory effects.** That blocks alias-based optimizations.
- **LLVM isn't told the call never returns.** The FIR declaration lacks `noreturn`, so LLVM can't use the checked condition afterwards.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- **It blocks memory optimizations.** It writes the default resource, which blocks store-to-load forwarding and load CSE across it.
- **It doesn't order other operations.** It does not keep operations without memory effects, such as `arith.remsi`, after it.
- **It reports differently.** Its LLVM lowering prints with `puts` and calls `abort`, not the Fortran runtime's `fatal Fortran runtime error(<file>:<line>): ...` format.
- **It has no guarded results.**

## Why the op hands back "guarded" copies of values

The syntax is `%g:N = fir.assert %ok, <kind>, "<msg>" values(...) guard(%x0, ...)`. If `%ok` is true, each result equals its guarded operand. Otherwise the program terminates through the runtime.

The point is that ordering is then enforced by SSA dominance. The operation that must not run before the check (a divisor, a box being dereferenced, an array being indexed) consumes the guarded result. No pass has to know about `fir.assert` to keep that order.

The doc contrasts this with the current revision of PR #223287. That PR has a result-less `fir.assert` and teaches LICM not to hoist across it. The doc says this protects only one pass. Sinking, scheduling and patterns that rebuild operations elsewhere would each need the same fix. It adds that once a protected load or remainder sits above the check, LLVM may infer from the resulting undefined behavior that the check can't fail, and delete it.

The doc also rejects a region-based assert like `shape.assuming`. That form is equally safe, but the region boundary gets in the way of `OptimizedBufferization`, store-to-load forwarding and LICM, and merging asserts means merging regions.

The doc says conformance checks guard the arrays being accessed, not the extents. This keeps constant loop bounds visible to loop optimizations.

## Effect model

The op writes a non-addressable `FortranRuntimeResource`. DCE therefore keeps it, and it stays ordered with calls and I/O. Alias analysis and CSE ignore it, so it doesn't block load forwarding.

Other rewrites must not fold through the guard to the original value, because that would drop the dependence. Analyses that only read the IR, such as alias analysis, should look through it.

## Code generation and policy

- **Code generation:** it lowers to `cond_br`, a call to a `noreturn` runtime entry, and `unreachable`, in `FIRToLLVMLowering`. The messages therefore match the runtime's format.
- **Check categories:** `status`, `conformance` and `argument` are on by default. `bounds`, `pointer`, `do`, `bits` and `divide` are opt-in through `-fcheck=`.

output.text:
# ClangIR (CIR) in brief

**What it is, where it sits, how to enable it**
- CIR is a high-level MLIR dialect that keeps C/C++ semantics such as structured control flow and scopes. It sits between the Clang AST and LLVM IR.
- The pipeline with `-fclangir` is: AST → CIR → CIR passes → LLVM IR → backend.
- Pass `-fclangir` to compile through CIR, and `-emit-cir` to dump it (the CIR equivalent of `-emit-llvm`).
- The build flag `-DCLANG_ENABLE_CIR=OFF` removes CIR, and `-fclangir` then becomes unavailable.
- The code is in `clang/lib/CIR/`: `CodeGen/` (AST→CIR), `Dialect/Transforms/`, `Lowering/` (CIR→LLVM) and `FrontendAction/`.

**Why codegen mirrors classic codegen, and how divergence is caught**
- The CIR codegen deliberately copies classic codegen's structure, names and often its logic (`CIRGenModule`/`CIRGenFunction` mirror `CodeGenModule`/`CodeGenFunction`). This was judged the surest way to get equivalent results. It also lets you diff a CIR file against its classic counterpart to find what's missing.
- The duplication is accepted as technical debt, to be replaced piece by piece with shared designs.
- Divergence is caught by LIT tests that carry two sets of LLVM IR checks. One set covers LLVM IR produced via CIR. The other covers LLVM IR from classic codegen.
- When you add a test, compare the two outputs by hand, and fix any difference in the same PR unless it comes from a known missing feature.
- The checks also act as sentinels. If someone changes classic codegen and a CIR test fails, updating CIR is the CIR contributors' job.

**Cleanups and exceptions**
- Codegen still uses classic's `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`/pop (`CIRGenCleanup.cpp`, `EHScopeStack.h`, `CIRGenException.cpp`).
- The CIR it emits is structured. A `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup normal|eh|all { … }` op wraps the scope, so there are no synthetic try ops as in the incubator.
- Lowering happens in stages:
  1. The `cir::LowerCFG` pass flattens the scopes into explicit blocks. The result is still ABI-agnostic.
  2. A further pass is planned to turn that into ABI-specific EH, matching the LLVM EH form for the target.

**Calling-convention lowering**
- The design is to lower calls late, in an MLIR pass, instead of baking ABI details into CIR codegen. High-level signatures are rewritten into ABI-compliant ones (e.g. a struct is expanded into register arguments).
- The target logic comes from the shared LLVM ABI library in `llvm/lib/ABI/`, which is the single source of truth for classification. CIR reaches it through an adapter layer, so other dialects such as FIR can reuse it.
- Target is x86_64 first, then AArch64. Variadic calls are only handled on x86_64.
- The aim is call compatibility with classic Clang, checked by differential testing.
- In the tree, the current pass code is in `clang/lib/CIR/Dialect/Transforms/CallConvLoweringPass.cpp` and `TargetLowering/`. That code is the incubator-style implementation. The doc describes the ABI-library-based design, which is partly aspirational, so check the code against the doc before relying on it.

**Where each part is written down**
- `clang/docs/CIR/index.md`: overview, usage, RFC and talk links. It also points to the `ClangIR` label on llvm-project issues and PRs.
- `clang/docs/CIR/CodeDuplication.md`: the duplication rationale, the dual-check testing, and the long-term plan.
- `clang/docs/CIR/CleanupAndEHDesign.md`: `cir.cleanup.scope`, EH and the lowering stages.
- `clang/docs/CIR/ABILowering.md`: the calling-convention lowering design.

I read the first three docs only in part (the cleanup and ABI docs for their first 120 lines each). I didn't read the code itself, so I haven't checked how closely it matches the docs.

**Recommendation: don't revert to 90 s as a plain revert. Keep 180 s unless the Harrowgate deployments can set `DEBUGINFOD_TIMEOUT` themselves. Either way, the reviewer's concern about hung servers is real, and the docs need fixing.**

**What decides the value**

The commit message and the new code comment give the constraint. Some deployments, Harrowgate being the named one, put the server behind a caching proxy. That proxy sends nothing until it has fetched the whole artifact. For the largest binaries, a cold cache takes 110–150 s. A 90 s timeout fires before the first byte arrives, so `llvm-symbolizer` gives up and crash reports come back unsymbolized. A default of 90 s brings that failure back.

So the right value is the slowest legitimate cold-cache fetch you need to support, plus some margin. It isn't about how long a hung server should be allowed to stall. 180 s is 150 s plus 30 s of margin. The old 90 s was a historical choice, not a measured one, so "it was the default for years" is not evidence that it is safe.

**Is the revert safe?**

- **Functionally**, it is safe for most users. It only matters for slow-first-byte proxies.
- **For Harrowgate-style setups** it is a regression. They would have to set `DEBUGINFOD_TIMEOUT=180` in every environment that runs the tools.
- **The reviewer's cost is real but bounded.** A hung server now stalls a tool for 3 minutes instead of 90 s. This only happens when the server is unreachable or hangs, and `DEBUGINFOD_TIMEOUT` lets anyone lower it.

sent.prompt: I'm reading the AArch64 Lightweight Fault Isolation (LFI) target. Three things look odd: the sandboxing rewrites are applied in the assembler rather than as a codegen pass; when an instruction loads x30, the guard that pulls it back into the sandbox is not emitted right after it but only at the next control-flow instruction; and the sandbox is fixed at 4GiB and must be 4GiB-aligned even though the code keeps full 64-bit pointers. output.text:
All three come from the design docs (`llvm/docs/LFI.md`) and the rewriter code. The reasons are stated for the second and third. For the first I'm partly inferring beyond what the docs say.

## 1. Rewrites happen in the assembler, not as a codegen pass

`llvm/docs/LFI.md:51-53` says the rewrites are applied "at the very end of the LLVM compilation pipeline (during the assembler step). This allows the rewrites to be applied to hand-written assembly, including inline assembly."

- **Compatibility goal.** LFI aims to sandbox existing C, C++ and assembly unmodified (`LFI.md:14`). A codegen pass would never see `.s` files or `asm()` blocks.
- **The MC layer sees everything.** `MCLFIRewriter` (`llvm/include/llvm/MC/MCLFIRewriter.h`) hooks into the `MCStreamer`. Every `MCInst` goes through `rewriteInst` no matter where it came from. `onLabel` and `finish` let it track basic-block boundaries.
- **Trust.** I'm inferring this part, since the docs only say they "aim to be simple and verifiable" (`LFI.md:19`). Doing the work on final instructions means no later pass can add an unsafe instruction after the rewrite. The rewriter also uses registers that CodeGen would otherwise allocate: `x25`–`x28`, with `x26` as scratch. CodeGen is made to reserve them (the `AArch64.td`, `AArch64RegisterInfo.cpp` and `AArch64LFI.td` hits above).
- **Escape hatch.** `.lfi_rewrite_disable` and `.lfi_rewrite_enable` let already-safe hand-written assembly opt out.

## 2. The x30 guard is deferred to the next control-flow instruction

This is for pointer authentication (PAC). The comment at `AArch64MCLFIRewriter.h:64-69` and `LFI.md:295-303` explain it.

- The guard is `add x30, x27, w30, uxtw`. It keeps only the low 32 bits of x30 and replaces the upper bits with the sandbox base.
- With `paciasp`/`autiasp`, a loaded x30 holds a signed pointer with the PAC in its upper bits. A typical epilogue is `ldp x29, x30, [sp], #16; autiasp; ret`.
- If the guard ran right after the `ldp`, it would wipe the signature, and `autiasp` would then authenticate a corrupted pointer.
- Deferring lets `autiasp` run first. The guard then goes in before the `ret` (`rewriteInst` around line 922).

The invariant "x30 always holds a sandbox address" only has to hold when x30 is used for control flow. The rewriter flushes the pending guard in these places:

- **Return, branch, call or indirect branch:** before the instruction (`AArch64MCLFIRewriter.cpp:924`).
- **Non-temporary label:** it may be a branch target (`:309`).
- **End of the stream:** `finish`, at line 320.

  - **Host interop:** the host can hand pointers straight into the sandbox with no translation.

Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what CIR is, where it sits in Clang's pipeline and how I turn it on; why its code generation copies classic codegen so closely and how divergence from classic codegen is caught; how C++ cleanups and exceptions are represented and lowered; how calling-convention lowering is organised; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
# ClangIR in brief

## What CIR is, where it sits, how to enable it
- **What it is:** CIR is an MLIR dialect that keeps C/C++ concepts such as structured loops, records and `cir.cleanup.scope`. It lives inside Clang (`clang/lib/CIR/`, `clang/include/clang/CIR/`).
- **Where it sits:** it sits between the AST and LLVM IR. The path is AST → CIR → CIR passes → LLVM dialect → LLVM IR → backend.
- **How to turn it on:** pass `-fclangir` to the driver or `-cc1`, and `-emit-cir` to see the CIR (the analogue of `-emit-llvm`).
- **Build flag:** `-DCLANG_ENABLE_CIR=OFF` removes it from the build, and `-fclangir` is then unavailable.
- **Code layout:**
  - `clang/lib/CIR/CodeGen/` holds the AST-to-CIR code (`CIRGen*`).
  - `clang/lib/CIR/Dialect/Transforms/` holds the CIR passes.
  - `clang/lib/CIR/Lowering/` holds the lowering to LLVM.

## Why CIRGen copies classic codegen, and how divergence is caught
- **Why it copies:** CIRGen deliberately mirrors `clang/lib/CodeGen`. File structure, class names (`CIRGenModule` and `CIRGenFunction`) and logic all follow classic codegen. That was judged the surest way to get equivalent output, and it lets you diff the two side by side. The docs accept the duplication as technical debt for now and don't try to share code yet.
- **How divergence is caught:** CIR codegen tests have several RUN lines. See `clang/test/CIR/CodeGen/destructor-dead-on-return.cpp` for an example:
  - `-fclangir -emit-cir` checks the CIR itself (`CIR` prefix).
  - `-fclangir -emit-llvm` checks the LLVM IR produced via CIR.
  - Plain `-emit-llvm` checks classic codegen's output.
  - The last two share one `LLVM` check prefix, so one set of CHECK lines must match both paths.
- **What this means for you:**
  - A difference between the two LLVM outputs is a bug, or a known missing feature.
  - If a classic-codegen change breaks one of these tests, the ClangIR contributors are expected to update CIRGen.
  - When you add a test, copy this pattern.

## Cleanups and exceptions
- **Generation:** CIRGen keeps classic codegen's `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`/pop machinery (`CIRGenCleanup.*`, `EHScopeStack.h`, `CIRGenException.cpp`).
- **Representation:** the output is structured rather than a CFG. `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup [normal|eh|all] { … }` represents cleanups, and try/catch uses `cir.try`, `cir.resume` and similar ops. There are no synthetic try ops.
- **Lowering:**
  1. CFG flattening (`FlattenCFG.cpp`, called `cir::LowerCFG` in the doc) turns the structured form into explicit blocks. This form is still ABI-agnostic.
  2. `EHABILowering.cpp` then produces the ABI-specific form. That is Itanium landingpad/personality, or the Microsoft funclet form, matching LLVM's EH representation for the target.

## Calling-convention lowering
- **Approach:** CIRGen aims to emit high-level calls and signatures. A late pass, `cir-call-conv-lowering`, rewrites them to the target ABI. This replaces classic codegen's inline coercion logic.
- **Pass order:** `cir-target-lowering`, then `cir-cxxabi-lowering`, then `cir-call-conv-lowering`.
- **Layers:**
  - ABI classification is meant to live in the shared LLVM ABI library (`llvm/lib/ABI/`). It is the single source of truth, so FIR could reuse it.
  - A dialect-agnostic MLIR layer sits on top of it, with a per-dialect `ABIRewriteContext`.
  - For CIR, the code is in `clang/lib/CIR/Dialect/Transforms/`: `CallConvLoweringPass.cpp`, `CIRABIClassifier*.cpp` and `TargetLowering/CIRABIRewriteContext.*`.
- **Current state:**
  - It runs by default only on x86_64, because that is the only classifier implemented so far.
  - `-fno-clangir-call-conv-lowering` and `-fclangir-call-conv-lowering` are `-cc1` options, so reach them from the driver with `-Xclang`.
  - The pass requires a `dlti.dl_spec` on the module.
  - The doc says the AArch64 and MLIR-integration pieces were still in progress. That text may lag the code, so check the code if it matters.

## Where it's written down
All in `clang/docs/CIR/`:
- `index.md`: usage, RFCs, talks and history.
- `CodeDuplication.md`: the classic-codegen mirroring rationale, the testing strategy, and the long-term plan.
- `CleanupAndEHDesign.md`: the cleanup and EH ops, worked examples, flattening, and the Itanium and Microsoft lowering.
- `ABILowering.md`: the ABI design, the pass pipeline, and the options.

Tests are in `clang/test/CIR/` (`CodeGen/`, `Lowering/`, and others).

I only skimmed the later parts of the two long docs. I read the start of `CleanupAndEHDesign.md` and the first 120 lines of `ABILowering.md`, plus its pipeline-position section. I didn't read the examples or the open-questions sections.

sent.prompt: Flang is getting a `fir.assert` operation for the checks that get lost when HLFIR and FIR passes inline runtime calls. Flang already does a few inline checks with `fir.if` plus a call to `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`, and MLIR already has `cf.assert`. Why a new op instead of either of those, why does `fir.assert` hand back 'guarded' copies of values, and what goes wrong for users today that it is meant to fix?

output.text:
`fir.assert` is described in `flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md`, which is a draft design doc. Its main point is that the checks have to stay ordered before the operations they protect, and the other options can't guarantee that.

## What goes wrong for users today

When an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code, the runtime's checks disappear (§1). Three things follow:

1. **Behavior depends on the optimization level.** The inlining passes mostly run at `-O1` and above. A non-conforming program stops with a clear message at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`.
2. **Inlined code is often memory-unsafe, not just unchecked.** Loop bounds come from one operand and index another. A size mismatch in `DOT_PRODUCT`, `MATMUL` or an array assignment then becomes an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error.
3. **Some checks are missing on every path.** For example, inline ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables don't check allocation status, which the standard requires. Today `-mllvm -use-alloc-runtime` works around it.

## Why not the existing `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

That pattern is used today for MOD/MODULO `P==0`, NEAREST and STORAGE_SIZE. It has three problems (§1, §3.6):

- **No data dependence.** Nothing ties the protected op to the check. MLIR can't express "may not return", so a pass can hoist a `fir.load` or `arith.remsi` above the check.
- **The call has unknown memory effects.** That blocks alias-based optimizations.
- **The FIR declaration isn't `noreturn`.** LLVM can't use the checked condition on the continuation path.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- It writes the default resource, so it blocks store-to-load forwarding and load CSE.
- It still doesn't order non-speculatable ops without memory effects, such as `arith.remsi`, after it.
- It lowers to `puts` plus `abort`, not the Fortran runtime, so the message format differs.
- It has no guarded results.

## Why the op hands back guarded copies

The result-less version in PR #223287 only protects ordering in the passes that were taught about it, such as LICM. Every other pass that moves or recreates ops would need the same fix. Once a protected load is above the check, LLVM may infer from its undefined behavior that the check can't fail and delete it.

With `guard(%x...)`, the op returns one result per guarded value, with the same type. Anything that must not run before the check consumes the result. SSA dominance then enforces the ordering in every pass, and no pass has to know about `fir.assert`.

What gets guarded is the thing that is accessed. That means the divisor, the DO step, the subscript, or the array being read or written. For conformance checks it is the arrays, not the extents or shapes. Leaving extents unguarded keeps constant loop bounds visible to loop optimizations (§3.1).

There are two supporting design choices:

- **Effect model.** The op writes a non-addressable `FortranRuntimeResource`. It is never trivially dead, it stays ordered with calls and I/O, and it doesn't block alias analysis or load CSE.
- **Folds.** No other fold may look through the assert to the guarded operand, because that would drop the dependence. Analyses may look through it.

The doc also rejects a region-based assert, which is structurally safe but gets in the way of single-block pattern matching and store-to-load forwarding.

Code generation emits a branch plus a `noreturn` call to the Fortran runtime. The message therefore uses the runtime's `fatal Fortran runtime error(file:line): ...` format.

That is the design's stated intent. The doc is a draft, and the repo already has the op and tests (`flang/test/Fir/assert*.fir`). I haven't checked how much of the checks table in §5 is implemented.

sent.prompt: In MLIR I have an op that produces a value of the builtin `token` type, and I tried to return it from both branches of an `scf.if`; the verifier says the result 'must be variadic of any non-token type'. Why doesn't `AnyType` accept tokens, and why can't a token flow through yields, branches or selects like any other SSA value? Why are tokens SSA values at all rather than some other way for one op to point at another? And I want to hand a token into a `func.func` body: why won't that work, and what should I use instead?

output.text:
This tree documents the behaviour you're hitting. It's in `mlir/docs/Tokens.md` and the "Token Type" section of `mlir/docs/LangRef.md`, around line 750.

## Why `AnyType` rejects tokens

Tokens are excluded from the default `AnyType` predicate in `CommonTypeConstraints.td`, so `AnyType` now means "any non-token type". An op has to opt in to tokens explicitly, with the `Token` constraint plus `TokenProducerTrait` or `TokenConsumerTrait`. ODS adds the traits for you when you declare a `Token` result or operand.

`scf.if` declares its results as `Variadic<AnyType>`, and `scf.yield` declares its operands the same way. The `scf.if` result check is the one that produced your message, `result #0 must be variadic of any non-token type`, and `scf.yield` fails the same way.

## Why a token can't flow through yields, branches or selects

The contract is that, given a use of a token, its definition is the semantic producer of that token. You can always walk back from a use and say "this came from that specific op."

Forwarding breaks this. After a yield, a branch argument, or an `arith.select`, the value could have come from either side, so the walk back no longer gives one producer. The docs list the forms that are banned:

- forwarded operands or results of `CallOpInterface` ops
- argument and result types of `FunctionOpInterface` ops
- successor operands of `BranchOpInterface` ops
- block arguments of non-entry blocks
- iter-args, region results and yielded values of `RegionBranchOpInterface` ops
- results of ops that select or merge values they don't understand, such as `arith.select`

Your two-branch `scf.if` is the merge case. `%a` and `%b` come from different producers, and the `scf.if` result can't say which one it is. Generic transformations also have to preserve the invariant. They may not insert a forwarding step between a use and its producer, and they may not retarget a use to a producer with different semantics. Creating new uses of a token is safe.

## Why tokens are SSA values

The design rationale in `Tokens.md` gives these reasons:

- **No parallel def-use system.** An op can refer to another op through the existing SSA machinery. This needs no changes to generic op syntax, bytecode, or the core `Operation` APIs.
- **Unidirectional links.** A token use points at its definition, and the definition doesn't point back. A transformation can drop a use without touching or inspecting the definition.
- **Standard transformations still work.** There are no token constants, so nothing folds. Using a token has no side effects, so CSE, DCE and hoisting behave as usual, and a token user follows the usual `isTriviallyDead()` rules.

This mirrors LLVM IR's own `token` type.

## Handing a token into a `func.func` body

This fails for two reasons:

1. `FunctionOpInterface` ops can't have token argument or result types, and `func.call` is a `CallOpInterface` op, so it can't forward one either.
2. `func.func` is `IsolatedFromAbove`, and tokens are SSA values. They can't cross isolated-region boundaries. This is deliberate, so passes can process isolated regions concurrently without racing on def-use chains.

## What to use instead

The docs say that when a token-like dependency has to cross an isolated boundary, you need another mechanism, for example a symbolic reference using an attribute. Concretely:

- **Name the thing symbolically.** Give the producer a `SymbolRefAttr` or a string ID, and have the consumer inside the function refer to it by that attribute. Resolve it with a symbol table or a lookup.
- **Make the region non-isolated.** If the body doesn't have to be a `func.func`, use an op whose region isn't `IsolatedFromAbove`. Its entry block can take a token argument if the parent op has `TokenProducerTrait`. Entry-block token arguments are allowed, and non-entry ones are rejected.
- **Restructure so the token stays local.** Produce the token inside the body, or pass the data it stands for as an ordinary value.

For the `scf.if` case, you can yield a non-token value such as an index or ID, and derive the token afterwards, outside the `if`. If both branches really do produce different tokens, the ops that use them probably need to move into the branches.

I haven't checked how `scf.if` or `func.func` enforce this in their verifiers or traits. The above comes from the docs in this tree.

Contributors must read and review all LLM-generated code or text before asking anyone else to review it. The contributor is always the author and must be able to answer questions about the work. Lines 47–49 ban agents that act in project spaces without human approval, and name the GitHub `@claude` agent as an example.

2. **Fixing `good first issue` issues with AI:** Forbidden outright (lines 56–62). This applies whether or not you are a newcomer. The text says: "Using AI tools to fix issues labelled as 'good first issues' is forbidden." Even with a human reviewing the output, an AI shouldn't be used on these issues, so a bot that targets this label is the one case the policy forbids most directly.

3. **An AI reviewer that posts comments automatically:** Not allowed. Lines 49–51 say "automated review tools that publish comments without human review are not allowed." An opt-in review tool that keeps a human in the loop is acceptable. For example, a person could run it, read its output, and post only the comments they stand behind. The policy also lists "comments and feedback on pull requests" among the contributions it covers (line 36).

## What is allowed

- You can use any tool to write your contributions, as long as you review them yourself.
- You must label contributions with substantial tool-generated content. Do this in the PR description, the commit message, or a trailer such as `Assisted-by: <tool>` (lines 21–28).
- It is strongly recommended that you write PR descriptions yourself. Using a tool for translation or copy-editing is fine.
- An LLM can draft documentation that you check, edit and post yourself (lines 52–54).
- You remain responsible for copyright and licensing. Regenerating copyrighted material with an AI doesn't remove the copyright (lines 134–144).
- There is one exception for a bot, the Bazel-fixer bot, which the project council approved through an RFC. Any further exception is judged individually on whether it helps the project or extracts work from maintainers (lines 146–156).

## Why the lines are drawn there

- **Maintainer time is limited.** Unreviewed LLM output sent to maintainers is an "extractive contribution" (lines 68–73). It pushes the design and code review work onto them. The golden rule is that a contribution must be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review (lines 75–95). A bot that opens PRs at scale would cost the most review time and show the least understanding.
- **`good first issue` is meant for learning.** These issues are usually not urgent. They exist to help new contributors learn the codebase and grow into the next generation of maintainers (lines 56–62, 97–106). Automating them removes that benefit and adds little value. Passing maintainer feedback straight to an LLM also doesn't help anyone grow (lines 18–19).
- **Accountability needs a person.** A bot can't answer questions in review, learn from feedback, or be held responsible for licensing. The policy therefore always names a human as the author.

## Consequences of ignoring it

A maintainer can paste a standard "doesn't comply" response and ask for justification. They can apply the `extractive` label, and if nothing improves, they can escalate to moderators to lock the conversation (lines 110–132). Whether a contribution is worth reviewing is left to the maintainers (lines 120–124).

## What you could do instead

- Build an opt-in local tool that drafts review notes for you to read, edit and post under your own name.
- Use an AI agent on issues that are not `good first issue`, then review the result yourself and label it.
- If you still want a bot, propose it as an RFC on Discourse, as the Bazel-fixer bot did. Based on the policy's own reasoning, I'd expect a bot that picks up `good first issue` items to be rejected.
